headline: The Line on Ohio State–Texas Is a Point and a Half.
deck: Twenty-two times this fall, two playoff contenders will line up across from each other. But not all collisions are equal. The Saturdays that actually decide the bracket are the ones where nobody can call the winner — and there is a formula for exactly how much a game like that is worth. The Sports Page · The Columnist · CFB Roadmap, Part III · 2026 schedule and opening lines via CollegeFootballData 22
methods: The books have already opened a handful of 2026 games, and one number stands out. Ohio State, ranked No. 1 in the country by nearly everyone, opens as a 1.5-point underdog at Texas on September 12. A point and a half is oddsmaker shorthand for “we truly do not know.” And here is the counterintuitive part: a game we cannot call is not a nuisance to be avoided. It is the single most valuable game on the schedule — the one that, when it ends, will have taught us the most. Information has a unit. Flip a fair coin and the result carries exactly one bit — the most a single yes-or-no event can hold — precisely because, beforehand, you had no idea. Flip a coin you already know is weighted 99-to-1, and the result barely registers; you learned almost nothing, because you already knew the answer. A blowout is || METHODS: Notes & sources Schedule and opening point spreads from CollegeFootballData (apinext.collegefootballdata.com), cross-checked against the schools’ official 2026 schedules, ESPN, and FBSchedules. Ohio State at Texas (Sep 12, Week 2) and the Red River rivalry (Texas–Oklahoma, Oct 10, AT&T Stadium, Dallas) were verified against the participating athletic departments. The “contender” set is the frontrunner / in-the-hunt / dark-horse board from Part II; a game counts as a collision when both teams appear on it. Twenty-two such games appear on the 2026 regular-season schedule. Win probabilities are derived from opening spreads via a standard normal margin model calibrated to typical college-football scoring margins; information content is the Shannon entropy of that probability, H = −p log₂p − (1−p) log₂(1−p), measured in bits, where a coin-flip = 1 bit. As of mid-July only the September games carry posted lines; the remaining collisions are identified by matchup, and their probabilities are pending. Spreads move; treat every number here as a preseason estimate, not a settled fact. See the companion Roadmap pieces, Parts I and II, for the contender board itself. headline: The Standings Say the Mets Should Bounce Back. The Franchise Says Otherwise.
deck: Regression to the mean is supposed to rescue a bad team — drag the strugglers back up toward respectability. But every club regresses toward its own mean, not the league’s. And the Mets’ mean, across twenty seasons, is eighty-two wins. Dead average. No matter what they spend. The Sports Page · The Columnist · The dog days, and the teams that make them longer 82
methods: The Mets are on pace for a season in the mid-60s in wins — a face-plant for a roster carrying the second-biggest payroll in the sport — and every fan who has lived through a July like this reaches for the same consolation. It has a name and it is real: regression to the mean i . A team this far below water is partly the victim of bad luck, and bad luck does not renew its lease. Run the numbers on twenty years of standings and the pattern is clean: a club keeps only about half of its distance from average from one season to the next, and gives the other half back. The Mets will climb. That part is not in doubt. The doubt is about the destination. Because “the mean” in regression to the mean is doing quiet, load-bearing work, and almost everyone hears it wrong. They || METHODS: Notes & sources Franchise win levels are the mean of each club’s regular-season winning percentage across the 2006–2025 seasons, from MLB regular-season records (MLB Stats API), expressed as wins per 162 games. The Mets’ twenty-year mean is a shade over .500 (about 82 wins), with 11 of 20 seasons finishing below .500. The 2026 team spent the back half of July well under .500, on a mid-60s win pace; those figures move daily, and this piece is about the destination of the climb, not its existence. “Keeps about half its distance from average” refers to the year-over-year persistence of team winning percentage across the same window: regressing next season’s win rate on this season’s gives a slope of roughly one-half, the standard signature of regression to the mean. The comparison to the Mets’ payroll draws on this newsletter’s earlier finding that money explains only a modest share of who wins. Championship drought lengths (Cubs, 108 years to 2016; Red Sox, 86 to 2004) are historical record. All numbers rounded; see the archive for the companion pieces on payroll and wins. headline: Every NFL Team Spends the Same. The Jets Still Can’t Find January.
deck: Baseball at least lets you blame the checkbook. The NFL has a hard salary cap — every team spends inside the same narrow band — so money cannot explain who wins and who rots. What’s left is the organization. And every franchise regresses toward its own mean, not the league’s. The Jets’ mean is under seven wins a year. The Sports Page · The Columnist · The dog days, and the teams that make them longer 15
methods: Fifteen years. That is how long it has been since the New York Jets last played a snap in the postseason — the longest active playoff drought not just in the NFL but in all of North American pro sports. And here is the part that should keep an owner awake: the Jets have spent that decade and a half operating under the exact same financial rules as the teams playing in January. Football’s salary cap is a hard ceiling. Nobody outspends anybody by much. The Jets have had, every single year, the same money to work with as the Chiefs and the Eagles. They have simply not turned it into wins. Every fan of a team like this reaches for the same medicine, and it is real medicine: regression to the mean i . A team stuck in the cellar is partly the victim of bad luck, and bad || METHODS: Notes & sources Franchise win levels are each club’s mean regular-season winning percentage across the 2006–2025 seasons, from regular-season game results (nflverse), expressed as wins per 17-game season. Relocated franchises are tracked as one club (Raiders, Chargers, Rams). The Patriots lead at about 12 wins per 17, the Browns trail near 6 — a gap of roughly six wins under a shared salary cap. The Jets rank 29th of 32, near 7 wins. The Jets’ 15-season playoff drought (since the 2010 season) is the longest active drought in the NFL and, after the Buffalo Sabres reached the postseason, the longest in the four major North American pro leagues, per ESPN. Buffalo’s prior drought ran 17 seasons (1999–2016) before its 2017 rebuild. The Jets’ lone championship is Super Bowl III (January 1969). Championship drought lengths for the Cubs (108 years to 2016) and Red Sox (86 to 2004) are historical record. headline: Indiana Just Won It All. Its Four-Year Average Still Says .500.
deck: A rolling average is supposed to reveal where a program is really headed — to smooth away the lucky bounces and show the underlying trend. But an average is a rearview mirror: it confirms a rise only after the rise is over. To catch a program in the act, you need its slope. To catch it early, you need the bend in the slope. Here is who is actually moving. The Sports Page · The Columnist · CFB Roadmap, Part V · program trajectories 14–0
qa: Indiana just won the national title. Its four-year average still reads .500. Which number tells us where the program is actually going?
methods: The question: Indiana just won the national title. Its four-year average still reads .500. Which number tells us where the program is actually going? The answer: neither, on its own. A level tells you where a program has been. A slope tells you where it is. Only the bend in the slope tells you where it is headed. Why that is surprising. A rolling average is sold as the sober, trend-revealing number. It is a rearview mirror; it confirms a rise only after the rise is over. Indiana won the national championship. The Hoosiers went unbeaten, the best team in the country, the story of the season — and their four-year average still says .500. || METHODS: Notes & sources Trajectories are each program’s four-year rolling regular-season winning percentage, from season records via CollegeFootballData, over 2006–2025 (the rolling window reaches back to 2003). The analysis covers programs that have been in the top division continuously across the window, so recent arrivals from the lower division are excluded to avoid transition artifacts. “Slope” is the linear trend of the rolling average over the last six seasons; “acceleration” compares the most recent slope to the prior one. Indiana’s raw win rate ran roughly .33, .25, .85, and a perfect 2025, so its four-year average sits near .60 despite the title — the lag described above. Kansas’ rolling average bottomed near 13% around 2017; Stanford peaked near 85% in the early 2010s before its decline; Nebraska’s recent slope reversal is the largest among long-standing programs. Figures rounded. This piece extends the newsletter’s earlier work on rates of change; see the archive for the companion pieces on regression and on acceleration as a metric. headline: They Called It “a Fool’s Errand.” Then They Ranked 138 of Them.
deck: A new list ranks every projected college quarterback from 1 to 138 — and it opens by admitting the whole exercise is guesswork. It is right to admit it. The list refutes itself twice over: the scouts don’t agree with each other, and even if they did, you cannot rank a quarterback out of the offense he plays in. The Sports Page · The Columnist · The Reader’s Defense · a field guide to a bad ranking 138
methods: Every summer the rankings arrive, and this one is ambitious: not a top 10, not a top 25, but a full census — all 138 projected starters, sorted into a strict order from first to last. The authors are candid up front that projecting quarterbacks is close to a fool’s errand, which is the most honest sentence in the piece. Then they spend the rest of it doing the errand anyway, with the confidence of a number line. Their tool was not a formula or a vote; it was roughly three dozen anonymous coaches, general managers, and scouts, with the tiers drawn wherever the “separations felt natural.” Feel is doing a great deal of load-bearing work here, and it cannot hold the weight. Start with the raters, because the piece hands you the evidence itself. On one quarterback, a Big Ten executive shrugs that he’s “just a game manager” and || METHODS: Notes & sources The ranking discussed is Antonio Morales and Sam Khan Jr., “College football quarterback tiers 2026,” The Athletic, July 21, 2026, which sorts 138 projected starters into seven tiers using the assessments of roughly three dozen anonymous coaches, general managers, and scouts, with no formal scoring system. All quotations, tiers, ranks, and the pressure figure (reported there as the highest in its conference) are as presented in that piece; this is a work of commentary and criticism, not a re-reporting of it. Figure 1’s bars illustrate the range of the opposing assessments the article prints for each player, on a qualitative scale; they are our reading of the piece’s own quotes, not new measurements. The statistical ideas named here have their own primers: reliability and how a metric can disagree with itself (Measurement), the unit-of-analysis problem and what a design can support (Research Design), and the value of reporting ranges over false precision (Communicating Uncertainty). headline: The Cubs Waited 108 Years. The Red Sox, 86. The Same Man Ended Both.
deck: A curse is the most comforting explanation a fan has, because it lets the waiting be nobody’s fault. But the two longest title droughts in baseball did not lift on a lucky bounce or the arrival of a savior in cleats. They ended the same way, run by the same executive. And the win column tells you the drought really broke years before the trophy. The Sports Page · The Columnist · The Reader’s Defense · how a curse actually breaks 108
qa: how does an 86-year curse actually end?
methods: The question: how does an 86-year curse actually end? The answer: on purpose, and years in advance. Both famous droughts ended the same way. Boston in 2004, the Cubs in 2016, the same executive doing the same unglamorous work: tearing the club down and building it back. Why that is surprising. We expect a drought to lift the way a spell does — a lucky bounce, a savior in cleats. Both of these ended with a plan, and you could have seen it coming. Consider the coincidence, then decide with me that it is not one. || METHODS: Notes & sources Win totals are regular-season records from the MLB Stats API. The Cubs’ championship drought ran from 1908 to 2016 (108 years); the Red Sox’ from 1918 to 2004 (86 years) — the two longest in the sport at the time each ended. Theo Epstein became Boston’s general manager in November 2002 (title in 2004) and Chicago’s president of baseball operations in October 2011 (title in 2016). Chicago’s deliberate rebuild bottomed at 61–101 in 2012 before climbing to 103 wins in 2016. The ideas here have their own primers: a rebuild bends the trajectory before it lifts the record (Rates of Change — level, velocity, acceleration), and a drought belongs to the institution rather than any single roster (The Unit of Analysis). headline: A Good Week From Your Receiver Is 10× a Bad One. That’s Where the Season Is Decided.
deck: A fantasy matchup is not won by whoever averages the most points. It is won where the two rosters differ — and they differ where the scoring swings. A slot that reliably delivers the same number every week cannot win or lose you anything; it cancels out. The whole game lives in the volatile positions, and most managers spend their energy everywhere else. The Sports Page · The Professor · a statistics lesson, dressed as fantasy advice 10×
qa: which player on your fantasy roster actually decides whether you win?
methods: The question: which player on your fantasy roster actually decides whether you win? The answer: not your best one. A matchup is decided where the two rosters differ , and they differ where the scoring swings. Your quarterback averages seventeen points and both of you will get roughly seventeen. Why that is surprising. We draft and fret over the biggest scorers. A number that never moves cannot separate two teams, however large it is. Here is a claim that sounds wrong and is not. The highest-scoring player on your roster is often the least important one you own. || METHODS: Notes & sources Figures are 2024 regular-season weekly fantasy points (standard scoring) for genuine starters — players with at least twelve games — from nflverse weekly data. “A good/bad week” is the mean plus or minus a typical player’s week-to-week swing (one standard deviation): a quarterback runs about 17 points with a swing near 7; a running back about 7 with a swing near 5; receivers and tight ends carry the largest swing relative to their scoring. The touchdown decomposition uses the same starters, splitting each back’s points into yardage and touchdowns. The general principle — that a predictor only carries information to the extent it varies, and that in an additive score the variance of the total is the sum of the parts’ variances — has its own primer (Variance). A companion caution applies in real prediction: variance is necessary for a predictor, but not sufficient — a variable also has to actually relate to the outcome. Fantasy is the clean case because the categories are the outcome by construction. See the archive for the companion pieces on communicating uncertainty and rates of change. headline: Pulling the Goalie Makes Your Team Worse. That’s Exactly Why You Do It.
deck: Down one, ninety seconds left. Pulling your goalie makes your team worse — you will be scored on more often than you score. It also lifts your chance of winning from about 3% to about 5% . That is not a paradox. The favorite and the underdog are not trying to maximize the same thing. The Sports Page · The Professor · part two of the variance lesson −0.14
qa: when is it correct to deliberately make your team worse?
methods: The question: when is it correct to deliberately make your team worse? The answer. Down one with ninety seconds left, pulling your goalie lowers your expected goal margin; you will be scored on more often than you score. It also lifts your chance of winning from about 3% to about 5% . Why that is surprising. We are trained to maximise the average. Here the right move makes the average worse, and it is still right. Yesterday’s piece argued that a matchup is decided in the slots that swing , not the ones that score most; variance is where the outcome lives. || METHODS: Notes & sources Fantasy figures use 2024 regular-season weekly fantasy points (standard scoring) for genuine starters — at least twelve games — from nflverse weekly data, the same source as the companion piece. Win probabilities come from treating the margin between two lineups as normally distributed and reading off how many swings above zero the projection sits. The matched comparison is deliberate: across all flex-eligible starters, weekly average and weekly swing correlate at about 0.9, so the volatile players are usually just the better players. Comparing only within a narrow projection band (six to nine points) is what isolates volatility from talent — otherwise you would be measuring the wrong thing entirely. The possession table and the goalie calculation are models, not observed results, and are labeled as such: a favorite worth a quarter-point per possession with a typical per-possession scoring spread, and a hockey team down one with ninety seconds left whose pulled goalie doubles its own scoring rate and quadruples its opponent’s. Both conclusions are robust to reasonable changes in those inputs — the direction is arithmetic, the exact percentages are not gospel. Two primers sit underneath this one: Variance (Concept No. 23) for why swing decides outcomes at all, and The Objective Function (Concept No. 24) for the difference between maximizing an average and maximizing your chance of finishing ahead. headline: The Royals Won Two. The Mets Won One. The Mets Spent $830 Million More.
deck: That is the ledger since 1985. And on the one occasion the two franchises actually settled it — the 2015 World Series — the small-market team from Kansas City had the bigger payroll. Before you reach for the obvious conclusion about money, though, look at what both teams have won across their entire histories. It is the same number. And it is almost exactly the number chance owes them. The Sports Page · The Columnist · titles verified via the MLB Stats API; payrolls 1985–2016 $830M
methods: Start with the game itself, because it is the cleanest test anyone could design. In October 2015 the Mets and the Royals met in the World Series. Kansas City won it in five. And the payroll that season ran the wrong direction for the story everyone tells: the Royals opened the year around $114 million, sixteenth in baseball, and the Mets around $101 million, twenty-first. The plucky small-market club was the expensive one. The New York team was, that year, cheap and young and thin. Forty-one years after the first of those trophies and eleven after the last, the two clubs have arrived at this July indistinguishable. Within a game of each other near the bottom of the standings, losing at the same rate: the roster costing about $380 million and the roster costing about $120 million, producing the same thing. Widen it out to every season for which consistent || METHODS: Notes & sources Championships and pennants were verified game-by-game through the MLB Stats API rather than taken from a summary page: the Mets won the World Series in 1969 (over Baltimore) and 1986 (over Boston) and also took pennants in 1973, 2000 and 2015; the Royals won in 1985 (over St. Louis) and 2015 (over the Mets, four games to one) and also took pennants in 1980 and 2014. Payroll totals are the sum of player salaries by team and season, 1985–2016, from the standard public salary database — one consistent definition applied across all thirty-two years, which matters more here than matching any single site’s opening-day snapshot. The 2015 comparison was checked against two independent opening-day tables, which put the Royals at about $114 million (sixteenth) and the Mets at about $101 million (twenty-first); the database used here gives $112 million and $97 million. All three agree on the direction, which is the claim being made. Figures are nominal and not inflation-adjusted. That matters less than it sounds for the comparison being made: both clubs are measured across the identical thirty-two years, so inflation inflates both ledgers alike and largely cancels out of the ratio between them. It would matter enormously for comparing 1985 dollars to 2026 dollars, which this piece does not do. For scale in the present day, the 2026 Mets are near $380 million and the Royals near $120 million — a far wider gap than over the historical window, and the trophy count across that recent stretch is nil to nil. headline: Twenty-Six Baseball Franchises. Not One of Them Runs in Cycles.
deck: Every fan believes their club rises and falls on some hidden clock — a good decade, a lean decade, a rebuild, a window. It is the most natural story in sports and it is not in the data. I tested all twenty-six long-lived franchises against a proper null and found zero real cycles. What is there instead is simpler, and you can use it. Every franchise has a level it returns to, and a speed at which it returns. The Sports Page · The Professor · a methods piece, in plain English 0
qa: does your team really move in cycles — a good decade, a lean decade, a window that opens and shuts?
methods: The question: does your team really move in cycles — a good decade, a lean decade, a window that opens and shuts? The answer: no. I tested all twenty-six long-lived franchises against a fair comparison, and the clock is not in the data. Why that is surprising. Everyone can name their team’s cycles. The trap is that a casual look will always find one; any series with a little year-to-year momentum looks wavy to the eye. Here is the belief, stated plainly enough to test. A franchise is supposed to move in waves: it climbs for some years, peaks, falls, and comes back. || METHODS: Notes & sources Season records come from the MLB Stats API, 1901–2025; the analysis window is 1970–2025 and covers the twenty-six franchises with at least forty seasons in it. Persistence is the lag-one autocorrelation of a club’s winning percentage around its own mean — a first-order autoregressive coefficient. The cycle test compares each club’s largest periodogram peak against four thousand simulated series matched on that same persistence and variance, which is the fair null: it already contains all the wave-like wandering that momentum alone produces. One club came in under five percent, at a period equal to the full length of the record, which is a trend rather than a cycle; across twenty-six tests roughly one such result is expected by chance. The NFL comparison uses public regular-season game results, 1999–2025, and the same calculation. Both leagues realigned, expanded and changed schedule length over these windows, which adds noise but cannot manufacture a periodicity that is absent. The companion primer is Regression to the Mean (Concept No. 3). A dedicated primer on autocorrelation — why a wandering line grows fake cycles, and how to test one honestly — is coming. And a reader-facing toy built on exactly this machinery, which will draw your own fandom trajectory from the teams you pick, is in the works; the arithmetic above is its engine. headline: The Deepest Wound in Sports Is Always the Same Shape.
deck: A team good enough to win 71% of a full season is only a 52% bet in one sudden-death moment. That single fact explains why the worst memory in your rooting life is always the same shape: the favorite, at the summit, losing by inches. The Sports Page · The Professor · a piece about where it hurts, and why 71%
qa: why is your worst memory as a fan always the same kind of loss?
methods: The question: why is your worst memory as a fan always the same kind of loss? The answer. A team good enough to win 71% of a full season is only a 52% bet in one sudden-death moment. A favorite’s edge needs repetition, and the summit takes the repetition away. Why that is surprising. We assume the biggest games are where the better team proves itself. They are the opposite; they are where its advantage is smallest. Ask any fan for the worst moment of their rooting life and notice what they never say. You never hear about a blowout. || METHODS: Notes & sources The three games are on the record. Boston College 41, Notre Dame 39 (Nov. 20, 1993, South Bend): No. 16 Boston College defeated the No. 1 Fighting Irish on David Gordon’s 41-yard field goal as time expired, one week after Notre Dame had beaten the No. 1–ranked team in the country. Chiefs 42, Bills 36 (Jan. 23, 2022, AFC Divisional Round): Buffalo led by three with 0:13 left; Kansas City tied it, won the overtime coin toss, and scored a touchdown on the opening possession, so Buffalo’s offense never took the field in overtime — the game the NFL cited when it changed its postseason overtime rule that offseason. 2011 World Series, Game 6 (Oct. 27, 2011): Texas was one strike from its first title in the ninth inning and again in the tenth; St. Louis rallied both times and won Games 6 and 7. The win-probability figures are a model, and a deliberately simple one. Treating each “chance” as an independent trial with a fixed edge, a team’s probability of winning scales with the square root of the number of trials: an edge calibrated to about 71% over a 162-game haul falls to roughly 52% in a single sudden-death moment. The exact percentages depend on the calibration; the direction — that fewer chances collapse a favorite toward the coin flip — is arithmetic, and is the same result behind the earlier issues on variance and on when to pull a hockey goalie. Real games add correlation and momentum this model ignores, which changes the numbers but not the shape. The underpinnings have their own primers: Variance (Concept No. 23) for why fewer chances mean more noise, and The Objective Function (Concept No. 24) for why the pain is the gap between hope and outcome. headline: The Sweetest Moment in Sports Is the Same Shape Too.
deck: A weak team wins 29 games out of 100 over a full season. Put that same team in one sudden-death game and it wins 48 out of 100. That one jump explains every upset you have ever loved. It also explains why the fan who expects nothing has the best seat in the house. The Sports Page · The Professor · part two — the mirror, and a happier one 29%
qa: why does an upset feel so much better than an ordinary win? Not slightly better. Categorically better — the kind of thing people still talk about forty years later.
methods: The question: why does an upset feel so much better than an ordinary win? Not slightly better. Categorically better — the kind of thing people still talk about forty years later. The answer is one number. A team that wins 29 games out of 100 over a full season wins 48 out of 100 in a single sudden-death game. Almost a coin flip. Here is the surprising part. Most people assume a one-game playoff simply fails to protect the better team. It does something stronger. It actively hands the underdog the best odds it will ever see — and it does that at the exact moment the stakes are highest. What you get from it: two things at once. Why the greatest upsets almost always happen at the very top. And why the fan who expects nothing is the happiest person in the building. || METHODS: Notes & sources The three moments are on the record. United States 4, Soviet Union 3 (Feb. 22, 1980, Lake Placid): a United States team of amateur and college players beat the four-time defending Olympic gold medalists in the medal round, Mike Eruzione scoring the winner midway through the third period; the Americans clinched the gold two days later against Finland. Giants 17, Patriots 14 (Feb. 3, 2008, Super Bowl XLII): New England entered 18–0 chasing a perfect season; the underdog Giants won on a late touchdown four plays after David Tyree’s “helmet catch,” ending the bid one game short. 1969 World Series : the Mets, a 100-to-1 preseason long shot who had never finished above ninth, went 100–62 and beat the 109-win Baltimore Orioles four games to one, clinching on Oct. 16. The win-probability figure is the same simple model as the companion piece, now showing both teams: treating each chance as an independent trial, a team’s probability of winning scales with the square root of the number of trials, so a matchup calibrated to 71%–29% over a 162-game haul narrows to roughly 52%–48% in a single sudden-death moment. The favorite’s fall and the underdog’s rise are the same movement, mirror-imaged about the 50% line. Real games carry correlation and momentum the model leaves out, which shifts the numbers but not the symmetry. This is the second of a pair; the first, on why the favorite’s loss is the deepest wound in sports, ran in the previous issue. Both rest on the primers for Variance (Concept No. 23) and The Objective Function (Concept No. 24). The full archive is at thesportspage.net . headline: A Math Teacher Invented the Point Spread. It Took Forty Years to Reach Your Living Room.
deck: A seven-point favorite wins about 70 games out of 100. You can read that straight off the number in the corner of your screen. A Chicago math teacher invented it around 1940. It may be the most accurate forecast most people ever see, and almost nobody knows what it is. The Sports Page · The Professor · a history of the number in the corner of the screen 70%
qa: how good is the most common number in American sports? Not who it favors — how accurate is it?
methods: The question: how good is the most common number in American sports? Not who it favors — how accurate is it? The answer. That little number beside the team name is a probability in disguise. Minus three means the favorite wins about 59 times out of 100. Minus seven means 70. Minus fourteen means 85. Why that is surprising. You would expect a number invented by bookmakers to be tilted in the house’s favor. It is not tilted at all. It is the most accurate everyday forecast most people ever encounter — and for forty years nobody was allowed to say so on television. What you get from it: a way to read any point spread as a probability, and a working defense against the most common mistake in sports talk. || METHODS: Notes & sources Charles Kline McNeil (1903–1981) earned a master’s at the University of Chicago and taught at the Riverdale Country School, where John F. Kennedy was among his students, before leaving to gamble full time and opening a Chicago book in the early 1940s; his “wholesale odds” are widely credited as the origin of the modern point spread. Jimmy “the Greek” Snyder began a syndicated betting column in 1963 and appeared on CBS’s The NFL Today from 1976 to 1988. By the mid-1980s a large majority of U.S. newspapers printed NFL lines. The 1992 federal law is the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act; it was struck down by the Supreme Court in Murphy v. NCAA (2018). The spread-to-probability figure is a model, stated plainly: it treats the final margin as normally distributed around the spread with a standard deviation of about 13.5 points, the long-run scatter of NFL game margins, and reads the favorite’s win probability as the share of that curve above zero. This is the same normal-margin model behind this newsletter’s earlier pieces on variance; empirical spread-to-win-rate tables track it closely. The cover-rate figure — NFL favorites at roughly 48% against the spread over the last ten seasons, a losing proposition after the standard vig — is the standard evidence that the market is efficient; exact figures vary by season and source. The underpinnings have primers: Variance (Concept No. 23) for the bell-curve machinery, and Communicating Uncertainty (Concept No. 18) for what a well-calibrated probability means. headline: The Bet Became a Stock. And a Stock Is Just a Probability With a Ticker.
deck: A contract trading at 38 cents means the market thinks it is a 38% chance. No decoding needed. The point spread hid that probability for eighty years. In January 2025 a federal exchange started printing it on the ticker — and now the courts have to decide whether it is a financial instrument or a bet. The Sports Page · The Columnist · markets, probability, and a fight over what to call them 38¢
qa: if a bet on a football game is now traded on a federal exchange, is it still a bet?
methods: The question: if a bet on a football game is now traded on a federal exchange, is it still a bet? The answer. On a prediction market you do not bet on Notre Dame. You buy a contract that pays one dollar if the Irish win and nothing if they lose. A price of 38 cents is a 38% chance, printed on a ticker. Why that is surprising. The point spread spent eighty years hiding the probability inside it. This prints it plainly — and in doing so it may have moved sports betting out of state hands and into Wall Street’s, without a single vote being taken. What you get from it: the ability to read a market price as a probability, and the reason a number that looks like a fact is the most dangerous kind. || METHODS: Notes & sources Kalshi, a Commodity Futures Trading Commission–regulated exchange, began offering sports event contracts on January 24, 2025; Polymarket operates a CFTC-regulated U.S. platform alongside a larger international one. On event contracts, a “YES” share pays $1 if the event occurs, so its price in cents is the market’s implied probability (38¢ ≈ 38%); the venue’s edge is taken either in the spread between the two sides or as an explicit trading fee, the analogue of a sportsbook’s vig. Combined quarterly volume on these platforms topped $3 billion in the third quarter of 2025, roughly five times the prior year, with sports the most-traded category. On the legal fight: several states — among them Nevada, New Jersey, Maryland and Massachusetts — sent cease-and-desist letters treating sports event contracts as gambling. On April 6, 2026, a divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit held that Kalshi was likely to prevail on its argument that such contracts are “swaps” under the Commodity Exchange Act and that federal law preempts state gambling law, affirming a preliminary injunction; the ruling is preliminary and binds only the Third Circuit (New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware and the Virgin Islands), with enforcement actions and conflicting orders continuing elsewhere. The legal landscape is moving quickly and may have shifted since publication. This is a companion to the earlier issue on the history of the point spread. Both rest on the primers for Communicating Uncertainty (Concept No. 18) — how to read a probability — and Variance (Concept No. 23). The full archive is at thesportspage.net . headline: No, Notre Dame Is Not About to Become Free.
deck: Notre Dame has about $20 billion. It is allowed to spend roughly $655 million of it a year. That covers 39% of the bills. And only about $85 million comes with no strings attached. The school is not about to go free, and the reason is the most seductive error in reasoning. The Sports Page · The Columnist · a media-literacy lesson, disguised as a fantasy about free college $20.1B
qa: Notre Dame has about $20 billion . Why does it still charge tuition?
methods: The question: Notre Dame has about $20 billion . Why does it still charge tuition? The answer. It can only spend about $655 million a year of that, and the school costs $1.67 billion to run. The endowment covers 39% of the bills. Of the part it does spend, only about $85 million comes with no strings attached. Why that is surprising. A $20 billion pile sounds like it should run the place forever. It does not even keep the lights on by itself. What you get from it: the reason big numbers so often lead to wrong conclusions — and a habit that stops it happening to you. || METHODS: Notes & sources Figures are from Notre Dame’s 2025 financial reporting. The endowment stood at about $20.1 billion, ninth-largest among U.S. universities; the endowment payout distributed for spending was about $655 million, roughly a 3.3% distribution rate. Of that payout, about 13% was allocated to general operations (on the order of $85 million) and the balance to designated purposes — academic programs, research, and athletics — reflecting the donor restrictions typical of large endowments. University operating expenses were about $1.67 billion (the most recent full-year figure), so the endowment payout covered roughly 39% of operating costs. Exact figures shift year to year with markets and reporting; the proportions are what matter to the argument. A note on the “free” thought experiment: making tuition free in perpetuity would require the endowment to fund the entire operating budget and replace tuition revenue out of unrestricted funds, which are a small fraction of the whole — implying an endowment several times the current size and of a very different (unrestricted) composition. This is illustrative arithmetic, not a Notre Dame plan; the university has not proposed anything of the kind. The underlying error — straight-line extrapolation of a large number past the constraints that bind it — is treated in the primer on Regression to the Mean (Concept No. 3). headline: Ohio State Football Cleared $33 Million. The Athletic Department Lost $38 Million. Both Are True.
deck: Ohio State football made $33 million last year. The athletic department it sits inside lost $38 million. Both are true. It is the same money seen from two heights. And once you set it next to the whole school, the runaway spending turns out not to be in the stadium. The Sports Page · The Columnist · a budget, read at the right altitude +$33M
qa: does college football make money or lose it? Both answers get quoted constantly, and both come with numbers.
methods: The question: does college football make money or lose it? Both answers get quoted constantly, and both come with numbers. The answer. In 2024 Ohio State football took in about $111.6 million and spent $78.6 million — a profit north of $33 million. The athletic department it belongs to took in $254.9 million and spent $292.3 million — a loss of $37.7 million. Same organization, same year. Why that is surprising. Both numbers are true. Which one you get depends entirely on where you draw the box. What you get from it: a habit. Once we draw the box properly, the spending that has really lost the plot turns out not to be in the stadium at all. || METHODS: Notes & sources Athletics figures are from Ohio State’s 2024 fiscal-year report to the NCAA (July 2023–June 2024), as reported by Sportico , Eleven Warriors , The Lantern and others: department revenue about $254.9 million, expenses about $292.3 million, deficit about $37.7 million; the football program about $111.6 million in revenue against about $78.6 million in expenses, one of only two Ohio State sports to turn a profit that year; athletic student aid about $26 million. FY2024 was a lighter revenue year — six home football games rather than eight — so the deficit is larger than in a typical season, but the structural point (football’s surplus subsidizing the non-revenue sports) holds every year. University scale: Ohio State’s operating budget is roughly $4.5 billion (FY2025); research expenditures were about $1.68 billion (FY2025, up from $1.58 billion the prior year); the Wexner Medical Center reports operating revenue above $4 billion and rising. Administrative figures — a non-instructional-to-faculty ratio above six to one, about 482 non-instructional staff per 1,000 students versus 281 at Texas and 323 at Wisconsin, and national growth of 164% (administrators) and 452% (professional staff) against 92% (faculty) from 1976 to 2018 — are from an American Enterprise Institute analysis of federal staffing data. Functional expense splits (instruction versus institutional support versus plant) are reported in the university’s financial statements and IPEDS filings; this issue characterizes administration by staffing rather than asserting a dollar line it cannot independently verify. The reasoning tool at the center of this piece — that the answer changes with the box you draw around the data — is developed in the primer on The Unit of Analysis (Concept No. 22). headline: Of 133 College Football Powers, Twenty-One Actually Pay for Themselves.
deck: Last year only 21 of the 133 top college athletic departments earned more than they spent. The other 112 covered the gap with student fees and university money. Ohio State cleared $33 million on football. Ohio State is not the rule. It is one of the 21. The Sports Page · The Columnist · the whole distribution, not the winners 21
qa: yesterday we saw Ohio State clear $33 million on football. Is that what college sports looks like?
methods: The question: yesterday we saw Ohio State clear $33 million on football. Is that what college sports looks like? The answer: no. Last year only 21 of the 133 top athletic departments earned more than they spent. The other 112 covered the gap with student fees and university money. Why that is surprising. Everything you hear about college sports — the TV deals, the coaching salaries, the enormous stadiums — comes from those 21. They are 16% of the tier and close to 100% of the coverage. What you get from it: a name for the trap, and the one question that defuses it. || METHODS: Notes & sources The central figures are from the NCAA’s Division I Athletics Finances: 10-Year Trends from 2015 to 2024 (December 2025). In fiscal 2024, generated revenue exceeded total expenses at 21 of the 133 Football Bowl Subdivision members. “Generated” revenue (tickets, media rights, donations, and the like) is distinguished from “allocated” revenue — student fees and direct institutional or government support, i.e., subsidies. Generated revenue covered about 89% of total revenue at FBS “autonomy” (power-conference) schools versus roughly 44% at non-autonomy FBS schools, and the median non-autonomy school was about 38% self-sufficient. The 133-dot figure fixes 21 as self-supporting and 112 as subsidy-dependent; it does not identify individual schools. On the new cost: the House v. NCAA settlement, approved in June 2025 and effective July 1, 2025, permits schools to share revenue directly with athletes up to a cap of about $20.5 million per school for 2025–26 — roughly 22% of the average power-conference athletic budget — rising over the ten-year agreement toward $30 million and beyond. Every Southeastern and Big Ten school committed to funding the full amount. Figures are subject to revision as reporting and the settlement’s implementation continue. This is the companion to the previous issue on reading a college athletic budget at the right altitude. The error at its center — generalizing from the visible winners — is treated in the primer on Survivorship Bias (Concept No. 4). The archive is at thesportspage.net . headline: Every Team Has Its Babe Ruth. The Mets Have Two.
deck: In 1971 the Mets traded a 24-year-old fireballer named Nolan Ryan for a third baseman they needed. In 2021 they traded a 19-year-old named Pete Crow-Armstrong for a shortstop they needed for two months. Ryan made the Hall of Fame. Crow-Armstrong is already a 30-30 All-Star. This is how a baseball team breaks its own heart, and it is always the same trade. The Sports Page · The Columnist · on the future, and the price of a bird in the hand ~81
qa: why does every baseball team have exactly one trade it cannot talk about?
methods: The question: why does every baseball team have exactly one trade it cannot talk about? The answer. Because they are all the same trade. A team with a hole to fill now gives up an uncertain future for a certain present. The Mets did it twice — Nolan Ryan in 1971, Pete Crow-Armstrong in 2021 — fifty years apart, for the same reason. Why that is surprising. These look like blunders. Mostly they are the sane move: almost every unknown 19-year-old stays unknown. The error is not stupidity. It is a bias so ordinary that it has a name in finance too. What you get from it: a way to spot the same mistake when it is not about baseball. || METHODS: Notes & sources Trades and outcomes are on the record. The Red Sox sold Babe Ruth to the Yankees in a deal agreed in late December 1919 and announced January 5, 1920, for $100,000 in installments plus a $300,000 loan secured by Fenway Park. The Mets traded Nolan Ryan (with three others) to the California Angels for Jim Fregosi on December 10, 1971; Fregosi lasted a season and a half in New York. The Cubs traded Lou Brock to the Cardinals for Ernie Broglio on June 15, 1964. The Tigers acquired Doyle Alexander from the Braves for John Smoltz on August 12, 1987; Alexander went 9–0 and helped Detroit win the AL East. The Red Sox sent Jeff Bagwell to the Astros for Larry Andersen on August 30, 1990. The Cubs acquired Pete Crow-Armstrong from the Mets for Javier Báez and Trevor Williams on July 30, 2021; Crow-Armstrong became an All-Star with a 30-homer, 30-steal season. Career value figures are Wins Above Replacement (Baseball-Reference), rounded to two significant figures: Ryan and Bagwell about 80 each, Smoltz about 66, Brock about 45. Crow-Armstrong, 24 years old, is in the single digits and rising. Ruth’s career WAR (well above 100, split between pitching and hitting) is off the scale of the chart and omitted from it. Ruth, Ryan, Brock, Smoltz and Bagwell are all in the Hall of Fame. The reasoning caution — that we judge these deals only by the prospects who became stars, not the many who didn’t — is the primer on Survivorship Bias (Concept No. 4). headline: How Many Stars Does It Take to Flip a Team? Baseball: Four. Basketball: One.
deck: You run a middling team. You may raid a superteam, but you must take as few players as you can. How many stars do you need? Baseball says 4 — about 12 wins’ worth. Basketball says 1 . Football says one, but only if he plays quarterback. The answer is not about the stars. It is about what each sport is. The Sports Page · The Professor · a thought experiment, settled with arithmetic 48
qa: you run a middling team and may raid a superteam, but you must take as few players as possible. How many stars does it take to actually change your fortunes?
methods: The question: you run a middling team and may raid a superteam, but you must take as few players as possible. How many stars does it take to actually change your fortunes? The answer. Baseball: about 4 . Basketball: 1 . Football: 1, but only if he plays quarterback. Why that is surprising. The answer has almost nothing to do with how good the stars are. It is set by how much of the game one player is allowed to touch. What you get from it: a single number that tells you how each sport shares out its power. || METHODS: Notes & sources The baseball arithmetic rests on two well-established facts about Wins Above Replacement. First, replacement level corresponds to about a .294 winning percentage — roughly 48 wins over a 162-game season — the record of a team of freely-available fill-ins. Second, WAR is approximately additive: summing a roster’s WAR and adding the ~48-win baseline lands within a few games of actual team records in most seasons (a full run of ten added runs equals about one win). A mediocre team of about 78 wins therefore needs roughly a dozen wins — a dozen WAR — to reach a ~90-win contender’s line, and an All-Star-caliber player supplies about 4–5 WAR, giving three to four such players. Figures rounded to two significant figures. The basketball and football answers are structural, not exact: their all-in-one value metrics (win shares, various WAR-style measures) are real but are not on the same additive footing as baseball WAR, so the piece argues them from how much of the game one player occupies — minutes and possessions in basketball, the quarterback’s presence on every offensive snap in football — rather than from a single cross-sport number. The chemistry caveat — that added production doesn’t always convert one-for-one — is the point of the closing section. The underlying idea — that a real answer needs more than the paper number — is the primer on Necessary vs. Sufficient (Concept No. 13). headline: The Pitcher We Started With Is “Struggling.” The Numbers That Matter Say He Isn’t.
deck: This newsletter began on a Paul Skenes number: a 67.5 ERA that looked like the end of the world and meant nothing, because it came from one ugly inning. A hundred issues later he is back in the headlines for “struggling.” Everything he controls says he is not. The Sports Page · The Professor · the founding subject, and the founding lesson 9–9
qa: Paul Skenes has a worse ERA and a .500 record. Is he actually declining?
methods: The question: Paul Skenes has a worse ERA and a .500 record. Is he actually declining? The answer: almost certainly not. Everything a pitcher controls — strikeouts, walks, home runs allowed — is where it has always been. The damage sits entirely in the parts he does not control. Why that is surprising. ERA and won-lost look like measures of the pitcher. Both are mostly measures of the eight men behind him and the nine who bat for him. The surface reads like a fall from grace, and the headlines have duly written it that way. You have probably seen one this week. || METHODS: Notes & sources Skenes’ figures are from the MLB Stats API for the 2024–2026 seasons, reconciled to his won-lost record per this newsletter’s standard. In 2024 he went 11–3 with a 1.96 ERA (Rookie of the Year); in 2025, 10–10 with a 1.97 ERA (Cy Young); in the current 2026 season he stands at 9–9 with a 3.90 ERA across 23 starts and about 124⅔ innings. His strikeout rate (about 11.3 per nine), walk rate (about 2.3 per nine), and WHIP (about 1.11) are in line with his first two seasons — the skill metrics a pitcher most controls have not declined, while the ERA and record, which fold in defense, luck, and run support, have. Home-run and sequencing variance and weak run support are the usual culprits for exactly this gap; public advanced metrics have also pegged his expected ERA well below his actual mark this year. The one genuine exception is velocity: his four-seam fastball has averaged about 98.8, 98.2, and 96.9 mph across 2024–2026 (MLB Stats API pitch-arsenal data) — a near-two-mph slide that, unlike ERA, is a sticky, leading signal worth watching, even though it has not yet dented his strikeout rate. The distinction at the heart of the piece — between a player’s own skill and the team-and-luck outcomes credited to him — and the expectation that results drift back toward skill are developed in the primer on Regression to the Mean (Concept No. 3). The 67.5-ERA reference is Issue No. 128, this newsletter’s first, published on MLB Opening Day 2026; find it in the archive . headline: The Radar Gun Knows Before the ERA Does. Some Numbers Predict; Most Just Revert.
deck: A companion issue argued that Paul Skenes isn’t really declining — his ugly ERA and .500 record are mostly noise. A sharp reader pushed back with one word: velocity . It is the perfect objection, because it opens the single most useful door in statistics. Some numbers become trustworthy almost the moment you begin counting. Others never do. Telling them apart is the whole difference between seeing a decline coming and being fooled by a mirage. The Sports Page · The Professor · on which numbers you’re allowed to believe yet 70
qa: can you see a decline coming before the results show it?
methods: The question: can you see a decline coming before the results show it? The answer: yes, but only from the top of the ladder. Strikeout rate settles after about 70 batters. Walk rate needs about 170. ERA needs a season and a half. Fastball velocity is trustworthy in a single start. Why that is surprising. The numbers we quote most — ERA, wins, batting average — are the slowest to mean anything. The ones that warn us early are the ones nobody puts on the broadcast. Every statistic is a mixture of two things: the player’s real skill, and the luck of the particular sample we happened to watch. || METHODS: Notes & sources The stabilization points are from the sabermetric work of Russell Carleton, popularized by FanGraphs and Baseball Prospectus: the sample at which a statistic correlates about 0.7 with a separate, equally-sized sample of the same player — roughly the point at which half its variation is repeatable skill rather than luck. For pitchers (measured in batters faced or balls in play): strikeout rate about 70, walk rate about 170, batting average against about 630, home-run rate about 1,320, and BABIP against about 2,000 — the last effectively unreachable within a season. Exact values vary slightly by study and metric definition. Velocity is not one of Carleton’s plate-appearance stabilization stats because it is measured per pitch, not per outcome; it is shown here at roughly one start to place it on the same axis, but its reliability is higher still — a pitcher’s average fastball velocity is trustworthy within a few dozen pitches, faster than any results-based number. The Skenes velocity figures (four-seam averages of about 98.8, 98.2 and 96.9 mph across 2024–2026) are from MLB Stats API pitch-arsenal data, and were the subject of the companion issue on his 2026 season. This is a follow-up to the previous issue on Paul Skenes, prompted by a reader’s question. It rests on the primers for Sample Size (Concept No. 6) and Regression to the Mean (Concept No. 3).
