headline: Detroit Traded the Best Pitcher in Baseball While Two and a Half Games Out. It Cost Them One Percentage Point.
deck: The Tigers sat 54–58 and inside the wild card race, and they sold Tarik Skubal anyway. Run the counterfactual — 200,000 simulated seasons, with him and without him — and the move that looked like surrender gave up nine-tenths of a point of championship odds. That was the whole prize.
qa: Detroit sat two and a half games out of a playoff spot and traded the best pitcher in baseball. What did that actually cost them?
methods: The question: Detroit sat two and a half games out of a playoff spot and traded the best pitcher in baseball. What did that actually cost them? The answer: about one percentage point. Run it 200,000 times, with Skubal and without him, and we find that selling him gave up nine-tenths of a point of championship odds. Why that is surprising. Every instinct says a contender does not sell its ace; the arithmetic says the ace was worth almost nothing to this contender. On Sunday the Tigers were 54–58, two and a half games out of the last American League wild card, and they traded Tarik Skubal to the Dodgers. || METHODS: How this was computed Records and stat lines are from the MLB Stats API as of August 3, 2026. Each team's true quality was drawn from a Beta posterior on its record with a Beta(34, 34) prior — a spread matching the roughly six-point standard deviation of real MLB team talent — then remaining games were simulated 200,000 times, with the bracket resolved by log5. Skubal's value was set at 1.5 wins over 10 starts. The model treats all remaining games as equally difficult; it does not use actual schedules, park effects, or head-to-head matchups, so treat the odds as well-calibrated in shape rather than exact to the decimal.

headline: The Mets Had the Third-Best Bullpen in Baseball. Nobody in Baseball Had Fewer Leads to Protect.
deck: A 3.1 ERA out of the pen — third of all thirty clubs. Thirty-two save opportunities — last of all thirty clubs. At the deadline the Mets sold the three arms at the center of it, and that was the correct thing to do, because a great bullpen on a 50-win team is the least useful good thing in sports.
qa: how can the third-best bullpen in baseball be the right thing to sell?
methods: The question: how can the third-best bullpen in baseball be the right thing to sell? The answer. A 3.1 ERA out of the pen, third of all thirty clubs. Thirty-two save opportunities , last of all thirty clubs. The Mets had a superb bullpen and almost nothing for it to protect. Why that is surprising. We rank bullpens by ERA as though the number stands alone. It does not; a reliever’s value depends entirely on how often his team hands him a lead, and we never check. You are looking at a 50–66 team. They are 20 games out of first and eleven and a half out of a wild card, and at Monday’s deadline they sold. || METHODS: How this was computed Player and team lines are from the MLB Stats API, 2026 season through August 3. “Bullpen” here means pitchers with zero games started — an unambiguous rule applied identically to all 30 clubs. That definition matters more than it looks: widen it to include swingmen who both started and relieved, and the Mets bullpen falls from 3rd to 12th, because Sean Manaea (9 starts, 4.4) and Tobias Myers (6.3) come in with it. Both figures are honest; they answer different questions. The 3rd-place number is the right one for “how good were the arms that only ever pitched in relief,” which is the group that was traded. Save opportunities are as recorded by MLB and are a proxy for high-leverage usage, not a perfect measure of it — a bullpen can also enter close games while behind or tied, which no save statistic counts. One last caution, and it is the reason every figure here is anchored to deadline day: if you run this query yourself now, you will not get our number. You will get a Mets bullpen around 3.3, ranked fourth. That is because the league's own database credits a traded pitcher's season line to his current club, so the innings Raley threw in Queens now sit under Philadelphia and Brazobán's sit under Chicago. The roster moved and the history moved with it. Ours is the bullpen the Mets actually ran out there — which is the only version that can answer what they gave up.

headline: 109 Teams Have Been Exactly Where Boston Was on July 3. One Made the Playoffs.
deck: Since 1998, 109 teams have sat where Boston sat on July 3. One made the playoffs. The Red Sox have gone 25–3 since — about a one-in-70,000 run — and are now 94% to reach October. This is not a story about belief being rewarded. It is a warning about every lesson drawn from the team that got lucky. By The Sports Page · 27 seasons, 109 comparable clubs
qa: the Red Sox were 37–48 on July 3 and are now 94% to reach October. What should we learn from that?
methods: The question: the Red Sox were 37–48 on July 3 and are now 94% to reach October. What should we learn from that? The answer: almost nothing. Since 1998, 109 teams have sat roughly where Boston sat. One made the playoffs. Why that is surprising. The run is real, and the odds against it were about one in 70,000; that is exactly why it cannot teach us anything general. On the morning of July 3 the Red Sox were 37–48 , eleven games under .500, going nowhere. || METHODS: How this was computed Records and results come from the MLB Stats API, filtered to regular-season games only. The comparison group is every team-season from 1998 through 2025 with a winning percentage between .415 and .455 measured in early July, between 78 and 92 games played; the shortened 2020 season is excluded as non-comparable. Postseason participation is taken from each season's actual postseason schedule, so “made the playoffs” means under that year's format, whatever it was — a moving target that the piece flags rather than hides. Boston's implied quality uses the newsletter's standard Beta-Binomial with a Beta(34, 34) prior, matching the observed spread of real MLB team talent; the streak probabilities integrate over that posterior rather than assuming a single fixed skill. The 94% figure comes from 200,000 simulated finishes to the American League season and, like every projection here, ignores schedule strength and injuries.

headline: The NCAA Is Expanding March Madness to 76. The Arithmetic Says Go to 365.
deck: In 2027 the field goes from 68 teams to 76. Invite all 365 instead, seed them off ten games, and run double elimination. You get 59% fewer games , ten times as many that end somebody’s season, and the best team in the country wins the title 55% of the time instead of 45%.
qa: the NCAA is expanding March Madness from 68 teams to 76. What would it actually cost to invite everybody ?
methods: The question: the NCAA is expanding March Madness from 68 teams to 76. What would it actually cost to invite everybody ? The answer. Invite all 365 Division I teams, seed them off ten games, and run double elimination. The tournament gets smaller and fairer at the same time. Why that is surprising. Everyone assumes a bigger field means more chaos. It is the reverse; a second life makes the tournament more reliable, not less. The NCAA has confirmed the change. From 2027 there are eight more at-large bids and a twelve-game “Opening Round” replacing the First Four. After that the familiar bracket of 64 carries on as before. || METHODS: Splitting into two divisions is free. Because the game count is linear, an 80-team elite bracket plus a 285-team second bracket costs 726 games against 728 for one combined field. A difference of two. Whatever you think of splitting the revenue programs off, the sums do not object. Ten games is not enough to seed anything, and that is a feature. A ten-game record tracks true team strength at 0.87 . That is genuinely useful. But it names the single best team in the country as the top seed only 4% of the time. Picking one maximum out of 365 from ten noisy games is close to hopeless, and you should not want it to be otherwise. Which settles a design question. If seeding is that unreliable, chasing it is a poor use of the opening slate. So a coach could spend those ten games sorting a rotation instead of stacking wins, and give up almost nothing. Under the current format, where one bad night ends everything, no coach can afford that. Under the current format, where one bad night ends everything, no coach can afford that. The new format would create a real choice where today there is only one sane answer. Which quietly settles a design question. If seeding is that unreliable, chasing it is a poor use of the opening slate — so a coach can rationally spend those ten games sorting a rotation instead of stacking wins, and give up almost nothing. Under the current format, where one bad night ends everything, no coach can afford that. The format would create a real strategic choice where today there is only one sane answer. What It Costs How this was computed Team counts and format details come from the NCAA’s expansion announcement and the 2026–27 Division I

headline: Every 12-Over-5 Number You Have Ever Heard Was Measured on a Bracket That Stops Existing in 2027.
deck: Expansion to 76 teams adds eight at-large bids, and those eight arrive on the bubble seed lines — which makes the 12-seed a better team than it used to be. Our model says the famous upset rate rises about five points. The part worth sitting with is the second finding: it would take roughly three hundred years of March Madness to prove it.
methods: Every March someone tells you how often a 12-seed beats a 5-seed. It is the most-quoted number in American sport, it gets repeated to the decimal point, and it is about to become quietly wrong. Not because anybody lied. Because the thing it describes is being replaced. There are 31 Division I conferences, so 31 automatic bids. That means today’s 68-team field carries 37 at-large bids ; the 2027 field of 76 carries 45 . Eight more. Those eight are the best teams currently being left out — bubble teams, not champions of small leagues. They do not land on the 1-line. They land in the middle, and everyone below them shifts down. The weakest automatic qualifiers get pushed toward the opening round, and the 11-, 12- and 13-seed lines fill up with better basketball teams than they hold now. || METHODS: How this was computed 365 Division I programmes were simulated across 31 conferences of unequal strength, with automatic bids decided by a noisy conference tournament rather than awarded to the best team, and at-large bids assigned by strength. Fields of 68 and 76 were then seeded and the 5-versus-12 matchups played 20,000 times. The game model is logistic in team strength and was calibrated so the 68-team upset rate reproduces the roughly one-in-three figure the tournament has actually produced — the finding is the five-point change and the mechanism behind it, not the level, which is an input rather than a result. The detectability curve is a standard two-proportion power calculation at 5% significance and 80% power. The 160-game figure counts four 12-versus-5 games in each of the 40 completed tournaments of the 64-team era, 1985 to 2025, excluding the canceled 2020. Datasets at data/cinderella-base-rate-shift.json and data/cinderella-detectability.json .

headline: Racing Fixed the Triple Crown’s Two-Week Problem by Moving It In Front of the Longest Race.
deck: From 2027 the Preakness runs three weeks after the Kentucky Derby instead of two — on a Sunday, a first in the history of the series. It is being sold as giving horses more room. The window from Derby to Belmont is unchanged at 35 days. All that moved is where the squeeze sits, and it now sits in front of a Belmont that is simultaneously getting 20% longer.
methods: The change is real and it is confirmed. The 2027 Preakness runs on Sunday 23 May , twenty-two days after the 1 May Derby rather than the traditional fourteen. It is the first Triple Crown race ever run on a Sunday, and from 2028 through 2031 it locks to the Sunday of Memorial Day weekend. The reason is not in dispute either. Trainers stopped bringing Derby horses back on two weeks’ rest. In 2026 the Derby winner, Golden Tempo, skipped the Preakness altogether — the third time in five years the Derby winner has done exactly that. A middle leg that the best horse keeps declining is a problem worth solving. So they gave the horses another week. Except they did not. Traditionally the Triple Crown runs Derby, then Preakness fourteen days later, then Belmont twenty-one days after that. Thirty-five days end to end. || METHODS: How this was computed Dates are the announced 2027 schedule: Kentucky Derby 1 May, Preakness 23 May, Belmont 5 June, checked against the traditional pattern of Derby on the first Saturday in May, Preakness two weeks later, Belmont three weeks after that. Gaps are simple date arithmetic. Distances are 1¼ miles for the Derby (10 furlongs), 1⅓⅙ for the Preakness (9½), and 1½ for the Belmont (12) — the Belmont having been run at 1¼ miles at Saratoga from 2024 to 2026 during the Belmont Park rebuild, returning to 1½ in 2027. “Rest per furlong” is days since the previous race divided by the length of the next one; it is a rough index of recovery demand, not a physiological model, and no claim is made about how horses actually recover. The count of thirteen Triple Crown winners runs from Sir Barton in 1919 to Justify in 2018. Dataset at data/triple-crown-spacing-2027.json .

headline: Notre Dame Gets Talked About All Summer. So Does Everybody Else.
deck: In a dead June, Notre Dame draws 18,884 Wikipedia lookups. In a live October it draws 70,836 . That is a floor of 27% . Across twelve blue bloods the median floor is 26.8% . Every program keeps the same share of its attention when nothing at all is happening. The Sports Page · The Professor · measuring hype instead of asserting it 27%
qa: every Notre Dame fan believes the Irish get talked about all year, however small the news. Are they right?
methods: The question: every Notre Dame fan believes the Irish get talked about all year, however small the news. Are they right? The answer: yes, and it is not special at all. In the dead months of March to June, Notre Dame holds 27% of the attention it gets from September to December. The median across twelve blue-blood programs is 26.8% . Notre Dame ranks seventh of twelve. Here is the surprising part. How much attention a program gets varies a lot; Alabama’s in-season months run 2.6 times Nebraska’s. The shape hardly varies at all. Every ratio lands between 21% and 31%, and whether a program is big or small predicts nothing about it (r = +0.01). What you get from it: a way to tell real distinctiveness from the ordinary feeling of caring a lot. || METHODS: Notes & sources Pageviews are English Wikipedia, user traffic only (bots excluded), monthly, January 2021 through August 2026, from the Wikimedia REST pageviews API. The article for each program is its football page, not the university page. In-season is the median of all September–December months; dead season is the median of all March–June months; the floor is the ratio. Medians rather than means, because a playoff run puts a long tail on the in-season months. Floors: Nebraska 30.9%, Texas 29.1%, USC 28.2%, Clemson 27.8%, Ohio State 27.5%, Alabama 27.0%, Notre Dame 26.7%, Michigan 26.5%, Georgia 26.4%, Penn State 25.5%, LSU 25.1%, Oregon 20.8%. Correlation between a program’s in-season level and its floor: r = +0.01, 95% CI −0.57 to +0.58, i.e. nothing. One limit worth stating. This measures people looking a program up, which is not the same behavior as watching a video about it. The specific claim that Notre Dame’s YouTube ecosystem is unlike anyone else’s is untested here — YouTube publishes view counts only through an API key we do not hold, and their robots file puts the feeds out of bounds. It remains a live question, not a settled one. The Almanac · A Milestone Observance

headline: Two Teams a Rank Apart? The Higher One Wins 48.7% of the Time.
deck: When #6 plays #7, the poll says one is better. The field says it is a coin flip, and slightly the wrong way. Two teams have to sit about ten places apart before a ranking tells you anything you could not have guessed. The Sports Page · The Professor · what a ranking can and cannot measure 48.7%
qa: how far apart do two teams have to be in the rankings before the ranking actually tells you who will win?
methods: The question: how far apart do two teams have to be in the rankings before the ranking actually tells you who will win? The answer: about ten places. Below that, you are reading noise. Teams one or two ranks apart split their games 48.7% to 51.3% — and the 48.7% belongs to the team the poll says is better. Here is the surprising part. We checked it two completely separate ways, and they agree. One asks the field; the other asks the raters. Neither knows about the other, and both land on ten. What you get from it: a way to look at any ranked list this autumn and know which gaps are real. || METHODS: Notes & sources Game data from the CollegeFootballData API: every regular-season game 2015–2025 in which both teams appeared in that week’s AP poll, 493 in total. Ties excluded. Of the 493, 190 were played at the better-ranked team’s home field, 219 at its opponent’s, and 84 at neutral sites. The gap is the absolute difference in AP rank; the outcome is whether the better-ranked side won. Confidence intervals are Wilson 95%: 1–2 apart is 48.7% [0.38, 0.60], 12–16 is 77.8% [0.67, 0.86]. Note that no single band clears 0.75 with its whole interval — the point estimate crosses in the low teens, and the honest reading is “around ten” rather than an exact threshold. Rating systems from a Massey Ratings composite export, 2026 preseason: 138 teams, 25 systems with sufficient coverage. Pairs required at least 15 systems rating both teams, giving 9,453 pairs. Agreement is the share of those systems ordering the pair the same way as the composite. Median across-system range per team, 41 ranks; median standard deviation, 10.2 ranks. The 75% criterion is Thurstone’s, from the law of comparative judgment (1927): two stimuli have a 50% chance of being ordered either way, so the halfway point between chance and certainty is 75%. The application of that idea to measures that are not physical — and the argument that a measure needs calibrating against behavior before its numbers mean anything — is from Sechrest, McKnight & McKnight, Calibration of measures for psychotherapy outcome studies , American Psychologist 51(10), 1996. One limit worth stating: preseason ratings are the noisiest of the year, so the 41-rank median spread should tighten as real games arrive. We will re-run this in November and report whether it did. The Sports Page · Vol. I, No. 152 What a ranking measures August 27, 2026 ·

headline: Home Field Is Worth Thirteen Ranks. Most of It Is the Road Team Losing Them.
deck: A ranked college football team at home wins 77% of the time. The same sort of team on the road wins 48% . Split that gap three ways and the crowd turns out not to be doing the work. The Sports Page · The Professor · what a stadium is worth 13
qa: how much is home field worth? Not in points. In ranks — the unit fans already argue in.
methods: The question: how much is home field worth? Not in points. In ranks — the unit fans already argue in. The answer: about thirteen ranks. A team playing at home wins about as often as a team thirteen places better playing away. Here is the surprising part. We split that thirteen into its two halves. Playing at home helps a little. Playing away hurts almost twice as much. We named the thing after the wrong team. What you get from it: one adjustment you can do in your head. Before you pick a game, take thirteen ranks off whoever is traveling. || METHODS: Notes & sources Games from the CollegeFootballData API: every regular-season game 2015–2025 in which both teams appeared in that week’s AP poll, 493 in total, ties excluded. Venue is taken from the API’s neutral-site flag rather than inferred from the home-team field, which matters more than it sounds: 84 of the 493 are neutral-site games, and counting them as home games for the listed host is what produced the earlier, wrong figure of 75% at home. One logistic regression, all 493 games, neutral site as the reference category. Rank gap +0.11 per rank (SE 0.020); home +0.52 (SE 0.30, p = 0.08); away −0.89 (SE 0.28, p = 0.001). The conversion is (home − away) divided by the gap coefficient: 13.2 ranks , 95% confidence interval [7.2, 19.2] by the delta method. That interval is wide, so the honest reading is “somewhere around a dozen,” not thirteen exactly. Fitted rates track the raw bands within 3.4 percentage points in all six venue-by-gap cells. Mean rank gap by venue: 7.8 home, 7.7 neutral, 8.3 away. The 75% criterion is Thurstone’s, from the law of comparative judgment (1927). The argument that a measure has to be converted into a unit somebody can act on before its numbers mean anything is from Sechrest, McKnight & McKnight, Calibration of measures for psychotherapy outcome studies , American Psychologist 51(10), 1996. Notre Dame vs. Wisconsin, Lambeau Field, Sunday, September 6, 2026, 6:30 p.m. Central, confirmed against the Notre Dame athletics announcement, ESPN, and the CollegeFootballData schedule. Preseason ranks are the Massey composite of 25 rating systems. A limit worth stating plainly. A rank is not a fixed amount of quality. The distance between first and second is far larger than the distance between fiftieth and fifty-first, so “thirteen ranks” is a rough currency and not a

headline: A Winning Streak Is Worth Twice as Much in May as in April. And Nothing at All in August.
deck: Boston won 14 in a row in July and it saved their season. If the Mets won 14 in a row tomorrow, their playoff odds would move by 1.6 points. Same streak. Different month. The Sports Page · The Professor · when a hot streak is worth having +26
qa: when is a hot streak worth the most?
methods: The question: when is a hot streak worth the most? The answer: the middle of the season. A 14-game winning streak would have bought the Mets 26 points of playoff probability on May 18. Today it buys 1.6. Here is the surprising part. Earlier is not better. On April 20 that same streak was worth only 12.5 points — less than half of May’s. Get hot too early and it washes out. What you get from it: two questions to ask the next time somebody tells you a team is red hot. || METHODS: Notes & sources Standings, schedules and results from the MLB Stats API, current through the morning of August 22, 2026. Every team’s games played plus games remaining was checked to equal 162 before any simulation was run; postponed games that had not been rescheduled were excluded, which is what made the first pass fail that check. Method: each team’s strength is a 50/50 blend of its actual winning percentage and its Pythagorean expectation from runs scored and allowed, regressed toward .500 by 69 games. Game probabilities use log5 with a home-field adjustment set at a .535 league home win rate. Every remaining game in both leagues is simulated, division winners and three wild cards per league are taken from the final standings, and ties are broken at random rather than by the real tiebreaker rules. 100,000 seasons for the headline odds, 20,000 for each point in Figure 1. The result is not sensitive to the regression choice. With no regression at all the Mets come out at 0.001% and Boston at 98.6%; with heavy regression, 0.007% and 97.0%. The figures quoted above use the middle setting. Franchise history covers all 10,255 regular-season games the Mets have played from 1962 through August 22, 2026, taken game by game rather than from a summary. Stretches are counted within seasons, never across an off-season, giving 8,175 windows of 33 games. Two overlapping windows reach 27–6, both inside the same June–July 1990 run. One limit worth stating. Forcing a team to win fourteen games does not make it a better team in the simulation; it simply hands over the results. A real fourteen-game streak might carry information we are throwing away — a returning starter, a fixed bullpen. If so, these numbers understate what a streak is worth, and they still do not save

headline: The Mets Must Pass Seven Teams. They Play Two of Them.
deck: Twenty of their last 33 games are against clubs whose losses do them no good at all. A comeback needs games you can take from the people ahead of you; the schedule decides whether you have any. The Sports Page · The Professor · the games that count double 2 of 7
qa: which of the Mets’ remaining games actually matter?
methods: The question: which of the Mets’ remaining games actually matter? The answer: one series. Four games against Philadelphia, September 17 to 20, at home. Sweeping it is worth more than sweeping every other series put together. Here is the surprising part. We rate a stretch run by how hard it is. Hardness is the wrong axis. The Mets’ schedule is not too hard; it is aimed at the wrong people. What you get from it: a better question to ask about any team chasing from behind. || METHODS: Notes & sources Standings, schedules and results from the MLB Stats API, as of the morning of August 23, 2026. Records move; the schedule does not. Whatever the standings say when you read this, the Mets do not play San Diego, Arizona, St. Louis, Pittsburgh or Cincinnati again this season, and that was settled before the year began. Method as in the companion piece on streak timing: team strength is a 50/50 blend of actual winning percentage and Pythagorean expectation, regressed toward .500 by 69 games; game probabilities use log5 with a home-field adjustment at a .535 league home win rate; every remaining game in both leagues is simulated, and ties are broken at random rather than by the real tiebreaker rules. The series comparison forces the Mets to exactly 25 wins in all cases, sweeps the named series, and distributes the remaining wins at random across the other games, so every row is the same record differing only in placement. 200,000 seasons per row gives a 95% interval of about ±0.07 points. Philadelphia at +0.63 clears that comfortably; Miami at +0.09 is small but separates from the control series; Washington at −0.18 sits alongside the Yankees at −0.20 and Milwaukee at −0.21. An earlier pass at 40,000 seasons per row put Washington third and showed every series as a gain. That ordering was noise. It is quoted here because it is the ordinary way this kind of table goes wrong: the differences being measured were smaller than the error on the measurement, and nothing in the output says so. One limit. Forcing a sweep hands over results without making the team better, and a real September sweep of a rival might carry information this exercise throws away. The direction of that bias favors the Mets, and it does not

headline: Kansas City Has Won Seven Straight. They Are a .435 Team.
deck: The Royals and the Phillies have the identical record over their last ten games. Stretch the window to fifty and one is a contender and the other is 57–74. Hot is not a fact you look up; it is a choice about how far back you count. The Sports Page · The Professor · how to spot a real hot streak 8-2
qa: who is the hottest team in baseball right now?
methods: The question: who is the hottest team in baseball right now? The answer depends entirely on how many games you count. Fix the window and it is Milwaukee; they have not been below .600 over any span you care to measure. Here is the surprising part. You would think hot is something you look up. The typical club can be made to look .200 better or worse just by changing where you start counting. Over a full season that is 32 wins, conjured out of nothing. What you get from it: two questions that take ten seconds and settle the argument. || METHODS: Notes & sources Every completed regular-season game through the morning of August 23, 2026, pulled game by game from the MLB Stats API — 1,949 games in all. Each club’s game log was checked against the official standings before anything was computed; all thirty reconciled exactly. Windows are the last 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 40 and 50 games for each club, counted from that morning. The “swing” is the difference between a club’s best and worst window. Median swing .200; largest Kansas City at .540; smallest Baltimore at .125. Over five games, 7 of 30 clubs sit at .800 or better and 7 at .200 or worse; over fifty games, none reach .800. Run differentials are raw runs scored minus runs allowed over the window. Where the piece says the runs and the record agree, that is a Pythagorean expectation with a 1.83 exponent compared against actual winning percentage. Milwaukee over thirty games: expected .598, actual .600. Detroit over thirty: expected .648, actual .500. Kansas City over twenty: expected .505, actual .550. Schedule adjustment is the Simple Rating System: each club’s rating is its run differential per game plus the mean rating of its opponents, solved by iteration until the ratings are consistent, then centered on zero. Full-season strength of schedule spans only −0.05 to +0.09 runs per game; across a 20-game window it spans −0.57 to +0.48. Playoff prediction uses all 223 postseason series from 1998 through 2025, with 2020 excluded for its 60-game season. For each series we ask whether the club ahead on a given measure won. Win percentage 50.9%; last-20 raw 53.4%; last-20 schedule-adjusted 57.4%; season run differential 57.8%. Two cautions. headline: We Built 252 Ways to Predict the Playoffs. The Best One Lost to the Simplest One.
deck: Our winner picked 59.2% of postseason series correctly. Shown a season it had never seen, it fell to 48.9% — worse than a coin. A plain run differential, with nothing tuned at all, beat it. The Sports Page · The Professor · how a good number goes bad 59.2%
qa: can you build a number that tells you who wins in October?
methods: The question: can you build a number that tells you who wins in October? We tried 252 of them. The answer is no. Here is the surprising part. The failure was not that our metrics were bad. The best one looked excellent . It only fell apart when we showed it a season it had not already studied. What you get from it: the single question that separates a prediction from a story. || METHODS: Notes & sources All 223 postseason series from 1998 through 2025, built game by game from the MLB Stats API. 2020 is excluded for its 60-game season and 16-team field. Each series is scored by whether the club ahead on a given measure won it; series are labelled by team identifier rather than by seed, so no home-field or seeding information leaks into the comparison. Schedule adjustment is the Simple Rating System: a club’s run differential per game plus the mean rating of its opponents, solved by iteration until consistent, centered on zero. The grid is every combination of window length in {5, 10, 15 … 60} and season weight in {0.00, 0.05 … 1.00}, giving 252 candidates. Single-measure results: won-lost record 50.9%, last-20 raw 53.4%, last-30 adjusted 52.9%, season SRS 56.5%, last-20 adjusted 57.4%, season run differential 57.8%, Pythagorean 57.8%. The apparent gap between raw and schedule-adjusted recent form rests on only 21 series where the two disagree; a McNemar exact test puts it at p = 0.19. We report it as a direction, not a result. Honest testing: leave-one-season-out re-selects the window and weight on the other 26 seasons and predicts the held-out one, scoring 48.9% over 223 series. The walk-forward version selects only on seasons already played and predicts the next, scoring 56.4% over the 181 series from 2004 onward; plain run differential scores 58.3% over that same subset. The two honest tests differ by more than we would like, which is itself a sign of how little any of these numbers are pinned down. One limit, stated plainly. None of this proves recent form is worthless in October. It shows that with the data baseball actually produces, we cannot tell whether it helps — and that a search over 252 options will hand you a confident

headline: Kickers Make 80% From 43 Yards. That Told Chicago Nothing.
deck: Gene, a Bears man, asks a good question. If the long run is so reliable, why does it seem to quit at the last second? Kickers make 80.3% from 43 yards. It never quit; it was never a fact about one kick. The Sports Page · The Professor · answering Gene 80.3%
methods: The question, roughly as Gene put it: a team wins 75% of its games over a season. So why, at the nitty-gritty last second, is the probability something else entirely? The answer: nothing about the team changed. That 75% was a fact about a crowd of games. It was never sitting inside the team like a fuel gauge, waiting to be read off on Sunday. Here is the surprising part. Most of us have it backwards. We treat the long-run percentage as the real thing and the single game as a wobble around it. It is the other way round. The single game is the only real thing; the percentage is a summary of a crowd that game happens to belong to. What you get from it: two questions that make any quoted probability behave. || METHODS: Notes & sources Kicking data is every field goal attempt in the nflverse play-by-play files for the 2015 through 2024 seasons, regular season and postseason: 10,624 attempts. Overall 84.6% made. By distance: under 30 yards 97.7%, 30–39 92.5%, 40–49 77.9%, 50 or longer 66.0%. From exactly 43 yards, 285 of 355, or 80.3%, with a 95% interval of [76.1%, 84.4%]. The clutch comparison uses the 40–49 yard band, because exactly 43 yards leaves too few late-game kicks to say anything. Last two minutes of a game within three points: 113 of 159, or 71.1%. All other 40–49 yard attempts: 2,351 of 3,006, or 78.2%. The gap is 7.1 points, z = −1.94, p = 0.052. That is a hint and not a finding, and it is used here to show a reference class narrowing rather than to argue that kickers choke. The kick: Philadelphia at Chicago, NFC Wild Card, 6 January 2019, Soldier Field. Cody Parkey, 43 yards, ten seconds left, Chicago trailing 16–15. The official play-by-play records it as blocked by Treyvon Hester; it struck the upright and then the crossbar. Parkey also made a 43-yard attempt in the fourth quarter of a one-point game in week three that season, with the same holder and long snapper. Two kicks as alike as two kicks get, and two different colors on the chart. The terms are Wilhelm Windelband’s, from an 1894 address: nomothetic for knowledge that seeks laws across cases, idiographic for knowledge of the individual case. Gordon Allport carried the pair into psychology, where the argument is still going. headline: Tampa Bay Leads the AL East by Six. By Runs Scored, They Are Third.
deck: The Rays have outscored their opponents by 47 runs. Both clubs chasing them sit near +100 . The team in first is the third-best team in its own division — and it is going to win the thing anyway. The Sports Page · The Professor · a deficit is a fact, superiority is a rate +7.5
qa: how can the best team in a division have almost no chance of winning it?
methods: The question: how can the best team in a division have almost no chance of winning it? The answer: because a deficit is a fact and superiority is only a rate. Boston is genuinely the better club. That edge pays out at 0.046 games per game, and six games of arrears takes 131 games to clear. Here is the surprising part. We read a standings table as a ranking of how good teams are. By late August it is mostly a record of what already happened. And what already happened does not change, however well you play from here. What you get from it: two questions to ask about any team said to be surging. || METHODS: Notes & sources Standings and results from the MLB Stats API through the morning of August 27, 2026. AL East: Tampa Bay 79–54 (591 runs scored, 544 allowed), New York 75–57 (583/479), Boston 73–60 (595/494), Baltimore 65–68, Toronto 65–69. Earned records use the Pythagorean expectation with a 1.83 exponent: Tampa Bay 71–62 against an actual 79–54, New York 77–55 against 75–57, Boston 78–55 against 73–60. The rate comparison uses those Pythagorean winning percentages, .537 and .583, whose difference of .046 is the expected games gained per game played. Six divided by .046 gives 131. Division and playoff odds come from 60,000 simulated seasons over the 426 remaining league games, with team strength a 50/50 blend of actual and Pythagorean winning percentage regressed toward .500 by 69 games, game probabilities by log5 with a .535 home-field adjustment, and ties broken at random rather than by the real tiebreaker rules. Every club’s games played plus games remaining was verified to equal 162 first. Two days earlier this piece said Boston had the division’s best run differential. New York has since passed them, +104 to +101, which is why the argument here rests on the gap between the leaders and Tampa Bay rather than on which chaser is fractionally ahead. Numbers this close move daily; the seven-and-a-half-game gap between Tampa Bay’s record and its runs does not. One limit. The 131-game figure assumes both clubs keep playing at their season-long rate against average opposition, which no schedule obliges them to do. It is a way of sizing an edge, not a forecast. The simulation, which does use the actual remaining schedule, reaches the same verdict by a different road. headline: The Best Season to Watch Is Not the Best Season to Have.
deck: Clubs that surged from nowhere win 44.6% of their playoff series. Clubs that were never in doubt win 57.4% . The anxiety is not the price of success. You just pay it. The Sports Page · The Professor · what a season is worth to live through 1.1
methods: The question, from a reader looking at our odds board. Shade in the area under a club’s playoff-odds curve: what have you measured? The answer: how much of the season the fans got to enjoy. Not whether the club succeeds. Those turn out to be different numbers. Here is the surprising part. He guessed that the ideal shape is nothing early and a great swelling late — hope rising, everything feeling better. He is right that it feels best. It is also, if anything, the shape that wins least . What you get from it: a way to separate how good a season was from how good it felt. || METHODS: Notes & sources Weekly playoff odds were rebuilt for every season from 1998 through 2025, excluding 2020 for its 60-game schedule: 27 seasons, 810 club-seasons, roughly 23 weekly snapshots each. Records and run totals at each cutoff come from game-by-game results rather than from a summary, and the number of wild cards is set to the era — one per league through 2011, two through 2021, three since 2022. Each snapshot simulates every remaining game 4,000 times, with team strength a blend of record and Pythagorean expectation regressed toward .500, log5 game probabilities, and a .535 home-field adjustment. The hope index is the mean of a club’s weekly playoff probabilities across the season, expressed 0–100. It correlates +0.788 with reaching the playoffs across all 810 club-seasons, which is the check that it measures something. The test uses the 250 clubs that reached the postseason and the 446 series they played. Shape is taken as the club’s playoff probability at the midpoint of its season — deliberately not the centroid of the curve, because a curve that ends high is dragged late by that ending, and the centroid would then be partly a restatement of the outcome. Quartile series-win rates: 44.6% (45 of 101), 52.9% (64 of 121), 43.1% (44 of 102), 57.4% (70 of 122), Wilson intervals as drawn. Bottom against top quarter: z = 1.92, p = 0.055. Across all 250, r = +0.086, p = 0.175. A limit worth stating. Playoff clubs win exactly half their series by construction, so these groups are being compared against each other rather than against a fixed standard. And 446 series is not many: an effect would have to be larger than about fifteen points for us to catch it reliably. The honest summary is a null with a lean in it,

headline: Two Teams Have Everything the Contenders Have. They Are Ranked 33rd and 35th.
deck: Bringing your players back is worth about 1.2 wins a season, on top of whatever talent you had. Eight clubs this year have both. Six of them are ranked in the top fifteen. The other two went 4–8. The Sports Page · The Professor · what a preseason ranking is looking at .691
qa: which teams are better than their preseason ranking says?
methods: The question: which teams are better than their preseason ranking says? The answer: Florida and South Carolina. Both have top-thirty talent and bring back most of last year’s production. Historically that combination wins about seven of every ten games. Here is the surprising part. A preseason ranking is mostly a memory. It leans on last season’s record, and both of these teams went 4–8. The roster that produced that record is not the roster arriving in September. What you get from it: two names to watch, and a reason that is not a hunch. || METHODS: Notes & sources Talent is the 247Sports composite of recruiting rankings as served by the CollegeFootballData API. Returning production is that API’s percentage of prior-season PPA — predicted points added — returning to the roster, which counts what players actually contributed rather than merely how many came back. The model is ordinary least squares on 1,297 team-seasons, 2015 through 2025 with 2020 excluded for its shortened and uneven schedule. Winning percentage = 0.213 + 0.000392 × talent + 0.161 × returning production. The returning-production term carries SE 0.024 and p = 3.7 × 10⁻¹¹. R² is 0.136, which is worth stating plainly: these two things together explain about a seventh of the variation in winning, and the other six sevenths are coaching, health, schedule and luck. The corner comparison uses the 70th percentile of talent and the 75th of returning production: 87 club-seasons meet both and won .691; 302 club-seasons have the talent without the continuity and won .595. Difference 1.2 wins over twelve games, z = 3.83, p = 0.0001. Conference check, because it would have broken the argument: residuals by conference run from −0.038 (Pac-12) to +0.046 (independents). The SEC sits at −0.013, about a fifth of a win, with a 95% interval of [−0.042, +0.017] that includes zero. Applying it anyway gives Florida 7.9 wins and South Carolina 7.8. 2026 figures: Florida, talent 891.1 and 69% returning, Massey composite 33rd with systems ranging 16th to 65th. South Carolina, talent 862.9 and 69% returning, 35th, ranging 22nd to 71st. Both finished 4–8 in 2025. One limit we will be held to. Returning production is measured in PPA share, which can exceed 100% or turn negative when a club loses productive players and keeps unproductive ones; the extreme tails are noisy and were clipped to [−20%, 130%] before fitting.

headline: The Mets Cannot Ruin Anybody. The Athletics Can Ruin Four Seasons.
deck: Both clubs are finished. One of them plays the Yankees, the Rays and the Phillies down the stretch; the other plays Seattle seven times. Only one of them still decides anything, and it is not the one you are watching. The Sports Page · The Professor · famous is not the same as important 201
qa: which eliminated team can still do the most damage?
methods: The question: which eliminated team can still do the most damage? The answer: the Athletics, and it is not close. Their remaining games can move 201 points of other clubs’ playoff chances. The Mets can move 93. Here is the surprising part. We expected the Mets. They play the Yankees, the Rays and the Phillies, on national television, in the loudest market in the sport. They turn out to be the fourth-most consequential dead team in baseball. What you get from it: a way to tell a game that is watched from a game that matters. Look for it tonight. || METHODS: Notes & sources Standings and schedules from the MLB Stats API on the morning of August 30, 2026. Playoff probabilities come from simulating all remaining games 80,000 times, with team strength a blend of record and Pythagorean expectation regressed toward .500, log5 game probabilities and a .535 home-field adjustment; ties are broken at random rather than by the real tiebreaker rules. Damage is measured by conditioning inside that single simulation: for each remaining game, the opponent’s playoff rate across the seasons where the home side won is compared with the seasons where it lost, and the absolute difference is summed across the club’s schedule. Conditioning this way is exact because games are independent given team strength, and far cheaper than re-simulating each game twice. Totals for clubs under 1%: Athletics 201 points over 26 games, Royals 162 over 25, Rockies 152 over 26, Mets 93 over 26, Reds 66, Angels 61, Nationals 61, Giants 52, Pirates 26. Per game the Athletics average 7.7 points against the Mets’ 3.6. A limit worth naming. This counts how much a club can move, not how much it will; a team that loses out moves nothing. It also treats all opponents alike, so it says nothing about who deserves to win. And the probabilities themselves shift daily — a club at 14% today may be settled within a week, and the leverage on its remaining games would vanish with it. headline: One Game Told Us More Than the Whole Summer Did.
deck: Recruiting rankings and returning starters explain about 14% of how a college season turns out. Add a single opening result and it climbs to 21% . We expected the opposite, and we were wrong in an interesting way. The Sports Page · The Professor · what a small sample is worth +1.5
qa: after one weekend, what do we actually know?
methods: The question: after one weekend, what do we actually know? The answer: a surprising amount. A club that wins its opener finishes about 1.5 wins better than one that loses it — and that is after accounting for talent and returning production. Here is the surprising part. We came to this expecting to write that one game tells you almost nothing. That is usually the lesson. This time the data said the opposite, and the reason is not flattering to August. What you get from it: a better sense of when a small sample is worth listening to. || METHODS: Notes & sources Every FBS team-season from 2015 through 2025, excluding 2020 for its shortened and uneven schedule, and requiring at least nine completed games: 1,297 in total. Games, recruiting-talent composites and returning-production figures all from the CollegeFootballData API. The opening result is each club’s first completed regular-season game by date. Naive comparison: week-one winners finished .583 (n=843), losers .429 (n=454), a gap of .154 or 1.8 wins over twelve games. Mean talent 606 against 519, and talent correlates +0.22 with winning the opener, which is why the naive figure cannot be taken at face value. Controlled model: ordinary least squares of final winning percentage on talent and returning production gives R² = 0.1357. Adding a week-one indicator gives R² = 0.2058, with a coefficient of +0.1251 (SE 0.0117, p = 1.4 × 10⁻²⁵) — 1.50 wins over twelve games. By talent quartile the raw gaps are +1.5, +1.4, +1.6 and +1.9 wins. Misdirection: 244 of 843 week-one winners (29%) finished under .500; 50 of 454 losers (11%) finished 8–4 or better; 294 of 1,297 seasons in total, or 23%. Two limits worth stating. Returning production is measured in PPA share and its extreme tails are noisy, so values were clipped to [−20%, 130%] before fitting. And this measures how much the opener predicts , not why: a club that wins week one may be better than August thought, or may have drawn an easier opponent, and this model cannot separate those. Opponent strength in the opening game is the obvious next thing to add. headline: The SEC Has an Edge. It Is 0.4 Points.
deck: A reader wanted one number with no thumb on the scale. So we used a method that has never heard of a poll, a recruiting class or a conference. The SEC still finishes first — by 0.4 points . And for five straight seasons, the top league has not been separable from the second. The Sports Page · The Professor · answering Patrick jr 0.4
methods: The question, and it came in almost word for word: can you give me a strength of schedule that does not cater to the SEC? The answer: yes, and the SEC still wins it. Just by far less than anyone says. Its schedules rate 0.4 points harder than the Big Ten’s. That is about a fifth of a field goal. Here is what surprised us. We expected to find a rating that flatters the SEC. Instead we found that the whole question is aimed at the wrong thing. Which league you play in is the small part of how hard your season is. What you get: a way to test any ranking someone hands you. || METHODS: Notes & sources Every regular-season game from 2015 to 2025 with a final score, from the CollegeFootballData API: 24,730 games. The 2025 figures use 136 top-level teams. Sub-division opponents are pooled into a single rating rather than dropped, so that beating one still counts for something small. The rating is a Simple Rating System — each team’s value is the average of its game margins plus the value of the opponent it faced, solved by iterating to a fixed point. Margins are capped at 28 points so that one blowout cannot dominate, and 2.5 points are removed for home field. It takes no input other than scores, dates and sites. Strength of schedule is the mean rating of a team’s opponents. 2025 conference schedule means: SEC +4.1, Big Ten +3.7, Big 12 +2.9, ACC +1.5, American −3.2, Mountain West −4.8, Sun Belt −5.3, Conference USA −7.7, Mid-American −8.2. Team strength means run higher (SEC +9.3, Big Ten +7.0) because a schedule averages in the weak opponents too. Intervals come from resampling only the cross-conference games, 600 times, and re-solving the ratings each time — those games alone fix where a league sits relative to the rest of the country. SEC minus Big Ten: +2.3 in team strength, 95% interval −1.6 to +5.9. SEC minus ACC: +6.0, interval +2.8 to +9.5, which does clear zero. Seasons 2021 through 2025 each gave a top-two gap whose interval contained zero. Variance split among the 67 power-conference teams: 18.6% between conferences, 81.4% within. Across all 132 rated teams in graded conferences the between share rises to 87.5%, because the Mid-American really does play an easier schedule than the SEC. Both numbers are true; the first is the one that answers the question asked. Two limits. This is a completed-season rating, and it has to

headline: Where Do They Find These Guys? Five Thousand High Schools Never Made One.
deck: A reader asked what stock the great linemen come from. We looked at 49,242 recruits over eleven years. One boarding school in Florida produced 83 blue-chip players. The median state produced 40 . And 5,755 high schools produced none at all. The Sports Page · The Professor · answering Patrick jr 83
qa: where do the freakish ones come from? Is there a place, a population, a stock?
methods: The question: where do the freakish ones come from? Is there a place, a population, a stock? The answer: there is a place, and it is smaller than a state. Elite production is concentrated so hard that fifty high schools out of eight thousand supply a sixth of everybody. Why that is surprising. We expected the answer to be regional — the South, the Islands, Texas. It is not. It is institutional . And the most productive place in America does not grow its players. It admits them. What you get: a test you can run whenever someone tells you a group is naturally good at something. || METHODS: Notes & sources All recruiting figures from the CollegeFootballData API, high-school classes 2015 through 2026: 49,722 rated recruits, of whom 49,242 list a United States home state. “Blue-chip” means a four- or five-star rating, 4,969 players. Offensive line groups OT, OG, IOL and C; defensive line groups DL, DT, DE, EDGE, SDE and WDE. State populations are the 2020 census. South is the Census South region. Blue-chip rates per million: offensive line 3.29 South against 1.39 elsewhere; defensive line 5.24 against 1.42. Ratio of offensive to defensive linemen 0.63 South, 0.98 elsewhere. Across all recruits rather than blue-chips only, the ratio is 0.83 against 1.11 — same direction, smaller gap. Concentration: 8,018 distinct high schools appear; 2,263 produced at least one blue-chip and 5,755 produced none. Top 10 schools 6.6% of all blue-chips, top 50 16.3%, top 100 23.9%, top 500 55.3%. Gini across all 8,018 schools is 0.838. The most productive is IMG Academy in Bradenton, Florida, with 83; it is a private boarding school that enrols nationally, which is the point rather than an aside. Median state output was 40. Hawaii: 367 recruits, 30 blue-chip, 20.6 per million against a national 15.0. Trench share 38.1% against 30.4% elsewhere, and 43.3% among its blue-chips. Five of 38 schools account for 58% of the state’s recruits. Comparable top-five shares: Nevada 63% of 44 schools, Utah 27% of 82, Iowa 20% of 140. On ACTN3: the R577X variant in its XX form removes functional alpha-actinin-3 from fast-twitch fibre. Population frequency of XX is roughly 18% worldwide and varies substantially between populations. Studies of elite sprinters have found the XX genotype to be rare or absent among them, but the samples are small and the variance the gene explains in ordinary populations is a few percent at most. Treat it as necessary-ish

headline: 209 of Every 1,000 Never Pitch Again.
deck: Out of 1,000 professional pitchers who have the operation, 791 pitch again. Only 735 get their level back. Same surgery, same pitchers, two different finish lines — and only one of them makes the headline. By Sean McKnight · numbers run by The Sports Page 791
qa: everyone says Tommy John surgery has a 90% success rate. Ninety percent of pitchers successfully did what ?
methods: The question: everyone says Tommy John surgery has a 90% success rate. Ninety percent of pitchers successfully did what ? The answer depends entirely on where you draw the line. A pitcher throws again. A pitcher returns to college baseball. A pitcher gets his old velocity back. All four might be called a success. They are not the same thing. Here is what is surprising. The famous number is not wrong. The question it answers is incomplete. And the gap has grown into something worse than confusion — a belief among some players and parents that the surgery makes you better , and that a torn ligament is a door to an upgrade. What you get: one extra question that changes almost any percentage you will ever be handed. || METHODS: Notes & sources Headline counts from Meta F, Meister K, Griffith TB, et al., “Epidemiology of Elbow Medial Ulnar Collateral Ligament Surgeries in Major and Minor League Baseball Pitchers: A Descriptive Study of 2281 Cases,” Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine 2025;13(7). 2,281 pitchers, 2010–2023; MLB 380 (16.6%), minor league 1,907 (83.4%); primary 2,093 (91.5%), revision 194 (8.5%). Return to play at any level 79.1% (mean 470 ± 135 days); return to the same level 73.5% (mean 499 ± 153 days); revision 71.1% against primary 79.8%. Percentages are converted to counts per 1,000 and rounded, so the figure’s 735 / 56 / 209 sum exactly. Ranges across all levels from Hones KM, et al., “Variable Return to Play and Sport Performance After Elbow Ulnar Collateral Ligament Reconstruction in Baseball Players: A Systematic Review,” Arthroscopy 2024;40(7):1997–2006 — 25 studies, about 2,100 elbows. Primary return to play 57–100%, same level 61–95%. High school and college: 73–85% and 55–74%. Revision: 67–98% and 42–78%. The width of those ranges is the argument of this piece, not a flaw in it. On performance after return: both Hones et al. and Coughlin RP, et al. (“Return-to-Play and Competitive Outcomes After Ulnar Collateral Ligament Reconstruction Among Baseball Players: A Systematic Review,” Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine 2021) report most studies finding reduced innings pitched after reconstruction, with several reporting decreased fastball velocity and mixed results on ERA. We could find no study reporting that a reconstructed ligament outperforms an uninjured one. The “comes back stronger” belief appears to be a cause-and-effect swap: a year of supervised strength work and mechanical rebuilding gets credited to the graft. On definitions: Buchanan et al., “Current Definitions of Return to Play After Medial Ulnar Collateral Ligament Injuries and Surgery in Professional Baseball Players Prohibit Cross-Study Comparison: A Systematic Review,” Arthroscopy 2025. headline: We Were Wrong About Cleveland.
deck: Out of 1,848 players who changed clubs, the ones who joined Cleveland were more likely to still be playing two years later, not less — ninth of 32. Among established starters, fourth. This is a correction, and the mistake was ours. The Sports Page · The Professor · marking our own homework 9th
qa: do some franchises actually ruin players, or do they just sign players who were already falling?
methods: The question: do some franchises actually ruin players, or do they just sign players who were already falling? The answer: we could not find the effect we predicted. Cleveland sits in the top third for keeping careers going, and does not work its players harder than anyone else works them. Why that is surprising: we said the opposite, out loud and on the record, and said the numbers would back us. What you get: the single question that separates a place making people worse from a place attracting people already in decline. || METHODS: Notes & sources Snap counts for every player and game, 2013–2024 regular seasons, from the nflverse public data release: 24,923 player-seasons across 6,682 players, of which 21,663 seasons involve at least four games. Franchise moves are merged, so Oakland and Las Vegas, San Diego and Los Angeles, St Louis and Los Angeles are each one club. The arrival sample is 1,848 moves: a player at a different club than the previous season, having played four or more games the previous season, whose first season on record is 2014 or later so that experience is measured rather than guessed, and moving early enough to allow two full seasons of follow-up. Outcome is appearing in any regular-season game in either of the next two seasons. Logistic model with experience, experience squared, previous-season snap share and season fixed; club effects are the mean residual, reported in percentage points against a league rate of 73.1%. Cleveland: 81.1% raw, +6.4 points adjusted, standard error 3.9, ninth of 32. Restricted to prior snap share of 50% or more (n = 680): +9.6 points, standard error 4.1, fourth of 32. Jets +4.2 (11th), Cincinnati +2.8 (13th). Extremes: New England +14.9, Philadelphia +12.8, Dallas +12.0; Arizona −15.8, Washington −13.8, Tampa Bay −8.6. Workload uses each player-season’s primary-role snap share with player and season means removed by alternating projection, plus a quadratic in years of experience. Cleveland +0.28 snap-share points, standard error 0.59, 15th of 32. Jacksonville +1.58 highest; Baltimore −2.42 lowest. Change in snap share on arrival at Cleveland: −0.2 points, 17th of 32. Four limits, and the first is the big one. “Still in the league” measures employment, not excellence — a man hanging on as a backup counts as surviving. headline: Nobody Wins 102% of the Time.
deck: Home field in baseball is worth one number: +0.14 . That single constant buys a coin-flip club 3.5 percentage points and a dominant club only 1.2 . Percentages cannot hold a constant like that. Log-odds can, and that is the whole reason the log is there. The Sports Page · The Professor · answering a question we were asked +0.14
qa: because two advantages have to be added together, and probabilities refuse to be added.
methods: The question, asked plainly: why do statisticians take the log of the odds instead of just using the odds? And what is an odds ratio actually for? The answer: because two advantages have to be added together, and probabilities refuse to be added. Why that is surprising. Most people assume you can just add a few percentage points for home field. You cannot, and the reason is not fussiness — do it and you will eventually claim a club wins 104% of the time. What you get: the ability to read the phrase “odds ratio” correctly, which most reporting does not. || METHODS: Notes & sources Definitions. Odds are p/(1−p). Log-odds, also called the logit, are ln(p/(1−p)); the inverse is p = 1/(1+e −x ). An odds ratio divides one group’s odds by another’s; a risk ratio divides one group’s probability by another’s. They are different quantities and coincide only when the outcome is rare in both groups. Home field: major league home clubs win about 53.5% of games between evenly matched opponents, so the home-versus-away gap is ln(0.535/0.465) = 0.140 in log-odds, applied as ±0.070 to the two sides. Converting back: a club at .500 goes to .535 (+3.5 points), at .700 to .729 (+2.9), at .900 to .912 (+1.2). These are the figures marked on the chart. The odds ratio worked example uses the same 1,297 FBS team-seasons (2015–2025, excluding 2020) behind our week-one piece. Winners of the opener: 599 finished at .500 or better, 244 below, odds 2.455. Losers: 205 and 249, odds 0.823. Odds ratio 2.98; log odds ratio 1.093 with standard error √(1/599 + 1/244 + 1/205 + 1/249) = 0.121; 95% interval 2.35 to 3.78. Risk ratio 0.711/0.451 = 1.57. The overstatement is 2.98/1.57 − 1 = 89%, and it is a property of how common the outcome is rather than a mistake in either number. Both are computed correctly; they answer different questions. A limit worth stating: the interval above assumes these team-seasons are independent, and they are not entirely — the same programmes recur across years. A proper interval would cluster by programme and would be somewhat wider. It would not move the point estimate, and it would not touch the argument about odds ratios against risk ratios, which is arithmetic rather than inference. See the bracket this piece came from on the Odds Board . Got a question the numbers could settle? thesportspage.net/ask.html .

headline: Rutgers Was Favored by Twenty-Nine. It Lost by Sixteen.
deck: Across all 47 rated games, week one missed its preseason number by 14.3 points a game. That is 28% worse than the last two seasons. The openers were not just loud — they were measurably the hardest to predict in three years. The Sports Page · The Professor · the week, against what was expected of it 1%
qa: was week one genuinely strange, or does every opening weekend feel that way?
methods: The question: was week one genuinely strange, or does every opening weekend feel that way? It was genuinely strange, and here is the number. Ratings missed by 14.3 points a game against 11.2 across the previous two openers. Why that is surprising. Openers are supposed to be the easy week; big programmes play small ones and win by forty. Instead the mismatches were the games that broke. What you get: a way to tell a loud week from an unusual one. || METHODS: Notes & sources Results and preseason SP+ ratings from the CollegeFootballData API, pulled the morning of 6 September 2026. Week one played 412 games; 47 had both clubs carrying an SP+ rating, and only those are counted, because a game against an unrated opponent has no expectation to beat. Expected margin is the home club’s SP+ rating minus the away club’s, plus 2.5 points for home field, with the adjustment dropped at neutral sites. Surprise is the actual margin minus that. Win probability converts the expected margin through a normal distribution with a 16.5-point spread, the same setting the odds board uses so the two never disagree. Mean absolute miss: 14.3 points in 2026, against 12.4 in 2024 and 10.0 in 2025 — a prior-year mean of 11.2, so this week ran 28% above it. Medians move the same way, 11.8 against 9.9 and 8.9, so a single blowout is not carrying the result. Outright upsets: 8 of 47 (17%), against 8 of 39 (21%) in 2024 and 6 of 48 (12.5%) in 2025. Massachusetts 37, Rutgers 21, at SHI Stadium on 3 September, verified against the game feed and against three published spreads — Bovada −29, DraftKings −29.5 twice, mean 29.3. SP+ made it 38.1. The implied chance of the result was about 1%. Two limits. Preseason ratings are at their least informative in week one by construction — they have no current-season evidence in them — so some elevation is expected every year; the comparison against the same week in prior seasons is what controls for that. And 47 games is a small sample for a mean, so treat 28% as a strong hint rather than a settled fact until a few more weeks agree with it. Reproduce it: python3 scripts/cfb_week_review.py . headline: We Found a Pattern in Forty Games. Then We Killed It.
deck: Penn State returned 7.6% of last year’s offense, hired a new coach, lost 48 players — and won 45–0. Clemson returned 41% , kept everybody, and lost by 41. The pattern held across the whole week. Then we gave it eleven seasons and it fell apart. The Sports Page · The Professor · how to lose an argument with yourself −0.28
qa: does a club that keeps last year’s players beat its preseason rating?
methods: The question: does a club that keeps last year’s players beat its preseason rating? The answer, briefly: no. And for one week it looked like a resounding yes. Here is what is surprising. Not the result. The speed at which a very good story assembled itself out of nothing, and how nearly it got published. What you get: the test that kills a pattern before it costs you money. || METHODS: Notes & sources All figures from the CollegeFootballData API: game results, preseason SP+ ratings, returning-production shares (percent of prior-season PPA returning), transfer-portal moves and coach hire dates. Surprise is the actual margin minus the expected margin, where expected is the home club’s SP+ minus the away club’s plus 2.5 points for home field, dropped at neutral sites. Week one 2026: 49 games where both clubs carried a rating and a returning-production figure. Correlation between the difference in returning production and the surprise: −0.276, t = −1.97. The named cases — Penn State 7.6% returning with a first-year head coach, 38 transfers in and 48 out, beating Marshall 45–0; Clemson 41.4% returning, no coaching change, 11 in and 15 out, losing 51–10 at LSU — are real and verified, and were chosen after the fact because they pointed the way we already suspected. That is the problem with them. The eleven-season test covers every week one from 2015 to 2026, excluding 2020, on identical method: 495 games, pooled correlation −0.089, t = −1.98. Season by season: −0.376, −0.038, −0.303, +0.188, −0.271, −0.035, −0.099, −0.053, −0.000, +0.081, −0.276. Two honest limits. The pooled t clears the conventional threshold, so a very small real effect cannot be ruled out — we are claiming it is far too small and far too unstable to explain anything, not that it is exactly zero. And week-one games are not independent within a season, since the same programmes recur; a properly clustered interval would be wider still, which only strengthens the conclusion. The catalogue runs with python3 scripts/outlier_watch.py and reports the sample size beside every correlation, labelling anything under 150 games a rumor. headline: Detroit Outscored Its Opponents by 55 Runs. It Is Twelve Games Under.
deck: The Tigers have scored 641 and allowed 586 . A club that outscores people like that wins about 79 games. They have 67 . The whole gap sits in one column of the schedule. The Sports Page · The Professor · the standings are lying, politely +55
qa: can a team outscore everybody it plays and still finish twelve games under .500?
methods: The question: can a team outscore everybody it plays and still finish twelve games under .500? Yes, and Detroit is doing it right now. They have outscored their opponents by 55 runs and sit at 67–79 . Why that is surprising. Runs are how you win. A club that scores more of them than it allows, over 146 games, has essentially never finished this far under. Detroit is not slightly unlucky; it is close to the limit of the thing. What you get: a way to tell which parts of a record will still be there next year. || METHODS: Notes & sources All figures from the MLB Stats API, pulled 9 September 2026. Detroit: 67–79, 641 runs scored, 586 allowed, a differential of +55. One-run games 14–27; extra-inning games 5–9. Expected wins use the Pythagorean estimate with an exponent of 1.83, the standard fit for modern run environments: 641 1.83 / (641 1.83 + 586 1.83 ) = .541, which over 146 games played is 79.0 wins against an actual 67. The shortfall is 12.0. Clubs outscoring their opponents while under .500, same date: Detroit +55, Pittsburgh +26, Miami +10, Washington +8. Pittsburgh is 24–17 in one-run games, so whatever explains their gap is not this. Persistence test: every club appearing in consecutive seasons from 2021 through 2026, giving 150 club-season pairs. One-run winning percentage correlates with the next season’s at −0.117 (t = −1.43), an r-squared of 1.4%. Overall winning percentage, identical clubs and identical method, correlates at +0.567, an r-squared of 32.1%. The second figure is the control that makes the first mean something. Two limits. 2026 is incomplete, so its pairs use a partial season and will shift slightly by October. And a correlation near zero establishes that one-run records do not repeat on average; it cannot rule out a particular club having a genuine and lasting problem in close games. It says only that a single season’s record is not evidence of one, which is what the claim usually rests on. headline: Our Model Went 15 for 15. That Is How We Knew It Was Broken.
deck: A perfect backtest is not a triumph; it is a bug report. Rebuilt so that cheating was impossible, the same method beat the spread 51.0% of the time across 2,140 games — and the interval around that contains 50. The Sports Page · The Professor · marking our own homework, again 15/15
qa: can our ratings beat a betting line?
methods: The question: can our ratings beat a betting line? No. And for one afternoon we had convincing evidence that we could. Why that is surprising. Not the answer — the answer is what anyone should expect. What is surprising is how good the wrong evidence looked, and that the thing which exposed it was the result being too good. What you get: the smell test that catches this in your own work. || METHODS: Notes & sources The broken test: SP+ ratings from the CollegeFootballData API against mean closing spreads from the same source, on the 51 games of week one 2026 where both clubs were rated and a line existed. Fifteen of fifteen against the spread on the top-ranked card; correlation between our edge and the actual result against the spread +0.842. The endpoint serves current ratings and overwrites them as the season progresses; there is no historical snapshot. The honest test: a Simple Rating System solved from scratch by iterating each club’s value to the mean of its game margins plus its opponents’ values, margins capped at 28 points, 2.5 points removed for home field. For each week from week five onward it is rebuilt using only games from earlier weeks that season, then used to pick against that week’s closing line. 2,140 games across 2024 and 2025, pushes excluded. Result: 1,091 wins, 51.0%. Standard error on a proportion at this sample is 1.1 points, giving a 95% interval of 48.9% to 53.1%. Correlation between edge and result against the spread, +0.018. By season: 52.6% in 2024 (r = +0.039), 49.4% in 2025 (r = −0.004). By edge band: 0–3 points 49.3% (n=980), 3–6 points 53.5% (n=620), 6–10 points 51.1% (n=354), above 10 points 51.1% (n=186). Three limits. Beginning at week five means the early season, where a market is least settled and an edge most plausible, is excluded — that is a real cost of removing leakage, since a rating needs games before it exists. Our rating uses margins alone and no injury, weather or personnel information, so this bounds what a simple rating can do rather than what any model could. headline: Michigan Nearly Lost to Western Michigan. Eight Days Later It Beat Oklahoma.
deck: A team that badly misses the number tells you almost nothing about what it does next. We measured it across 236 teams and two weekends: last week explains three tenths of one percent of this week. The Sports Page · The Professor · on the thing everybody says on Saturday night −26.5
qa: a team wins ugly when it should have won big. Does that tell you anything about next week?
methods: The question: a team wins ugly when it should have won big. Does that tell you anything about next week? Almost nothing. Across 236 teams, the correlation between one week’s miss and the next is +0.06 . Why that is surprising. Everybody treats an ugly win as evidence. They should have lost; they are frauds; the ranking is a lie. That reasoning assumes the ugliness carries forward. It does not. What you get: a way to tell a real signal from a loud one, by Saturday night. || METHODS: Notes & sources Games and scores from the CollegeFootballData API. Closing spreads are the mean across that API’s books for each game, taken as a historical record of what was believed before kickoff — unlike a rating, a past line cannot be quietly updated by the result. A team’s miss is its final margin minus the margin the line implied, signed from that team’s perspective. Both clubs in a game therefore carry equal and opposite misses. Weeks 1 and 2 of 2026, every game where a line existed: 253 team-games in week 1, 240 in week 2, and 236 teams appearing in both. Correlation between a team’s week-1 miss and its week-2 miss: r = +0.058, t = +0.89, r-squared 0.3%. Fitted slope +0.051 points per point. Mean absolute miss: 13.4 points in week 1, 11.5 in week 2. Crowd against model, on the 49 week-2 games that had both a line and a rating for each side: mean absolute miss 10.76 for the closing line, 12.00 for SP+ frozen on 2026-09-10 by scripts/snapshot_ratings.py . Mean difference 1.24 points, standard error 0.64, t = 1.95 — not separable from zero. Three limits. Two weekends is a small window, and early-season lines are the least settled of the year, so the true correlation is probably somewhat higher than 0.06 once the market has more information. A correlation near zero measures only the LINEAR relationship; a team that changes for a real reason mid-season would not show up here. And this measures margin against expectation, not quality — a club genuinely transformed by an injury is exactly the case the method cannot see, which is why the piece asks for a mechanism rather than a number. headline: Oregon Lost One Game. Now Nobody Can Agree How Good They Are.
deck: Oregon lost once and the consensus dropped them from 4th to 19th. But one system still has them 5th and another has them 76th — and that gap tells you more than the ranking does. The Sports Page · The Professor · with thanks to Kenneth Massey, who publishes all of it 5th to 76th
qa: how much should one Saturday change your mind about a team?
methods: The question: how much should one Saturday change your mind about a team? Nobody agrees. Thirty-five rating systems looked at the same Oregon loss and moved them to somewhere between 5th and 76th. Why that is surprising. A ranking is presented as a fact — one number, printed, settled. Underneath it is an argument that nobody has won. What you get: a way to tell a solid ranking from a contested one, using a number nobody prints. || METHODS: Notes & sources Ranks are from Kenneth Massey’s published comparison, 35 systems carrying a rank for these teams, in the week beginning 14 September 2026. The composite rank is his; we do not claim to know how it is formed, and we checked — ordering our 30 teams by the mean of the published ranks does not reproduce his order, and neither does the median, so it is doing something else with more information than we have. The spread statistics are ours: best, worst, median and interquartile range computed directly from the published per-system ranks. We use the interquartile range rather than the full range because two dissenting systems should not be allowed to describe a consensus — Oregon’s range of 71 places and its middle-half spread of 12 are different claims, and the second is the honest one. Oregon at Oklahoma State, 31–39, 12 September 2026. The pregame spread was Oregon by 23.25, mean across books via the CollegeFootballData API and captured before kickoff by scripts/snapshot_ratings.py . The 0.3% figure is from Issue #155: the correlation between a team’s week-1 miss against the closing line and its week-2 miss, across 236 teams, r = +0.058. Two limits. We transcribed 30 of the 138 rated teams — Notre Dame, its 2026 opponents, the top twenty and the two clubs from Saturday’s largest upset — so nothing here describes the full board. And a wide spread is not evidence that a ranking is wrong; it is evidence that informed people disagree, which is a different and more interesting thing. headline: Home Teams Stopped Winning in 2019. The Crowds Left in 2020.
deck: NFL home teams won by 2.4 points a game from 2016 to 2018. In 2019, with every seat sold, the edge was minus 0.14 — and the empty-stadium season that followed looked exactly the same. The Sports Page · The Professor · on the experiment that arrived a year late −0.14
qa: does a home crowd win football games?
methods: The question: does a home crowd win football games? Probably not the way you think. NFL home teams won by an average of 2.4 points from 2016 to 2018. In 2019, in front of full stadiums, that edge was −0.14 . It was already gone. Why that is surprising. 2020 was supposed to be the test. Empty stadiums, no noise, a natural experiment nobody could have run deliberately. But the effect had vanished a year early, with the crowds still there. What you get: a worked example of the thing that ruins most natural experiments. || METHODS: Notes & sources Built from nflverse play-by-play, 2016 through 2025, aggregated to one row per team per game by scripts/build_nfl_history.py : 5,278 team-games with scrimmage plays, yards, drive-level possession, turnovers, points and result. Analysis in scripts/nfl_predictive.py . Home margin by season, points, with 95% intervals: 2016 +2.57, 2017 +2.48, 2018 +2.20, 2019 −0.14, 2020 +0.05, 2021 +1.71, 2022 +1.98, 2023 +2.68, 2024 +1.87, 2025 +2.07. Home win rates run 57.4%, 56.6%, 59.8%, 51.6%, 49.6%, 51.5%, 55.7%, 55.5%, 53.3%, 53.7%. Grouped: 2016–2018 +2.42 (n=768), 2019 −0.14 (n=256), 2020 +0.05 (n=256), 2021–2025 +2.06 (n=1,359). Differences with pooled standard errors: 2019 against 2020 is −0.20, SE 1.29, t = −0.15. 2016–2018 against 2019 is +2.56, SE 1.06, t = +2.42. 2016–2018 against 2020 is +2.36, SE 1.02, t = +2.31. Three limits, and the first is the big one. A single season is 256 to 272 games, so its interval spans roughly three and a half points; "2019 and 2020 are indistinguishable" is partly a statement about low power, not proof they were the same. The comparison carrying real weight is the three pooled seasons against 2019. Second, 2020 was not only crowdless — no preseason, altered protocols, disrupted travel — so even a clean 2020 effect could not be attributed to noise alone. Third, this is margin, not win rate, and the two disagree slightly in 2019 and 2020; we lead with margin because it uses the whole scoreboard rather than only its sign.
