headline: Your Team Held the Ball Longer. That Just Means They Were Ahead.
deck: Time of possession predicts a team’s second half at +0.216. Account for the point margin and it falls to minus 0.003. Teams hold the ball because they are winning. The Sports Page · The Professor · answering an argument about the Bills +0.216
qa: your team held the ball for 36 minutes. Does that tell you anything?
methods: The question: your team held the ball for 36 minutes. Does that tell you anything? Nothing you did not already have. Time of possession correlates with a team’s second half at +0.216. Account for the point margin and it falls to −0.003 . Why that is surprising. It is on the screen every week, so it must mean something. It does — it means the score, which is printed beside it. What you get: the difference between a number that matters and a number that repeats another number. || METHODS: Notes & sources Built from nflverse play-by-play, 2016 through 2025, aggregated to one row per team per game by scripts/build_nfl_history.py : 5,278 team-games with scrimmage plays, yards, drive-level possession, turnovers, points and result. Analysis in scripts/nfl_predictive.py . Each metric is a margin — own minus opponent — averaged over weeks 1 to 8, correlated with win rate from week 9 onward. 320 team-seasons with at least six games either side. Raw correlations: point margin +0.424, first-half win rate +0.414, yards-per-play margin +0.368, turnover margin +0.245, time of possession +0.216, plays run +0.117. Partial correlations, holding the point margin fixed: yards per play +0.081, turnover margin −0.016, time of possession −0.003. Point margin holding yards per play fixed is +0.240, so the dependence runs one way. Stable where you cut the season. Splitting at weeks 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11 leaves the ordering unchanged, with possession between +0.201 and +0.236 throughout. Two limits. This predicts a team’s remaining SEASON, not a single game; a piece claiming possession never matters in any particular game would be overclaiming, and this is not that piece. And a partial correlation near zero means possession adds nothing beyond the point margin — if you somehow knew the possession figures and not the score, you would still know something. Buffalo 36, Houston 31, 13 September 2026. Box score via ESPN. headline: Turnovers Win Games. They Do Not Win Seasons.
deck: A season’s turnover margin explains 3% of the next season’s. How a team moves the ball explains 15%. Turnovers feel like character and behave like weather. The Sports Page · The Professor · on the number everybody calls discipline 3.0%
qa: your team lost the turnover battle again. Is that who they are?
methods: The question: your team lost the turnover battle again. Is that who they are? Almost certainly not. A season’s turnover margin explains 3% of the next season’s. How a team moves the ball explains 15%. Why that is surprising. Turnovers feel like character — discipline, ball security, coaching. They behave like weather. What you get: a way to know which of this year’s numbers will still be true next year. || METHODS: Notes & sources Built from nflverse play-by-play, 2016 through 2025, aggregated to one row per team per game by scripts/build_nfl_history.py : 5,278 team-games with scrimmage plays, yards, drive-level possession, turnovers, points and result. Analysis in scripts/nfl_predictive.py . Year-over-year persistence across 288 consecutive team-season pairs, 2016–2025. Correlation of a team’s season average with the same team’s next season: yards-per-play margin r = +0.392 (t = +7.20), win rate r = +0.369 (t = +6.71), turnover margin r = +0.175 (t = +3.00). The percentages quoted are r-squared: 15.4%, 13.6% and 3.0%. Turnover margin is takeaways minus giveaways, counting interceptions thrown and fumbles lost. Fumbles FORCED are excluded from the giveaway side deliberately — a forced fumble recovered by the offense is not a turnover, and lumping the two together is what makes the statistic look more repeatable than it is. Three limits. Persistence across seasons is a low bar: rosters, coaches and schedules all change, which is why even the best figure here is only 15%. A low year-to-year correlation does not prove there is no skill in ball security — it shows that whatever skill exists is swamped by variance at a 17-game sample. And r-squared measures only the straight-line relationship; a team that genuinely fixed something would be invisible inside an average of 288. headline: The Crowd Splits Every Game in Half. You Still Lose a Thousand Dollars.
deck: A betting line is remarkably good: across 4,360 games, every simple rule we tried landed within a point of 50%. The catch is the price. Two sides at −110 add up to 104.76% , and that surplus never plays a down. The Sports Page · The Professor · on the one number nobody shows you 104.76%
qa: if a betting line is a fair guess at who wins, why does almost everybody lose?
methods: The question: if a betting line is a fair guess at who wins, why does almost everybody lose? Because the line is fair and the price is not. Both sides are offered at odds implying 52.38%, and 52.38 twice is 104.76. Why that is surprising. People assume they lose because the house knows more. The house does not need to know more. The arithmetic does the work. What you get: the ability to turn any price into a probability in your head, and to see what it costs you. || METHODS: Notes & sources The implied probability of American odds of −110 is 110/(110+100) = 52.381%. Both sides of a standard spread are offered at that price, so the two implied probabilities sum to 104.76%; the excess over 100% is the overround, commonly called the vigorish or juice. Normalized back to 100%, each side is exactly 50.00%. Expected profit on one bet at −110 is 100p − 110(1−p), where p is how often you win. That is zero at p = 110/210 = 52.38% and −$5.00 at p = 0.50. Note the stake is $110, not $100, so −$5.00 is 4.545% of the money risked. The season figure is 15 bets a week for 13 weeks: 195 × −$5.00 = −$975, against $21,450 risked, which is the same 4.55%. Two numbers here are close together and are not the same thing. The overround is 4.76 percentage points — the amount by which the two implied probabilities exceed 100. The hold , what the house keeps as a share of money wagered, is 4.76/104.76 = 4.545%. The headline rounds $975 to a thousand; the exact figure is here, as it should be. Rule records are from 4,360 FBS games, 2023–2025, graded against the mean closing spread across books via the CollegeFootballData API, pushes excluded. Our own model’s 51.0% is from Issue #154: 2,140 games, walk-forward, ratings rebuilt each week from earlier weeks only. Two limits. This piece is about the PRICE, not about how a line is set — the common account, that books simply balance the money on each side, is more complicated than it sounds and we are checking it properly before writing that piece. And −110 is the standard price, not a universal one; reduced-juice books and some markets differ, which is exactly why the habit of summing the

headline: The Booth Shows You Twelve Numbers. Eight of Them Mean Nothing.
deck: A game hands you a dozen stats. We tested all of them against 5,278 games. Four tell you something. The rest just tell you the score again. The Sports Page · The Professor · asked for by Tim, who wanted a fan’s guide 4
methods: Four of them can. Eight cannot. Here is the surprising part. You would expect the bad ones to look bad. They do not. Every single stat here looks useful at first; third down percentage, first downs and turnover margin all track winning teams closely. They fall apart only when you check them against something you already knew — the score. That is the whole answer. Here is how we know. We took ten years of games. For each team we measured every stat over the first half of its season. || METHODS: Notes & sources 5,278 team-games, 2016–2025, from nflverse play-by-play. Each stat is a margin — own minus opponent — averaged over weeks 1 to 8, then correlated with win rate from week 9 on. 320 team-seasons with at least six games either side. The second column is a partial correlation holding point margin fixed. On its own, every stat here looks useful: third down percentage +0.280, first downs +0.290, turnover margin +0.245, possession +0.216. Holding the score fixed they fall to +0.033, +0.031, −0.016 and −0.003. The four that survive are yards per play +0.081, explosive plays +0.070, completion percentage +0.068 and total yards +0.061. Penalties are credited to whoever committed them rather than assumed to be the offense. Red zone trips are counted once per drive, not once per play inside the twenty, which would reward stalling there. Three limits. This predicts a team’s remaining SEASON, not a single game; third down percentage plainly matters in the game you are watching. "Adds nothing" means adds nothing beyond the score — if you somehow knew the third down rate and not the result, you would still know something. And one oddity we are not explaining: penalty yards runs slightly the wrong way, so committing fewer penalties tracks a marginally worse second half. It is small, we have logged it, and we would rather leave it unexplained than invent a reason. Tools: scripts/build_nfl_broadcast_stats.py and scripts/rank_broadcast_stats.py . headline: Mississippi State Won by 25. The Numbers Say Minnesota Is Just Bad.
deck: Mississippi State beat Minnesota 38–13. The ratings moved Mississippi State up 0.6 and moved Minnesota down 4.9 . Same game. Almost all of it was about the team that lost. The Sports Page · The Professor · a reader asked who that game was really about +0.6
methods: Mississippi State went to Minnesota and won 38–13. Nobody saw it coming. The betting line had the game dead even. Most people read that one way: Mississippi State must be good. Here is the surprising part. You would expect a 25-point win to say most about the team that won it. It did not. The ratings moved the loser eight times further than they moved the winner — and the betting line for this week read the game the other way round. Maybe not. There is a second reading, and the ratings prefer it. Minnesota might just be bad. || METHODS: Notes & sources SP+ ratings before the game were frozen on 2026-09-10 by scripts/snapshot_ratings.py , so the "before" column cannot have seen the result. Mississippi State +9.4 to +10.0, Minnesota +9.6 to +4.7, South Carolina +16.7 to +16.9. Lines are the mean across books via the CollegeFootballData API. Minnesota–Mississippi State closed at Minnesota −0.33, effectively a pick. Week 3 has South Carolina −4.0 at home against Mississippi State. Transfers from the CFBD portal feed, 2026: 28 into Mississippi State, 27 into South Carolina; the figure quoted is the mean SP+ of the programmes those players left. Returning production is the share of last season’s output back on the roster. The blowout follow-up covers 2023–2025, 6,626 consecutive team-week pairs with a line in both weeks. Teams beating the closing number by 20+ went 307–334 the following week, 47.9%, with a 95% interval of 44.0% to 51.8%. Correlation between a team’s cover margin one week and the next: r = −0.006. Three limits. SP+ is one rating system and others weight recency differently, so "the ratings" here means this one. Two games is a tiny sample for any of these clubs, Mississippi State included — the argument is about what a result can support, not about who wins on Saturday. And the 47.9% lean is not separable from 50%; if it were a finding rather than a hint, we would have led with it. The Sports Page · Vol. I, No. 175 Who was that game about? headline: Our New Rule Beat Our Old One. Random Numbers Beat Them Both.
deck: We found a better way to order our picks. It gained eleven points. Then we checked it against pulling the order out of a hat, and the hat won by eleven more. Here is how a rule can look like it works and still be worthless.
methods: Does the order you put your picks in matter? We run an entry in a family pick'em pool. You choose fifteen games and hand out fifteen point values, 15 down to 1. We wanted to know whether a smarter ordering would win more. So we tested one. Over three weeks it scored 213 where we had scored 202. It would have moved us up in two of the three weeks. That looks like a win. Then we asked the question we should have asked first. What does the order score if you pull it out of a hat? The answer is 224 . Our clever rule lost to the hat by eleven points. So did our real entry, by twenty-two. Most people assume a rule that beats what you were doing before is an improvement. It is not. It is only an improvement if it beats doing nothing in particular || METHODS:

headline: The Same Fifteen Picks. Fifty Points Apart.
deck: Two people can pick every game the same way and finish fifty-six points apart, because of nothing but the order they ranked them in. Over a season that order is worth nothing at all to your score. It nearly doubles your chance of winning. Both of those are true, and the gap between them is one of the most useful ideas in statistics.
methods: Does it matter which of your picks you put the big numbers on? In a confidence pool you rank your games. Your best one carries 15 points, your worst carries 1. Everybody has a theory about the order. Here is the answer, and it comes in two halves that sound like they cannot both be right. The order is worth nothing to your score. Over the long run it adds exactly zero. And the order nearly doubles your chance of winning — 22 in 100 instead of 15 in 100. Most people hear "it does not raise your score" and stop. That is the mistake. Scoring more and winning are not the same goal, and once you see the difference you will start noticing it everywhere. Say you get 8 of your 15 right. Put those 8 on your top numbers and you score 92. Put them on your bottom || METHODS:

headline: Two Teams Are Tied With Losing Records. One Is Going to the Playoffs.
deck: Houston and Texas are both 79 and 80 with three games left, and one of them will win the AL West. In 57 years, 270 teams have won a division and not one finished with a losing record. There is a 70% chance this one is the worst ever.
methods: Can a team with a losing record win its division? Right now Houston and Texas are both 79 and 80 . Three games each. They do not play each other, and one of them is going to the playoffs. It has never happened. We pulled every division winner since divisions began in 1969 — 270 of them — and not one finished below .500. The worst was the 2005 San Diego Padres at 82 and 80. Most people assume a division winner is a good team. That is what the trophy is for. But a division is just five clubs, and if all five are bad, somebody still wins it. This week you get to watch that happen. Both clubs need to sweep to reach 82 and 80, which only ties the worst mark ever. Houston plays the Athletics, who are 63 and 96. Texas plays Minnesota, who are 74 || METHODS:

headline: Two Fans Spent the Same $84,000. One of Them Has $167,000.
deck: A hundred dollars a week, every week of the football season, for forty seasons. One of them put it through a betting pool. The other bought a plain index fund and did nothing. We ran it on the real market, every starting year since 1970, and the gap at the end is larger than everything either of them ever paid in.
methods: What does it really cost to bet on football? Not the losing weeks. The whole thing, measured against what the same money would have done somewhere dull. Take two fans. Both spend $100 a week through the season — eighteen weeks and the playoffs, about twenty-one weeks, $2,100 a year. One runs it through a pool at standard prices. The other buys a plain index fund and forgets about it. After forty seasons they have each paid in $84,000 . The bettor has $80,182 . The index fund has $167,377 . Most people expect the bettor to be the one who lost money. He is not — he is down less than four thousand dollars. What happened is that the other man's money was busy the whole time, and by the end you will see why that gap is bigger than the entire amount either of them spent. || METHODS:

headline: Three Hundred Million Tickets. One Expected Winner.
deck: There are 292,201,338 ways to fill in a Powerball ticket. If every person in the United States bought exactly one, you would expect a single winner. This is not a piece about people who buy tickets being foolish. It is a piece about who is selling them, and what the money they keep gets called.
methods: What are you actually buying when you buy a lottery ticket? Let us do the arithmetic properly, and then let us be careful about who the arithmetic is aimed at. We pulled every Powerball draw New York has published — 1,997 of them , back to 2010. Then we worked out the game from its own results, not from a press release. You pick five numbers from 69, plus one from 26. That gives 292,201,338 different tickets. Here is the number that makes it real. There are about 335 million people in the United States. If every single one of them bought one ticket, you would expect one winner. Not one each. One. People know the odds are long. What they do not have is a feel for how the odds respond when you try harder, so look at what happens as you buy more. || METHODS:

headline: Defense Moves More Than Offense. Measure It Better and It Does Not.
deck: You take over a bad team. Do you fix the offense or the defense? Counted in points, the defense is the one that budges — 4 points likelier to jump a full standard deviation, and the interval clears zero. Count the same 797 clubs in yards per play and the gap falls to 1.5 and stops being a gap at all.
methods: You take over a struggling team. Do you fix the offense or the defense? It is the most basic question in running a club, and it has a clean answer available — which is exactly why it is worth checking twice. Start with something settled. A point of offense and a point of defense are worth identically the same in win probability. Not roughly. Identically, always, in every league. Every game where one team scores 24 is the game where the other allows 24, so the two curves are mirror images and their slopes match everywhere. There is nothing to find there. So the only question left is which side actually moves . We took 797 NFL clubs with three straight seasons, scored every offense and defense against its own league year, and asked how often a unit jumped a full standard deviation. || METHODS:

headline: He Threw 104. The Box Score Said He Climbed Three Levels. It Did Not.
deck: A 22-year-old in Las Vegas threw seventeen fastballs and not one came in under 101.5. His season line reads Single-A, Double-A, Triple-A — a prospect tearing through the system. The transaction log says something else, and the difference is the whole lesson.
methods: What does one great pitch actually tell you? On September 26 I sat at Las Vegas Ballpark and watched number 44 throw seventeen fastballs. Every one came in at 101.5 or better. The fastest hit 104 . Two questions came with it. How often does a pitcher climb from Single-A to Triple-A in a single season? And does being tall explain throwing that hard? Most people assume the way to answer a question like this is to find other pitchers who did the same thing. That is the natural move and it is the wrong one, because it counts only the people you already noticed. The answer comes from counting everybody who belongs in the calculation — and once we did, it turns out the box score was describing something that never happened. The pitcher was Jarlin Susana, of the Rochester Red Wings. He is listed at six foot six || METHODS:

headline: He Inherited the Roster. He Wins One Game Fewer Than It Should.
deck: Everybody says give him three years. Nobody says what changes in those three years. So we counted the recruiting classes on every roster since 2000. A first-year coach finishes a full win below what his inherited talent should deliver. He climbs out of the hole at almost exactly the rate the roster becomes his.
methods: When does a team stop being the last guy's team? Everybody has an opinion and nobody has a number. So we built one. A college roster is roughly the last four recruiting classes. A class belongs to the new coach only if he signed it. That gives a share with no judgment in it. In his first season none of the roster is his. In his second, a quarter. Then half, then three quarters, and by his fifth season all of it. Then the question becomes answerable. Do coaches beat the talent they were handed, and does the answer change as the talent becomes theirs? First, the exchange rate. One standard deviation of recruiting — roughly the gap between the twentieth-best class in the country and the fiftieth — is worth 0.086 of winning percentage. About one win a season. That is what talent buys. || METHODS:

headline: Twenty-Four Times in a Hundred. This Was One of Them.
deck: Wisconsin fell behind No. 13 Penn State 17–0 and won 24–20. The market had given the Badgers about one chance in four. That is the whole point: a forecast that never lets the underdog through is not cautious, it is broken.
methods: When an underdog wins, was the forecast wrong? Almost everyone says yes without thinking about it. The answer is usually no, and once you see why, you will never hear a pundit the same way again. I am a Wisconsin alumnus. I always root for the Badgers and I almost never bet on them. Somewhere in the fan part of my brain lives the suspicion that my money causes the missed tackle. On September 26 that part of my brain had plenty to work with. Wisconsin fell behind No. 13 Penn State 17–0 , then won 24–20 . Two touchdown passes inside the last 3:31 finished it — an 11-yarder, then a 72-yarder with 1:13 left. The fan's reaction: unbelievable. The statistician's question: how unlikely was it, really? || METHODS:

headline: The Mets Got One Day of Hope. The Cubs Got 126.
deck: Which is worse — a season that was over by June, or one that carried you to October and then died in forty-eight hours? We can measure half of that question. Add up a club's playoff probability across every day it was alive and the Cubs banked 126 days of real hope. The Mets banked one. Both finished with nothing.
methods: Which season would you rather have lived through? One that was settled before the Fourth of July, or one that carried you all the way to October and then ended inside forty-eight hours? You can measure half of that. Since April this paper has stored every club's playoff probability on a weekly grid. Add those probabilities up across the days they cover and you get a number: hope-days . From 15 April to 26 September the Cubs banked 126 of them. The Mets banked one. Most people assume the Cubs fan got the worse deal, because the ending was so much uglier. Look again. The ending was identical. Both clubs finished with no championship, same as twenty-eight others. Everything that actually differed between those two seasons happened in the middle. By the end of this you will have a way to price any season you have sat through — by || METHODS:

headline: The New Coach Recruited None of Them. We Start Counting Anyway.
deck: Whose team is a new coach actually coaching? In his first season, none of it — every recruiting class on the roster was signed by the man he replaced. It is half his by year three and all his by year five. And the research says firing a middling coach makes the team worse .
methods: A new head coach holds up the jersey at the press conference. He talks about culture, discipline, development, a new direction. Then something strange happens: before he has recruited a single freshman or coached a single practice, we start keeping score. So ask the question plainly. Whose team is he actually coaching? That sounds like a philosophical question. It is really a question about counting, and you can answer it. A college roster is roughly the last four recruiting classes. In a coach's first season, every one of those four was signed by the man he replaced. None of it is his. Not some of it — none. By his third season about half the roster is his. By his fifth, all of it. That curve is the whole argument, and notice what it does not do: it never jumps. There is no moment when the team stops being inherited || METHODS: Where these numbers come from Recruiting-class ratings for every FBS program since 2000, standardized within each year, matched to coaching tenures from the same source. A roster is modeled as the four most recent classes; a class is the coach's only if it was signed in or after his arrival year. 2,685 coach-seasons with at least three classes on file, 441 coaches. What it cannot do. Recruiting rankings are a market forecast, not a measurement — they price the same hype a coach's reputation feeds. They ignore transfers entirely, which in the portal era is a widening hole. And attrition is not random: bad teams lose their best players. Every one of those pushes toward crediting a coach for talent he did not develop, so read this as generous to the coach, not harsh. On Friday we take the next step and ask what the inherited year actually costs him, in wins. Sources Adler ES, Berry MJ, Doherty D. Pushing “Reset”: The Conditional Effects of Coaching Replacements on College Football Performance. Social Science Quarterly 2013;94(1):1–28. Humphreys BR, Paul RJ, Weinbach AP. Performance expectations and the tenure of head coaches: Evidence from NCAA football. Research in Economics 2016;70(3):482–492. Johnson J, Matz D, Householder A, Jones J. Is Winning the Only Thing That Matters? An Analysis of Team Sport Head Coach Tenure in the NCAA Power Five and Group of Five Conferences. Journal of Sport Behavior 2023;46(2). NCAA Division I Council, decision of 9 October 2024, notification-of-transfer windows. Argued about something you could not settle? headline: Ninety-One Chances. Six Upsets.
deck: The Athletic reported this week that unranked teams have beaten ranked ones only six times through Week 5, the fewest since 2019. We checked it. The six is right. What nobody printed is the other number: there were more chances at an upset this season than in any year since 2019, and the favorites held anyway.
methods: Is this season really stranger than usual, or does it only look that way? The Athletic reported this week, from TruMedia, that unranked teams have beaten ranked ones just six times through Week 5. That is tied with 2023 for the fewest since 2019. We went and counted. The six is right. We get six too, using the AP Top 25 a team actually carried into the week, and counting only wins by teams that play in the same division. But the comparison is doing the wrong job. “Fewest since 2019” is a rank , and a rank hides the thing you want to know: fewest out of how many tries? Here is the number nobody printed. There were ninety-one chances at an upset this season, more than in any year since 2019 — and the favorites held anyway. By the end of this you will know why that distinction || METHODS: How we counted Every regular-season game from 2019 through week five of 2026 in which one team and only one appeared in that week's AP Top 25, from the CollegeFootballData API. An upset is a win by the unranked side. Winners outside the top division are excluded — one in 2021, Montana over Washington — because The Athletic's framing is about ranked teams losing to their peers. What it cannot do. It cannot tell you why . Fewer upsets could mean stronger favorites, weaker challengers, a softer schedule, or luck. A base rate says this season is unusual; it does not say what made it so. And 91 games is a small enough card that a single wild Saturday would move the number noticeably — two standard deviations is rare, not impossible.

headline: We Said Ninety Wins. They Won Seventy-Four.
deck: We published five forecasts about the Mets this season and the gloomiest one was the most accurate. Every time we talked ourselves up from a bleak number, we got further from the truth. The one thing that survived the year was not a number at all — it was an interval.
methods: How wrong were we about the Mets, and which kind of wrong was it? We published five forecasts this season. They finished 74–88 , fifth in their division and thirteenth of fifteen in the league. Our March number was ninety wins. We missed by sixteen. You are owed the whole list, so here it is. But the interesting failure is not the size of that miss. It is the pattern underneath, and you would probably guess it backwards. Our gloomiest number was our most accurate. Every time we talked ourselves up from a bleak figure, we got further from the truth. By the end of this you will have a cheap test for whether a forecast is being reasoned with or reasoned away. March, before a pitch. We ran a Beta-Binomial on a 3–3 start using a preseason prior of about ninety wins, and concluded six games was noise. That || METHODS: How this was graded, and what is missing Final record from the MLB Stats API: 74–88, 699 runs scored and 731 allowed, a differential of −32. Their Pythagorean expectation was about 77.7 wins, so they finished 3.7 below even that. Every forecast above is quoted from our own published archive, with the issue it ran in. No payroll figure appears in this piece, deliberately. Cost-per-win is the line everyone wants from a season like this. The roughly $375M in circulation is unsourced; it came from working notes, not a named source. Both references we tried refused automated access. Our own rule is two independent confirmations for any number a reader will quote, and we have zero, so it stays out until somebody can stand behind it. What this cannot show. Five forecasts is a tiny sample, and one season cannot tell you whether this paper is systematically optimistic or simply was about one club in one year. The pattern is suggestive and it is not yet evidence. The calibration curve in November, built on every forecast we have published, is the test that can actually answer it.

headline: The Upstarts Won 103 Games.
deck: Milwaukee swept Los Angeles, and it was not an upset: the Brewers had the best record in baseball. What they did was shut the Dodgers down — 11 runs in four games, under three a game, from a lineup that scored almost five all summer.
methods: How did a club of small-market upstarts sweep the stars? It didn’t. Milwaukee won 103 games , more than anyone in baseball. Los Angeles won 100. The better team won the series. You probably heard it the other way: the two-time champions against the plucky Brewers. That framing comes from rings and payroll, not from the season. A reputation is not a prior i you should be using. So here is what you will get from this: the one extra column of arithmetic that tells you whether a team collapsed, or whether October simply did to them what it does to everyone. Then you can watch the World Series the same way. Here is how we got the odds. Treat each game as a coin weighted by the two records. Milwaukee wins a single game about 52 times in 100 — barely better than a flip. That makes the Brewers || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Regular-season records and run totals from the MLB Stats API as of the final day, 27 September. Postseason rates from every completed game through 15 October: eight each for Milwaukee, Los Angeles and Cleveland, six for Tampa Bay. The single-game chance uses the log5 method on the two regular-season records and ignores home field, starting pitchers and injuries. These are tiny samples and the piece does not pretend otherwise. Eight games cannot show that a club has changed; they can only show what has happened so far. The point is not that Milwaukee’s pitching staff became a different staff — it is that the comparison most people make, against reputation, is worse than the comparison against a club’s own season. Nor does this explain WHY October scoring falls. Shorter rotations, better bullpens used earlier, colder weather and tighter umpiring have all been offered. This measures the drop; it does not diagnose it. Argued about something you could not settle? headline: A Coin That Hits Like Ohtani Slumps More Than He Does.
deck: Shohei Ohtani went 3 for 20 in his first six playoff games, with no home runs. Pure chance makes a hitter with his exact talent go that cold about four times a season. The real Ohtani does it about once. Streaks are not something extra on top of chance. They are what chance looks like up close — unless something hurts.
methods: Is Shohei Ohtani in a slump, or is this just baseball? Here is the answer, with its number. His first six playoff games: 24 trips to the plate, 3 hits, 7 strikeouts, no homers. A hitter with his talent, if every at-bat were a fair coin, would have a stretch that cold about four times a year. The real Ohtani has had about one a year since 2021. That should surprise you. Most people think a slump is something added to chance — a cold hand, a lost swing, nerves. The numbers say the opposite. Chance makes more slumps than he does. By the end of this you will have a two-question test for any slump you hear about on the broadcast. You have heard of the hot hand: the shooter who cannot miss. In 1985, Thomas Gilovich and two colleagues looked at basketball shots and found streaks no longer || METHODS:

headline: The Bills and Notre Dame Will Be Champions. Book It. We Are Probably Wrong.
deck: Our call: the Bills win the Super Bowl and Notre Dame wins the national title. Our own simulations make the Bills the single likeliest champion in the NFL and Notre Dame the second likeliest in college. Even so, the Bills win it about 15 times in 100 and Notre Dame about 16. Both at once: about 1 season in 40. We believe it. We do not know it. This piece is about the difference.
methods: How sure should you be when you say “book it”? Here is our answer, with its number. We are picking the Bills and Notre Dame, and our own models agree they are among the best bets on the board. The Bills are the NFL’s likeliest champion at about 15%. Notre Dame is college football’s second likeliest at about 16%. That should stop you. Most people think the favorite is likely to win. In a playoff, the favorite is the best single bet and still loses most of the time. It is one team against the whole field. By the end of this you will be able to tell, in your own head, what you believe from what you know. We said Notre Dame in July. Issue #109 called the 2026 national title for the Irish, dated so you could hold us to it. Six games later they are 6–0. They || METHODS:

headline: Who Did They Even Play?
deck: Kirk Herbstreit calls Notre Dame’s schedule an embarrassment. By Sunday’s poll the Irish have three ranked opponents, including No. 1 Miami and No. 2 BYU, which beat them Saturday. A week ago, the same schedule looked easier. But nobody can know how hard a schedule was until January: a third of the ranked teams the last twelve champions beat were unranked in August.
methods: How hard is Notre Dame’s schedule — and can anybody know yet? On Friday, Kirk Herbstreit called it “an embarrassment,” with two real tests: BYU and Miami. By Sunday’s AP poll it has three: No. 1 Miami, No. 2 BYU and No. 23 SMU . BYU beat the Irish 28–24 on Saturday. That is as many as Indiana, last year’s champion, and one fewer than Georgia. Ohio State has five; Texas has six. Now watch the schedule move without a single game changing. A week ago those same three teams were No. 8, No. 3 and No. 24. One Saturday later, two of them are the top two teams in the country. Notre Dame did not add anybody. The belief about who they play just went up. Most people assume a schedule’s strength is a fact, fixed the day it is printed. The polls say otherwise. So he is half || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do AP Top 25 polls and game schedules from CollegeFootballData. “August” is the preseason poll; “the end” is the final poll after the playoff; 2026 figures use the poll of 18 October, after Notre Dame lost at BYU. A ranked opponent is any team in the Top 25 at that moment. Regular season only, conference title games included. Champions are taken from each season’s title game. Top 25 is a hard edge. No. 26 does not count and No. 25 does; SMU, at No. 23, is one bad week from vanishing. A champion that beats everybody also drags its opponents’ final rankings down, so the “after” counts run a little low for the very best teams. And a poll is a vote, not a model: it leans on record and brand. It is the public’s belief, which is the thing being argued about. Updated October 19: the first version of this issue used the October 11 poll and went out before we added Saturday’s result. It called Georgia No. 1; Georgia lost to Auburn and is now No. 5. The numbers above use Sunday’s poll. Argued about something you could not settle? headline: We Bet Runs Go Up After a Pitching Change. They Do — Before It.
deck: Innings with a pitching change score about five times as many runs as innings without one. It looks like proof that the bullpen blew it. It is not. Once the new pitcher arrives, he gives up almost exactly what the situation was already worth. The runs cause the change.
methods: Do hitters feast after a pitching change? Our editor bet they do, at least in the 4th, 5th and 6th innings, before the best relievers come in. In the 8th and 9th, he guessed, the bullpen wins. We checked every play from five seasons, 2021 through 2025. In the 6th inning, an inning with a pitching change averages 1.3 runs . An inning without one averages 0.28 . That is nearly five times as many. Most people would read that as proof that changes go badly. Here is the surprise: watch what happens after the new pitcher arrives. He walks into runners and outs he did not create. That spot is worth 0.67 runs on average. He gives up 0.66 . The big inning was already happening. Managers pull pitchers who are getting hit. The runs cause the change, not the other way around. By the end of this you || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Every regular-season play from 2021 to 2025, from Retrosheet. A mid-inning change compares the runs scored from the change to the end of the inning with the expected runs for the runners and outs at that moment, built from the same five seasons. A start-of-inning change compares the new pitcher's inning with innings where the same pitcher came back out. The 9th inning uses top halves only, because walk-offs cut the bottom halves short. Position players pitching are left out. As a check, our parsed run totals matched MLB's official team totals in all eight seasons we tested. The yardstick is an average pitcher, not the one who was pulled. Nobody can see what would have happened if the manager had left him in. And late in a game, "the same pitcher continuing" is often a starter cruising or a reliever mopping up a blowout, which makes that group a little odd. Adjusting for the batting order and the score barely moves the 9th-inning result. The information used here was obtained free of charge from and is copyrighted by Retrosheet. headline: Nearly 200 Bad Teams Changed Coaches. One Did This.
deck: A new coach is supposed to be a fresh start. Across twenty seasons, bad college teams that changed coaches improved by about 3 points a year later. Teams that kept their coach improved by about the same. Indiana in 2024 improved by 28, more than any team in twenty years.
methods: How fast can a new coach turn a bad team around? Usually, not fast at all. We looked at 194 bad teams in major college football that changed head coaches between 2006 and 2025. On average they got about 3 points better the next year. Bad teams that kept their coach also got about 3 points better. That should surprise you. The new coach is supposed to be the reason things change. Mostly, he is not. Bad teams bounce back a little no matter who is in charge. Then there is Indiana. In 2024, its first year under Curt Cignetti, it got 28 points better. By the end, you will know what to compare the next big hire to, and why one Indiana should not fool you about the rest. We measure teams with SP+, a power rating built by Bill Connelly. It is counted in points: how many points || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Every major college (FBS) team that played FBS football two years in a row, 2005–06 through 2024–25: 2,512 team-seasons, 2,509 with an SP+ rating. A “bad team” is in the bottom third of SP+ that year; Indiana in 2023 was 42nd from the bottom of 133. A coaching change means the coach who led the most games was different from the year before. Records, ratings, coaches and transfers come from CollegeFootballData. Indiana’s records were checked against ESPN. Limits. SP+ comes from one source, and its scale drifts a little across eras. The 2020 season was shortened by COVID. Coach histories before James Madison joined FBS in 2022 come from general records, not the same feed. UCLA’s 2026 numbers are through October 18 and will move. We cannot see what Indiana would have done without Cignetti, so “the coach did it” is still a guess, just a much better one than usual. Argued about something you could not settle? headline: The Rays Were Supposed to Win 79 Games.
deck: They won 98, and they open the World Series against Milwaukee on Friday. Only 14 teams since 1999 beat their forecast by more. Here is the odd part: that is what champions look like. 22 of the last 25 beat theirs.
methods: What makes a team a surprise? Not being good. The Dodgers won 100 games and surprised nobody. A surprise is the gap between what you expected and what you got. So to measure one, you need to say out loud what you expected. Here is ours, and you can do it on a napkin. Take last year’s wins, and give back half the distance from 81. A 97-win team should win about 89. A 65-win team should win about 73. We fit that rule on 750 team-seasons since 1999, and it misses by about 10 wins either way. One honest note before we use it. We did not print this forecast in March; we built it this week. So we kept it simple enough that you can check it yourself, with no knobs for us to turn after the fact. The Rays went 77–85 in 2025. The rule said about || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do The forecast is a straight line fit to every pair of back-to-back seasons from 1999 to 2025, skipping 2020: this year’s winning share = 0.23 + 0.55 × last year’s. In wins, that is about 37 + 0.55 × last year’s wins. The typical miss is 10 wins. Records come from the MLB Stats API and were checked against ESPN. Champions come from the same postseason feed. This is a deliberately simple forecast. It knows nothing about trades, injuries or free agents, so real projection systems beat it. That is the point: it is the “reasonable fan” baseline, and anyone can check it. Payrolls are approximate and differ by source. The Rays figure is from Spotrac and ESPN reporting, and the Brewers figure is from Spotrac and team-beat reporting. The information used here was obtained free of charge from and is copyrighted by Retrosheet. Interested parties may contact Retrosheet at www.retrosheet.org . headline: The Mets Let Him Go. Then He Got Worse. Then He Won the Pennant.
deck: For four starts in Tampa his ERA was 7.2. Then came ten outings with five earned runs, an ALCS MVP, and a World Series against the team that traded him to the Mets. The devil did not move him. August did.
methods: Ah yes. The Mets. Did the Mets trade away a great pitcher, or did they trade away a bad month? Every Mets fan asked it this week, the way Mets fans ask everything. Who did we anger? What do they want? Some even had a theory: the ball through Buckner’s legs. We went through every outing he made this year, so here is the answer, with its number: the trade fixed nothing. In his first four starts as a Ray, Freddy Peralta gave up 17 earned runs in 21 innings. That is worse than anything he did in Queens. The magic, such as it is, started three weeks later and has lasted ten outings. That is the surprise. You were told a story about a change of scenery. The scenery changed, and for a month he got worse. By the end of this you will know what to say the || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Every 2026 outing is from the MLB Stats API game logs, regular season and postseason. His Mets and Rays lines were checked against the same feed’s season splits. The trades and the return are from the MLB transaction log and Associated Press reporting. The ALCS MVP is from MLB’s awards record. “Ball in play” is hits minus home runs, divided by batters faced minus strikeouts, walks, hit batters and home runs. That is close to the usual definition, not identical. What this cannot tell you: whether Tampa changed something real, like a pitch mix or a grip, that a box score cannot see. The fewer walks and home runs hint that they may have. Nor can it say what he would have done in New York in September. Nobody gets to see that game. Argued about something you could not settle? headline: Notre Dame Got a Week Off. It Bought About One Point.
deck: Across more than 13,000 college games since 2005, a bye added about one point to a team’s final margin. Home field is worth three. And for a team coming off a loss, like the Irish, the week off was worth close to nothing.
methods: Do bye weeks help? You hear it every fall. A team gets a week off. It heals, it studies film, and it comes back sharp. Notre Dame lost at BYU, 28–24. It sat out last Saturday, and it plays Navy this Saturday. So did the rest help? Here is the answer, with its number. A bye adds about one point. We checked more than 13,000 games between major-college teams since 2005. The rested team did about one point better than its rating said it should. Home field, by comparison, is worth about three. That should surprise you a little. Most fans talk about the bye like a weapon. It is a nudge. And here is the part that matters for the Irish: teams coming off a loss got almost none of it. By the end of this, you will be able to price a week off yourself. You will also || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do College: every regular-season game between two major-college (FBS) teams from 2005 to 2025, from CollegeFootballData. A “bye” means 12 to 16 days since the team’s last game; a normal week is 6 to 9. Season openers and longer gaps were left out. Strength is the pregame Elo rating; we checked it against each team’s season margin with that game removed. Short weeks and home field were accounted for. NFL: every regular-season game from 1999 to 2025, from nflverse, with rest days as that data records them. A bye means 13 or more days of rest. What it cannot tell you: schedule makers choose where byes go, so a bye is not a coin flip. We cannot see injuries, so we cannot say whether rest helps a hurt team more than a healthy one. And the after-a-loss split is one of several cuts we looked at; treat it as a lead, not a finding. Argued about something you could not settle? headline: One in Seven Coaches Goes Home to Coach. Home Gives Them No Edge.
deck: Since 1970, major-college programs have hired a former player as head coach 181 times. Those coaches won 47% of their games. Every other coach at those same schools won 46%. The real story is what they were handed.
methods: Chuck Amato died on October 19. He was 80. He played linebacker at NC State in the 1960s, spent years as an assistant elsewhere, and came home to run the program in 2000. His teams went 49–37 over seven seasons. The 2002 team went 11–3, which the Associated Press notes is still the only double-digit-win season in school history. His death raised a question we could count. Does a coach do better at the school he played for? Here is the answer, with its number: no. Since 1970, 181 of about 1,345 major-college head coaching hires had played at the school. That is about one in seven, and it has held in every decade. They won 47% of their games. Every other coach at the same schools won 46%. That should surprise you, because both of the usual stories predict a gap. One says a former player knows the place, || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Records: every head coach at a major-college (FBS) program from 1970 to 2025, season by season, from CollegeFootballData. A tenure is an unbroken run at one school. “Before he arrived” is the team’s record over the five prior seasons; tenures without five prior major-college seasons were left out of that comparison. Who “played there”: taken from each coach’s Wikipedia playing history. That is not a primary source, so a few may be wrong. A handful of coaches who attended a school without playing were counted as outsiders. The comparison covers wins and losses only. What it cannot tell you: this is observational. We cannot see recruiting, budgets, or why a school chose its man. The adjusted gap of about two points has a likely range that includes zero. Argued about something you could not settle? headline: The Best Hitter in Baseball Finished Fifth in Runs Batted In.
deck: In 2025 Salvador Perez and Carlos Correa hit almost alike. Perez drove in 100 runs; Correa drove in 52. Most people assume RBI measure the hitter. They also measure the men batting ahead of him and his manager — and only one of those is him.
methods: What does a run batted in actually tell you? It is the oldest argument-winner in baseball. “He drove in 120 runs” ends a lot of bar fights. Here is the answer, with its number. We took the 145 men who played every day in 2025. How well each one hit explains only 43% of the spread in their RBI. Add one more fact — how often he came to bat with runners on base — plus his power, and you can explain nearly 90%. That should bother you a little. Most fans read RBI as a hitter’s skill, maybe even his nerve. A big part of it is a seat at the table: who is on base when he walks up. By the end of this you will know how to read an RBI total. You will also have a new idea, one this whole series is built on: the || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Data: the 145 hitters who qualified for the 2025 batting title, from the MLB Stats API: season totals plus the “runners on” and “scoring position” splits. Totals for traded players are combined. Perez and Correa were checked against ESPN; the RBI leaders against ESPN and MLB.com. The 43% and the nearly 90%: simple regressions across the 145 hitters. OPS alone explains 43% of the variation in RBI. Home runs plus plate appearances with runners on explains 88%; slugging plus those plate appearances, 84%. What it cannot tell you: plate appearances with runners on is a rough count of chances; it does not say how many runners, or where they stood. One season of qualified hitters leaves out part-timers. And this says nothing about whether “clutch” is real — that question gets its own issue. Argued about something you could not settle? headline: Two in Three Home Run Hitters Do It Again. Most Doubles Hitters Don’t.
deck: Of the regular hitters in the top third for home runs one season, 67% were back in the top third the next. For doubles, 45%. Chance alone would keep 33%. Most people assume homers and doubles both measure power. They barely move together.
methods: Is a home run a clean sign of power? Ask any fan who the power hitters are and you will get a list of home run totals. So we checked whether that list means anything a year later. Here is the answer, with its number. We took every regular hitter in back-to-back seasons from 1997 to 2025. Of the men in the top third for home runs, two in three were still there the next year. For doubles, fewer than half. If the numbers were pure luck, one in three would stay. The surprise is in the doubles. You would think the double and the homer are cousins, two kinds of extra-base hit, both “power.” Across these seasons, a hitter’s home run rate told you almost nothing about his doubles rate. By the end of this, you will know which of the two to trust, and why. This is the || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Data: every hitter who qualified for the batting title from 1997 to 2025, from the MLB Stats API. We paired each hitter’s season with his next one when he qualified in both, which gives 2,516 pairs. Pairs that touch the 60-game 2020 season are left out. Each stat is per plate appearance; “top third” is set within each season. Other measures: the season-to-season correlation tells the same story: home run rate 0.75, batting average 0.51, doubles rate 0.33. Within a season, home run rate and doubles rate correlate at 0.10. The 1998 figures were checked against the same feed’s league leaders. What it cannot tell you: only hitters who kept a full-time job in both years are counted, so slumps that cost a man his job drop out. That flatters every stat a little, though not one more than another. Parks and the ball change over time, and we did not adjust for either. Argued about something you could not settle? headline: Navy Beats the Spread Two Times in Three. It Rarely Beats the Team.
deck: Notre Dame is a 30.5-point favorite over Navy on Saturday. The betting market gives Navy about one chance in 21 to win the game. But since 2013, when Navy has been a big underdog, it has lost by less than the line 13 times in 20. The option keeps games close. It almost never wins them.
methods: Does Navy have a chance on Saturday? Notre Dame comes off a bye, a loss at BYU still stinging. Navy is 2–5 and gave up 49 points to North Texas last week. They meet at noon in Foxborough, Massachusetts. Here is the answer, with its number. The betting market makes Navy about a 1-in-21 shot to win the game outright. The record is even harsher: since 2013, underdogs of 28 to 35 points have won 17 times in 710 tries, about 1 in 42. But that is the wrong question to ask about Navy, and the surprise is in the right one. You would think the market has Navy figured out; it sees the Midshipmen every year. Yet when Army, Navy or Air Force has been a two-touchdown underdog, the academy has beaten the spread 31 times in 47. By the end of this, you will know why a team || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Lines and results: every regular-season game with a betting line from 2013 to 2025 in CollegeFootballData (12,948 games), using the consensus line when present and the median of the books otherwise. Our line data starts in 2013 and misses some games, including the 2016 Navy–Notre Dame game; the series record comes from CollegeFootballData’s full head-to-head history. Saturday’s line is DraftKings and Bovada as of October 29; the 1-in-21 is DraftKings’ moneyline, Navy +2000, which Scores and Odds and Bleacher Nation also list. “Expected” wins come from how often all underdogs won at the same spread, in three-point bands. Run share is rushing attempts divided by all plays. What it cannot tell you: the academy numbers rest on 47 games, and the 24-point group on ten. We did not count drives directly; the short-game explanation fits the pattern but is not proven by it. And the line can move before Saturday. Argued about something you could not settle? headline: Allow 28 Points and Even Tom Brady Loses Six in Ten.
deck: Across 13,934 NFL starts since 1999, quarterbacks whose defense held the other team under 17 points won 86% of the time. When the defense gave up 28 or more, they won 16%. Most people assume a quarterback’s record measures the quarterback. A big piece of it measures the men he never shares the field with.
methods: Is a quarterback’s win-loss record really his? You hear it every Sunday. “He just wins.” “Look at his record as a starter.” No stat in football ends more arguments. Here is the answer, with its number. We took every regular-season start from 1999 to 2025, 13,934 of them. When the defense held the other team under 17 points, the quarterback’s team won 86% of the time. When it gave up 28 or more, 16%. The quarterback was the same kind of player in both piles. The defense was not. That should bother you a little, because the quarterback never plays a snap of defense. By the end of this you will know how to read a quarterback’s record, and you will see the same lesson the first issue of this series found in baseball’s runs batted in: a team stat with one man’s name on it. There is no official || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Data: every NFL regular-season game from 1999 to 2025 in the nflverse game records, which list each team’s quarterback and the final score: 13,934 starts. Ties count as half a win. Tom Brady’s 23 wins in 61 games when his defense allowed 28 or more were checked against ESPN’s scores. A data trap we hit: the quarterback listed for a game is not always the man who started it. In one 2007 Colts game, Peyton Manning started and left early, and the records list his backup. A handful of such games will not move rates built on thousands of starts, but it is why we did not quote any one quarterback’s perfect record. What it cannot tell you: points allowed is not purely the defense — a quarterback who throws an interception for a touchdown, or keeps his defense off the field, changes it. The season-to-season comparison is a correlation, not a controlled test. Across team seasons, points scored explains 55% of the spread in winning percentage and points allowed 44%; the quarterback shapes the first far more than the second. headline: A Thousand Games In, It Still Doesn’t Even Out
deck: Seventy-four college football programs have played at least 1,000 games. If every game were a coin flip, nearly all of them would sit close to .500 by now. Only 20 do. The other 54 are too good or too bad, for too long, to be luck. You can watch it happen, every program from 1869 on, on our new page.
methods: Is a program’s all-time record skill, or could luck have done it? Here is the answer, with its number. Seventy-four programs have played 1,000 or more major games. Luck could explain the records of 20. For the other 54, it can’t. That should surprise you, because you have heard the opposite your whole life: it all evens out. Over enough games, people figure, the bad bounces cancel the good ones and everybody drifts toward average. For a coin, that is true. For a football program, it mostly isn’t. By the end you will be able to look at any record and ask the one question that tells you how much luck is in it. How many games? Start with the picture, because it does the arguing for us. Open Every Program Since 1869 and press play. Each dot is one program. It moves right as the program plays more games, || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Records: James Howell’s College Football Historical Scores, 304 programs and 14,408 seasons from 1869 to 2025. These are results as played on the field: vacated wins stay in, so Alabama is 999–319–42 here against an official 985–345–43. Howell counts only the seasons a program played at the major-college level, so Notre Dame enters in 1899 and Yale leaves after 1981. Totals will not match a school’s own record book. Checked against CollegeFootballData for 2005–2025: 31,525 of 31,553 regular-season games match to the exact score, and none of the rest changes who won. Yale’s 1872–1981 record differs from Sports-Reference’s by one game. The funnel is .500 plus or minus two standard deviations of a fair coin, one over the square root of the games played. A tie counts as half a win. Leaving ties out moves no program across the line at 1,000 games. What it cannot tell you: a coin is the simplest kind of luck. Real luck in football is lumpier (injuries, schedules, a bad decade), so the funnel is a floor, not a full account. And it says nothing about why a program was good, only that it was. headline: Nobody Plays Better With Their Back to the Wall
deck: Since 1995, teams one loss from elimination in a best-of-seven won 58 of 125 of those games, 46%. Teams that survived one won the next game 30 times in 58, about half. A coin flipped once a game would have called the 3–1 series almost exactly.
methods: When a team is one loss from going home, does it play better? You have heard the line all week: the Rays are dangerous now, because they have nothing to lose. So we counted. Here is the answer, with its number. Since 1995, a team facing elimination in a best-of-seven series has won 58 of 125 of those games, or 46%. That is a little worse than a coin, which fits, because the team that is behind is usually the weaker team. The surprise is how little is left over. Most fans believe some teams have a gift for the comeback; you can probably name one. But a team that just survived an elimination game won the next one only 30 times in 58. No lift from the escape, no momentum. By the end of this, you will be able to read a 3–1 series the way the numbers do, || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Data: every playoff game from 1995 to 2025 in the MLB Stats API, grouped into series. Ninety-two series were best-of-seven, meaning one team reached four wins; one series that would not sort cleanly was left out. An elimination game is one where exactly one team has three wins; Game 7, where both do, is left out. That gives 125 elimination games. “Survived one” means the team facing elimination won, and we scored its very next game. Checks: the seven comebacks from 3–1 down in this window (1996 Braves, 2003 Marlins, 2004 Red Sox, 2007 Red Sox, 2012 Giants, 2016 Cubs, 2020 Dodgers) match Wikipedia’s list, team for team. The 2004 Red Sox count because they trailed 3–1 after four games, on the way back from 0–3. The ranges on the chart are 95% Wilson intervals: 38 to 55% for elimination games, 39 to 64% for the next game, 73 to 93% for 3–1 leaders. What it cannot tell you: a coin treats both teams as equal, and they are not; the trailing team is usually weaker, and home field shifts the odds a few points. A model with team strength would move each dash a little. It would not move it far, and 125 games cannot see an effect smaller than about eight points either way. The 2026 Series is not in the data; the Rays won one elimination game and lost the next, a perfectly ordinary week. Argued about something you could not settle? headline: Nine Traded Stars in Ten Fall Short. Four Trades in Five Do Not.
deck: Gene asked how many blockbuster trades pan out. We checked 474 baseball trades for a star since 1980. Only 43 stars played as well for their new team as they had before. Yet the team that got the star lost the trade only about one time in five.
methods: How many blockbuster trades actually pan out? Gene asked us that, and it is a better question than it sounds, because “pan out” means two different things. Here is the answer, with its number. We found 474 baseball trades for a star since 1980. Only 43 of those stars played as well for the new team as they had in their last three years. But the team that got him clearly lost the trade only 86 times , fewer than one in five. That is the surprise. You would expect a star who disappoints to mean a trade that failed. Usually it does not. By the end, you will know what to expect when your team lands a star. You will also know which football deal to fear before the trade deadline on Tuesday, November 10. A blockbuster , for us, is a trade that sends away a player who || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Baseball: every trade between big-league clubs in Retrosheet’s transaction file, 1980 to 2021, where its records end. A blockbuster sent a player with at least 8 Baseball-Reference WAR over the three prior seasons: 474 trades. Each player’s WAR counts only for the team that received him, over the next three seasons; a player who never played for them counts zero. “Matched his past” means at least his prior pace, adjusted for games in short seasons. The ranges: 9.1% matched (6.8 to 12%); won 45% (41 to 50%), even 37% (32 to 41%), lost 18% (15 to 22%). Football: nflverse’s trade file with Pro Football Reference Approximate Value, which stops in 2021, so trades run 2005 to 2019. Only 35 trades sent a veteran with 30+ AV in three seasons, so the football ranges are wide: won 40% (26 to 56%), lost 26% (14 to 42%). The 100 pick trades had no veteran over 24 AV; the side with the best first-rounder lost 53% (43 to 62%). Picks are valued by the player drafted with them. Choices that move the answer: the line for “even” matters. At 1 WAR, the star’s team wins 53% of baseball deals; at 4 WAR, it wins 28% and 58% come out even. Over six seasons instead of three, the star’s team still wins 41% and loses 26%. Our checks of famous deals (Santana, Griffey, Halladay, Stanton, Mack, Ramsey, Revis, Cutler) matched the record. What it cannot tell you: WAR and Approximate Value are rough, and Approximate Value is roughest for linemen. Prospects who reached the majors after 2022 count zero here, which slightly favors the star’s side in the latest trades. And “won the trade” ignores money: a team that took on a big contract may

headline: The Last Time Owners Asked for a Cap, Nobody Won the World Series
deck: Twelve times, a big league has fought over a new pay system like a cap. Ten of those fights stopped the games, and seven cost real games. Baseball’s owners want a cap now. History puts a lockout at about five chances in six, and lost games next spring at about one in three.
methods: Will there be baseball on Opening Day? The players’ labor deal runs out at midnight on December 1. The owners want a hard salary cap, and the union has said no to any cap at all. So we counted every time this has happened before. Here is the answer, with its number. Across baseball, football, basketball and hockey, a league has fought over a whole new pay system 12 times . Ten ended in a strike or a lockout. Seven cost regular-season games. The surprise is how long sports stoppages last. The typical big American strike is over in about nine days. Sports ones run for months, and the reason tells you exactly which date to watch this winter. Most labor talks are haggling inside a system both sides already accept: a higher minimum salary, a different tax line. We sorted all 33 negotiations since 1967 that ran to a || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Negotiations: every labor agreement in MLB, the NFL, the NBA and the NHL from 1967 that expired or was reopened, including the ones that ended in a handshake: 33 in all, 21 with a stoppage. First-ever agreements, court settlements and early extensions are left out. We could not date some NBA agreements of the 1970s or NHL agreements before 1991; none is known to have had a stoppage, so leaving them out makes stoppages look a little more common, not less. The kind of fight: we called it a new-system fight when one side demanded a cap, a fixed revenue split, or the end of free-agency limits. That sorting was done by us, knowing how each fight ended, which is a weakness; three cases were close calls, and flipping them moves the 83% to 92% and the 52% to 45%. The ranges (95%): stoppage in a new-system fight 55% to 95%; games lost 32% to 81%. Our forecast’s ranges: still going at day 75, 17% to 66%; games lost, 12% to 59%; past 232 days, 3% to 42%. Numbers: stoppage lengths are counted from the first day stopped to the day of the deal. Attendance is per game, from the Lahman baseball database, and matches MLB’s own totals to within half a percent. Sources disagree on games lost in 1994–95 (938 or 948); the schedule itself gives 920, and we use none of those here. The $12 billion is Forbes’s estimate of team revenue, reported by CBS Sports and others. The large-strike record is the Bureau of Labor Statistics list of stoppages with 1,000 or more workers. What it cannot tell you: the past cannot see this year’s people or this year’s money. Fights in one league are not independent of

headline: Outliving the Owner Won’t Save You. Ask the Raiders.
deck: Since 1980, 28 NFL owners have died while running their teams. Eighteen of those teams are still in the family. A Jets fan of 60 will very likely outlive Woody Johnson, and still has worse than even odds of seeing the Jets leave the Johnsons.
methods: Will you outlive your team’s owner, and would it help? Every long-suffering fan has done this grim little sum. Woody Johnson is 79. A Jets fan of 60 thinks: I’ve got him by nineteen years. Just wait. Here is the answer, with its number. Since 1980, 28 NFL owners have died while still in charge. Eighteen of those teams never left the family. Only three were sold within a year. That is the surprise: the fan is betting on the wrong event. The owner dying is close to a sure thing. The team leaving the family is a coin flip. By the end, you will know the difference, and why the Raiders already learned it. Al Davis ran the Raiders as owner and general manager for nearly forty years. He won three Super Bowls, then spent most of his last decade losing, and a lot of Raiders fans quietly did || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Owners: every change of controlling ownership of an NFL team from 1980 to October 31, 2026, 67 in all, each confirmed by two independent sources where we could (59 of 67). Twenty-eight owners died in control: 18 teams stayed in the family, 10 were sold, 3 within a year and 8 within five. Among deaths with five years of follow-up, 32% were sold within five years. Living owners sold at about 1.8% a year (22 sales over 1,300 franchise-years). Sources include AP, ESPN, the NFL and the teams; the Seahawks’ $9.6 billion sale was approved on August 26, 2026. Lifetimes: the Social Security Administration’s 2023 period life table for men. Woody Johnson was born in 1947; his age is confirmed by CBS and ESPN. The national table gives a man of 79 a median of 8.3 more years. The wealth adjustment cuts the death rate at every age by the same share, enough to match the life expectancy that Chetty and colleagues (JAMA, 2016) found for the richest 1% of men at age 40, 87.3 years; it gives a median of 13. The fan is a man on the national table; a woman fan lives longer, so her odds are better. The ranges (90%): team leaves the family in the fan’s lifetime: fan of 30, 56 to 76%; fan of 45, 46 to 68%; fan of 60, 35 to 56%. With the wealth adjustment, 33 to 52% for the fan of 60. What it cannot tell you: the Johnsons are not an average family, and history is a base rate, not a plan. A reported sale, a will that orders one, or a change in the family would move these numbers more than any table. Lifetimes are treated as independent, and

headline: Somebody Had to Be Last. It Didn’t Have to Be Seattle.
deck: Four clubs have never won a World Series, and one of them, Seattle, has never played in one. Pure luck would leave about three clubs without a title, so the list is ordinary. Seattle’s wait is not: in 50 seasons it has reached the playoffs 6 times, where an equal draw would send it 13.
methods: Is it just bad luck that some clubs never win a World Series? On October 28 the Brewers won their first, and left a short list. Four clubs are still on it: the Mariners, the Padres, the Rays and the Rockies. The Mariners have never even played in one. Here is the answer, with its number. Suppose you pulled a champion out of a hat every year since 1903, with every club getting the same chance. The hat would leave about three of today’s 30 clubs without a title. Four or more happens 23 times in 100. So the list itself is ordinary luck. That is the surprise: luck explains the list, but not who is on it. Seattle has reached the playoffs 6 times in 50 seasons. The hat would have sent it 13 times. By the end, you will be able to tell a curse from a team || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Data: the Lahman Baseball Database, Teams table, American and National Leagues, 1903–2025. The 2026 season is from the MLB Stats API: final standings and postseason results (the Brewers beat the Rays 4–1, final game October 28). Seattle’s six postseason runs were checked series by series against MLB’s game feed. Code: scripts/ws_droughts.py ; data in data/ws-droughts/ . The hat: each season, every club in a league has the same chance at its pennant (1 divided by the number of clubs in that league), and every club in the majors the same chance at the title. There was no World Series in 1904 or 1994. Clubs are counted from 1903 or their first season, so older pennants (the Dodgers’ and Giants’ 1890s flags, for instance) are left out. 100,000 simulated histories. Once in: each actual playoff trip is treated as an equal draw among that league’s playoff clubs that year. Wild-card game losers from 2012 to 2021 count as trips, which flatters them a little. What it cannot do: the hat is a yardstick, not a model of baseball. Real clubs are not equal, and the playoff format has changed several times. The coin comparison for Seattle’s record treats games as independent flips, which they are not quite; the gap is wide enough that this does not change the answer. headline: Does Working for a Great Coach Make You Better?
deck: Assistants of coaches who won 70% of their games go on to win 51 of every 100 in their first head job. Everyone else wins 46. But most of that gap was there before they arrived: they get handed better programs. What is left is small, less than half a win a season, and it may be nothing.
methods: Does working for a great coach make you a better coach? Every time a school hires a coordinator, you hear about his coaching tree. He learned under Saban. He came off the Bowden staff. The idea is that greatness rubs off. Here is the answer, with its number. We found 508 coaches who got their first major-college head job since 1970, and the head coach each one worked for just before. The 203 whose boss had won 70% of his games or more went on to win 51 of every 100 games in the new job. The rest won 46 . That looks like proof, and here is the surprise. Most of that 5-game gap was there before they showed up. The schools that hired a great coach’s assistant had already been winning 52 of 100. The schools that hired everyone else had been winning 48. By the end, you || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Data: head-coach records for every major-college (FBS) program from CollegeFootballData. For each coach whose first FBS head job began 1970–2025 (856 in all), the job he held just before came from the coaching list in his Wikipedia biography, checked against the article’s own text. 93% matched at high confidence, and a hand check of 15 at random found no errors. The boss is the head coach at that school in the assistant’s last season there. The sample: 508 coaches with a high-confidence prior job, a known boss record, and five seasons of program history; interim head coaches are left out. A “great coach” won 70% or more while the assistant was on staff. Cuts at 65% and 75% give the same answer. Two ways to be fair: subtracting the program’s past gives +1.2 games in 100 (95% range −2.1 to +4.4). Fitting the program’s past as a line gives +3.5 (+0.6 to +6.4); only about 43% of a program’s past carries into the new coach’s record, so subtracting all of it penalizes coaches who inherit strong programs. When two groups start in different places, those two methods can disagree; statisticians call it Lord’s paradox. We report both. What it cannot do: it sees only assistants who were hired, which is survivorship : the ones nobody hired are not here to count against a tree. It counts only the job held right before the first head job, so a coach who left Saban and made two more stops is not in Saban’s tree. Code: scripts/coach_tree.py . headline: Was He Just Propped Up by His Staff?
deck: When a head coach’s assistant leaves to run his own program, fans brace for the drop, and it comes: those teams slip 3.5 games in 100 the next year. But that is the slide every great season brings. Compared with teams that had just as good a year, the raided teams win more over the next three seasons, 75 of 100 against 69.
methods: When a head coach loses his best assistants, does his team fall apart? It is one of the oldest stories in college football. A coach wins big. Other schools hire away his coordinators. A few years later the wins dry up, and people say he was propped up by his staff all along. Here is the answer, with its number. We checked every major-college head coach from 1969 to 2024: 4,269 seasons. In 236 of them, an assistant left to take his first head job. The next year those teams did slip, by 3.5 games in 100. Teams that lost no one slipped 0.6. Now the surprise. The slip has nothing to do with the raid. Raids come after big seasons, and every big season is followed by a slide. Compare the raided teams with teams that had just as good a year, and the raided teams won more over || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Data: head-coach records for every major-college (FBS) program from CollegeFootballData, and the prior jobs of 856 first-time FBS head coaches from the study behind our earlier piece (Wikipedia coaching lists checked against article text; 93% high confidence). A raid: an assistant (coordinator or position coach) on the head coach’s staff whose next job, within a year, was his first FBS head job. We count it against the head coach’s season that the assistant finished. 454 such departures; 218 could not be used, mostly because the head coach left too, so there is no “after” to measure. The comparison: 4,269 head-coach seasons with at least one season before it and one after at the same school. The model predicts the next season (or the next three) from this season and the average of up to three before it, plus whether a raid happened. Next season: +2.1 games in 100 (95% range −0.2 to +4.5). Next three seasons: +3.3 (+1.2 to +5.4), from 2,410 seasons with three to follow. The 75%-or-better comparison uses 79 raided seasons and 607 others. What it cannot do: it only sees assistants who left for their first FBS head job. A coordinator who went to the NFL, like Joe Brady, or to the same job somewhere else, is invisible here, and so is who replaced him. A raid followed by a great replacement hire looks the same as no raid. Code: scripts/coach_drain.py . Argued about something you could not settle?
