headline: What Did the Bears Really Give Up for Simmons?
deck: Two first-round picks near the end of the round usually become about seven seasons of starters. A defensive tackle like Jeffery Simmons, at 29, usually has two or three left. Chicago did not trade one player for two. It traded later seasons for sooner, better ones.
methods: What did the Bears really give up for Jeffery Simmons? On October 29, Chicago sent its next two first-round picks to Tennessee for him. In his first game he had a sack and six tackles, and the Bears won 34–17 at Seattle. Everyone is grading the trade on this season. You should grade it on the next seven. Here is the answer, with its number. Defensive tackles who looked like Simmons at 28 started about 2.5 more seasons from 29 to 32. Two picks late in the first round started about 7 seasons between them in the years Chicago gave up. Most people see one star for two maybes. The surprise is that this is a trade in time . Chicago bought good seasons now and paid with more seasons later. By the end, you will be able to read any win-now trade the same way. Simmons is 29. Through || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do The unit: a starter season is 8 or more regular-season games playing at least half of his unit’s snaps (nflverse snap counts, from 2013). Sacks and games come from nflverse season stats from 1999; picks from the nflverse draft table. Simmons side: interior linemen born 1984–1993 with 25 to 60 career sacks and 10 or more games at 28, chosen only on what was known at 28; ten in all. A games-only version with 13 men agrees: about seven in ten played a full season at 29, under five in ten at 32. Pick side: picks 17–32, 2013–2018 (95 players); the Pro Bowl rate uses 1990–2017 (415). Trade terms from NFL.com and ESPN; the Seattle game from ESPN and nflverse. What it cannot do: a starter season is a count, not a grade, and Simmons’s seasons are worth more than an average starter’s. Ten comparison players is a small group. Where the picks fall depends on how Chicago finishes. And it leaves out money: rookie contracts are cheap and a star’s is not. Code: scripts/trade_counterfactual.py . headline: We Blamed the New Pitcher. We Were Wrong.
deck: After a manager pulls a pitcher in the middle of an inning, 66 runs score per 100 changes. An average inning gives 50. But the new man walks into the jam the old one made, and that jam was worth 67. Once you count the jam, the change itself adds nothing, in the 5th or the 9th.
methods: Do runs go up after a pitching change? You have seen it. The manager walks out, the new man warms up, and two batters later the inning is on fire. Our editor bet it happens most in the 4th to 6th, when the middle relievers come in. Here is the answer, with its number. We looked at every pitching change from 2023 to 2025: 13,966 made in the middle of an inning. For every 100 of them, 66 runs scored before the inning ended. An average inning gives 50 . So yes, runs go up. Now the surprise. The base runners and outs he inherited were worth 67 runs per 100 on their own. The change added nothing. Our editor was wrong, and so is the feeling. By the end you will be able to spot this trap anywhere someone is sent in to fix a mess. Think about when || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Data: play-by-play for all 7,289 regular-season games of 2023–2025 from the MLB Stats API, the pitch-clock seasons. A change is any plate appearance whose pitcher differs from the one before in the same half-inning (13,966), or a new pitcher starting a half-inning (28,513). The yardstick: for each of the 24 outs-and-bases spots, the average runs scored from that spot to the end of the half-inning, over all 123,861 complete regulation half-innings. Ranges are 95% bootstrap ranges over whole games. Mid-inning changes overall: runs minus the yardstick was −0.4 per 100 (−2.2 to +1.5). In the 4th to 6th: −0.6 (−3.5 to +2.3). Starting the 8th: −2.6 (−4.5 to −0.6). What it cannot do: extra innings and the bottom of the 9th are left out, because the free runner and walk-offs change the rules. The yardstick is for an average pitcher against an average lineup; late relievers often face the top of the order. A runner who steals before the new man’s first pitch counts against him. Code: scripts/pitching_change_runs.py . Argued about something you could not settle? headline: Two of Every Three Top-25 Pairs Have Nothing in Common
deck: Through Oct. 31, 199 of the 300 pairs of teams in the AP Top 25 had never played each other or a common opponent. Among the NFL’s 12 best records it was 9 pairs in 66, and by January it is none. Saturday’s Miami–Notre Dame game, the biggest of the month, will connect just two of the 300.
methods: When a college football ranking says one team is better than another, how often have they actually met on the field? Saturday night, No. 1 Miami plays at Notre Dame. The AP voters have the Irish fourth. The playoff committee, looking at the same games, has them eleventh. Somebody is reading the evidence differently, or there is not much evidence to read. Here is the answer, with its number. Take the 25 teams in the AP poll and make every pair: 300 of them. Through Oct. 31, 199 of those pairs had never played each other and had not played a single team in common. In the NFL’s top 12 it was 9 of 66 . You might expect the big games to fix that. They barely move it. By the end, you will be able to tell which parts of any ranking are results and which are opinions. Our || METHODS: How this was measured, and what it cannot do Data: every completed game and the AP Top 25 from CollegeFootballData, read Nov. 4; the “now” poll is the last one before week 10, and games run through Oct. 31. NFL games from nflverse through week 8; the top 12 is by record, ties broken by point differential. End-of-season counts use the final AP poll and every game, bowls and playoffs included, and the NFL’s full season with playoffs. The measure: each pair is “played,” “common opponent only” (any opponent, including lower-division teams), or “neither.” It counts links, not how strong each link is. A common opponent beaten by 3 and by 40 counts the same. The 2025 box score: ESPN and CollegeFootballData agree on the score, passing yards, first downs, turnovers and time of possession. They disagree on Miami’s total yards (339 or 332), its rushing (134 or 127), and third downs; we print a range or leave the number out. Yards per play comes out about 5.5 for Notre Dame and about 5 for Miami on either feed. Code: scripts/settled_on_field.py , with --game for any box score on both feeds. headline: We Called the Rays Lucky in July. They Won 98.
deck: We graded 15 things this paper worried about in baseball’s first half. Seven held up, four washed out, and four were half right. Worries about a team’s record held. Worries about a player’s first week mostly did not.
methods: Which of this spring’s baseball worries were real, and which were just noise? The season is over, so you and we can finally check. We went back through every storyline we ran from Opening Day to the All-Star break and graded each one against the final numbers. Here is the answer, with its number. Of 15 worries, 7 held up and 4 were nothing. The rest were half right. You would expect a paper that preaches small samples to dodge the small-sample traps. We did not. We even wrote the rule, in Issue #32 , and then broke it twice. By the end, you will know which worries to keep next April and which to let go. Start with the worst, so you can see we mean it. In mid-July the Rays were 56–37. In Issue #110 we said their first place was “bought on credit.” By the runs they || METHODS: How this was graded, and what it cannot do The list: every MLB issue from Opening Day (March 27) to late July that made a claim or a worry the season could settle; 15 in all. Pieces with nothing to check, like history or method pieces, are left out. The outcomes: final 2026 standings, season stats, game logs and injured-list moves from the MLB Stats API. The Rays’ 98–64 was also checked against ESPN and Baseball-Reference, Alonso’s line and Williams’s game log against ESPN. The full ledger, with each claim and outcome, is in data/mlb/worries-2026.csv ; code: scripts/mlb_worries.py . What it cannot do: the grades are ours, and “half right” is a judgment call. Fifteen worries is too few to say how often we are right in general. And the White Sox and Braves are measured against their 2025 records, not against what anyone expected in March.

headline: Will Toney Play? Two of Every Three Questionable Players Do.
deck: Miami’s best player hurt his ankle Wednesday, three days before No. 1 Miami plays at Notre Dame. In the NFL, where every injury report is on file, a player listed questionable has played 9,634 times out of 14,346 since 2016. That is two in three. The betting line moved half a point.
methods: Malachi Toney hurt his ankle at practice Wednesday. Will he play Saturday night, and how much should it change what you expect? Start here: in the NFL, a player listed questionable plays about two times in three. Most fans hear “questionable” as a coin flip, or worse. It leans the other way. And the people with money on the game barely moved. By the end you will be able to read an injury report the way a bookmaker does. Start at two in three. Then ask the one question that can move you. Toney hurt his ankle in practice Wednesday, the Associated Press reported. Miami said he is “undergoing further evaluation by the team’s medical staff.” The school did not say whether he will play. ESPN’s Pete Thamel reported that his status is uncertain and that Toney is expected to push to play. He has had ankle trouble earlier this || METHODS:

headline: Good Teams Answer Back. The 7–2 Bears Rarely Do.
deck: Gene’s rule: you can tell a good team by how fast it scores after the other side does. We checked about 30,000 answer drives since 1999. Gene is right that good teams answer. The reason is plainer than it feels: they score after a touchdown about as often as they score any other time.
qa: Gene teams are good teams, and the numbers back him. But the answer is not a separate gift. Since 1999, NFL teams have scored on 33 of every 100 drives right after giving up a touchdown, and on 34 of every 100 other drives that started with a kickoff. Same field position, same team, same rate.
methods: Does a team that answers a score show you something special, or just that it is good? Gene, a longtime reader, has a rule for it. The other team scores a touchdown. Now watch the next drive. A good team gets off the mat and scores right back. We will call a club that does that a Gene team , and his rule Gene’s Rule ; the idea is his, all of it. The answer: Gene teams are good teams, and the numbers back him. But the answer is not a separate gift. Since 1999, NFL teams have scored on 33 of every 100 drives right after giving up a touchdown, and on 34 of every 100 other drives that started with a kickoff. Same field position, same team, same rate. Why that is surprising: we all feel the answer drive reveals character. You can see it on the sideline. || METHODS: How we measured it Football. An answer chance is a drive that comes right after the other team scores a touchdown (on offense, defense or a return), in the same half, with at least two minutes left. It is answered if it ends in a touchdown or field goal. The comparison is the same team’s other drives that began with a kickoff. Same game, same opponent, the gap holds: 34 against 35. Source: nflverse play-by-play, regular season, 29,864 answer chances; 2026 counts checked against ESPN. Baseball. A chance is the half-inning right after the other team scores. Source: Retrosheet line scores. The information used here was obtained free of charge from and is copyrighted by Retrosheet. Interested parties may contact Retrosheet at www.retrosheet.org. Hockey. After every goal, whose goal comes next. Shootouts left out. Source: NHL play-by-play. Limits. A trailing team plays differently, and an answer drive is usually played from behind; we do not adjust for that. The 2026 table is nine weeks; treat it as a snapshot, not a verdict. Code and data: research/gene-rule . Argued about something you could not settle? headline: Is the Playoff Rigged Against Small Schools? Ask the Bowl Games.
deck: Over 12 seasons, the committee ranked small-conference teams about five spots lower than their scores earned. Then those teams met the big conferences in bowl games and fell six points short of the same math. The judges knew something. This week’s real argument is Miami, not Texas.
qa: is the playoff committee judging like a figure-skating panel, with a thumb on the scale? You’ve heard the charge. Notre Dame beat Boston College 41–7 on Saturday and slid from fifth to sixth, and Texas moved past them. across 70 rankings since 2014, the judges put small-conference teams about five spots below where their scores put them. That looks like a fix; it isn’t one. Here’s the surprise: when those same teams played the big conferences in bowl games, they lost by six points more than the math expected. You’d expect a biased panel to be wrong. This one was mostly right.
methods: The question: is the playoff committee judging like a figure-skating panel, with a thumb on the scale? You’ve heard the charge. Notre Dame beat Boston College 41–7 on Saturday and slid from fifth to sixth, and Texas moved past them. The answer: across 70 rankings since 2014, the judges put small-conference teams about five spots below where their scores put them. That looks like a fix; it isn’t one. Here’s the surprise: when those same teams played the big conferences in bowl games, they lost by six points more than the math expected. You’d expect a biased panel to be wrong. This one was mostly right. What you get: a way to tell a judge with a thumb on the scale from a judge who knows something your spreadsheet doesn’t. We’ll run this scorecard every Tuesday until Selection Day, December 6. The 2026 committee has 13 members. Six are sitting || METHODS:

headline: The Playoff Has a Favorite. Probably.
deck: We played out the rest of the college season and the 12-team bracket 400,000 times, and let the ratings themselves be wrong by as much as they plausibly could be. Georgia won the title about 28 times in 100: somewhere between 6 and 60, allowing for that. It came out the favorite in 6 of every 10 versions of the ratings. Below it, the field is close to a pile of coin flips.
qa: Georgia wins about 28 times in 100. It is the likeliest champion, and it still loses about three times in four. No other team tops 12 in 100. But we are less sure of even that than a ranking makes you feel. Allowing for how wrong the ratings could be, Georgia’s chance runs anywhere from 6 to 60. In about 4 of every 10 versions of the ratings, somebody else is the favorite. Below Georgia the field is close to a pile of coin flips. Pick any two of the other eleven teams in the top 12 and put them on a neutral field; 46 of those 55 games are 60–40 or closer.
methods: Who wins the national title, and how much better is No. 2 than No. 11? The committee put out its new top 25 on Tuesday. We took it, played out the last two weekends, the title games and the bracket 400,000 times, and counted. The answer: Georgia wins about 28 times in 100. It is the likeliest champion, and it still loses about three times in four. No other team tops 12 in 100. But we are less sure of even that than a ranking makes you feel. Allowing for how wrong the ratings could be, Georgia’s chance runs anywhere from 6 to 60. In about 4 of every 10 versions of the ratings, somebody else is the favorite. Below Georgia the field is close to a pile of coin flips. Pick any two of the other eleven teams in the top 12 and put them on a neutral field; || METHODS: How we measured it The format. From the College Football Playoff’s own site. Five conference champions get bids: the ACC, Big Ten, Big 12 and SEC champions, plus the highest-ranked champion of the American, Conference USA, MAC, Mountain West, Pac-12 or Sun Belt. Seven at-large teams fill the rest. Notre Dame gets in if it is ranked in the top 12. The top four are seeded 1–4 and get byes. Seeds 5–12 play on the higher seed’s campus. A champion ranked outside the top 12 goes to the bottom of the seeding, and there is no reseeding. The model. Win chance comes from the SP+ gap through a normal curve with a spread of 16.5 points, plus 2.5 points for the home team. We simulate every remaining regular-season game, send the top two in each conference to its title game, then rank the teams. Our stand-in for the committee starts from Tuesday’s order. Each new loss drops a team about six places (half that for a title-game loss), and conference champions move up a little. That part is judgment. On the printed ratings, doubling or halving the penalty moves Georgia only between 32 and 35 in 100. Uncertainty. Each team’s true rating is drawn from a normal curve centered on its SP+, with a spread of 16.5 ÷ √(games played), about 5.2 points this week. Each of 400 draws gets 1,000 simulated seasons; a team’s title chance is the average over all 400,000, and its 95% interval is the middle 95 of every 100 draws. The interval also carries a little simulation noise (about ±1.5 for Georgia), which is small beside the rating uncertainty. headline: In College, the Answer Drive Comes Up Short. Even No. 1 Georgia’s.
deck: Gene’s rule: a good team answers a touchdown with a score of its own. In college football since 2014, teams scored on 32 of every 100 drives right after giving up a touchdown. On their other drives that began with a kickoff, they scored on 35. The answer came up short in all 13 seasons. Most of that gap is the scoreboard, not the heart.
qa: it runs the other way, a little. In about 9,000 games between FBS teams, the answer drive scored 32 times in 100 and the comparison drive 35. Why that is surprising: you would expect the gap to favor the answer, or at worst to vanish, as it does in the pros. What you get: the reason, and this year’s top 12.
methods: Does Gene’s Rule hold on Saturdays? Gene, a longtime reader, says you can tell a good team by how fast it scores after the other side does. In Issue #232 we tested it in the pros : good teams answer, but no better than they score the rest of the time. If any football should reward heart, it is the kind played by 19-year-olds. The answer: it runs the other way, a little. In about 9,000 games between FBS teams, the answer drive scored 32 times in 100 and the comparison drive 35. Why that is surprising: you would expect the gap to favor the answer, or at worst to vanish, as it does in the pros. What you get: the reason, and this year’s top 12. Notice that the rust dot sits left of the steel one in every row. That many seasons in a row is not luck. || METHODS: How we measured it An answer chance is the drive right after the other team scores a touchdown (on offense, defense or a return), same half, two or more minutes left. It counts if it ends in a touchdown or field goal. The comparison is the same team’s other drives that began with a kickoff: the opening drive of each half and the drive after the other team’s field goal. FBS against FBS, regular season, 2014 to Nov. 17, 2026: about 50,000 answer chances. Games whose drive scores do not add up to the final were left out (145 of about 9,000). Source: CollegeFootballData; 2026 top-12 counts and records checked against ESPN. Limits. Trailing teams play differently; matching the score handles some of that, not all. The 2026 table is ten games; treat it as a snapshot. Code and data: research/gene-rule . Argued about something you could not settle? headline: Will We Still Cheer for Humans in 90 Years? Start With 1936.
deck: Jesse Owens won the 1936 Olympic 100 meters in 10.3 seconds. The 2024 winner was only about 5% faster. But in 1936, big-league pitchers finished 43 of every 100 games they started. This season, about 4 in 1,000 did. Ninety years changed the games far more than the people playing them.
qa: how different is sport from 90 years ago, and will we still be cheering for humans 90 years from now, when machines can do most of it better? the bodies changed less than the games did. Owens ran 10.3 seconds in Berlin; Noah Lyles won Paris in 9.79. That’s about 5%. Meanwhile, the complete game went from 43 of every 100 starts to about 4 in 1,000.
methods: The question: how different is sport from 90 years ago, and will we still be cheering for humans 90 years from now, when machines can do most of it better? The answer: the bodies changed less than the games did. Owens ran 10.3 seconds in Berlin; Noah Lyles won Paris in 9.79. That’s about 5%. Meanwhile, the complete game went from 43 of every 100 starts to about 4 in 1,000. Why it’s surprising: you’d expect the athletes to be the big change. They’re the smallest one. The rules, the strategy and the math moved far more. What you get: a way to think about the AI question with numbers instead of dread. Read the chart from the middle line. A dot on the line means nothing changed. The 100-meter dash sits right next to it. The dots far from it are mostly choices people made. || METHODS:

headline: Is Your Team Getting Hot at the Right Time?
deck: A team that has won five straight wins its next game about one time in 100 more than its strength already says. A hot November adds nothing to a playoff run once you know the whole season. Hot teams do win in January. They were good in October.
qa: Gene and Tim put it this way: in November you have no idea what’s going to happen, because it happens in December, when a team just clicks. So does a hot November make a hot January? Is there such a thing as momentum? we checked four sports and more than 200,000 times a team took the field. A team that has won five straight wins its next game about one more time in 100 than its strength predicts. In the playoffs, a hot finish adds nothing you can measure once you know the full season.
methods: The question: Gene and Tim put it this way: in November you have no idea what’s going to happen, because it happens in December, when a team just clicks. So does a hot November make a hot January? Is there such a thing as momentum? The answer: we checked four sports and more than 200,000 times a team took the field. A team that has won five straight wins its next game about one more time in 100 than its strength predicts. In the playoffs, a hot finish adds nothing you can measure once you know the full season. Here’s the surprise: hot teams really do win more in January. It just isn’t momentum. A streak is a team telling you how good it is. What you get: a way to tell a hot team from a good one, and the one number to check before you believe in either. || METHODS:

headline: Hockey Goals Fall Like Raindrops. Until Somebody Falls Behind.
deck: An NHL team scores just under three goals a game. Give that one number to a formula from 1837 and it tells you how often a team will score none, one, two or seven. Across 27,000 team-games since 2015, it is never off by more than about one game in a hundred. The places it misses are where the hockey is hiding.
qa: how often should your team get shut out? about 5 or 6 games in every 100. Over an 82-game season that is four or five shutouts, and you can work it out from one number: the average.
methods: The question: how often should your team get shut out? The answer: about 5 or 6 games in every 100. Over an 82-game season that is four or five shutouts, and you can work it out from one number: the average. Why that is surprising: a hockey game feels like a story. A hot goalie, a bad bounce, a tired line. You would expect a pile of stories to make a mess. It does not. Since the fall of 2015, NHL teams have scored zero, one, two or seven goals almost as often as a formula that knows nothing about hockey says they should. What you get: by the end you will be able to draw that curve yourself, see the two places where hockey bends it, and know what a good fit does and does not prove. || METHODS: The math, in three lines chance of k goals = e −λ × λ k ÷ k! λ (lambda) is the average. Try λ = 3. Zero goals: e −3 = 0.05, or 5 games in 100. Each next count is the one before, times λ, divided by k: one goal is 0.05 × 3 = 0.15; two goals is 0.15 × 3 ÷ 2 = 0.22; three goals is 0.22 × 3 ÷ 3 = 0.22 again. Notice that last step. With an average of 3, two goals and three goals come out dead even. Hold onto that; the real games do it too. 27,000 team-games against one formula How we did it Data. Every regular-season goal from 2015–16 through 2025–26, 13,512 games, from the NHL’s play-by-play feed (api-web.nhle.com). Goals in regulation and overtime count; shootout tries do not. An empty-net goal is one scored while the other side’s goalie was off the ice, from the feed’s strength code. Check against a second feed. For 2024–25 we counted 7,901 goals plus 77 shootout winners, which the league credits as one goal each: 7,978. The NHL’s standings feed, summed over all 32 teams, gives 7,978 goals for. Uncertainty. The intervals on the bars are 95% intervals from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of whole games. Shutouts per 100 team-games: 5.6 (5.3–5.9); eight goals or more: 0.75 (0.65–0.85), against 1.1 from the curve. The curve’s own uncertainty is smaller still, because it rests on one average from 27,000 team-games. Limits. The curve is drawn from one league-wide average, though teams differ; that difference should make the real counts scatter more than Poisson, which makes the shortage of eight-goal games harder to explain, not easier. headline: College Football’s Gini Coefficient Is 0.37 — Worse Than MLB, Approaching US Income Inequality
deck: Texas A&M spent $51.4 million on NIL. The average Group of 5 school spent $3 million. That’s a 14x gap. The executive order aims to compress it — and the math says it would push the entire sport toward Notre Dame’s spending level.
methods: The numbers above tell a story that doesn’t require a degree in economics to understand. The top school in the country spends more than 25 times what the average Group of 5 program spends. The top five schools alone account for roughly as much total NIL spending as the bottom 80 FBS programs combined. This isn’t competitive imbalance. This is structural inequality — the kind economists measure with a tool called the Gini coefficient. The Gini coefficient is a single number between 0 and 1 that captures how evenly a resource is distributed. Zero means perfect equality — every school spends exactly the same amount. One means perfect inequality — a single school has all the money and everyone else has nothing. The current NIL Gini for FBS college football is 0.37. For context, the United States income Gini is 0.39. College football’s spending inequality is approaching the level of || METHODS: The Math: Calculating the NIL Gini Coefficient The Gini coefficient measures inequality on a 0–1 scale. Zero means every school spends the same. One means a single school has all the money. The Gini coefficient formula: G = (1/2n²μ) × Σ|x_i - x_j| for all pairs i,j Where: n = number of schools (134 FBS programs) μ = mean NIL spending (~$12.8M) x_i = spending for school i Simplified calculation using the 28-school sample: Mean spending: $12.8M Median spending: $8.0M Top quartile avg: $38.2M Bottom quartile avg: $3.4M Ratio (top/bottom): 11.2x Lorenz curve: Bottom 50% of schools control ~22% of total spending Top 10% of schools control ~35% of total spending Gini = 2 × (area between Lorenz curve and equality line) Result: G = 0.37 Context: NFL Gini: 0.05 (hard cap works) NBA Gini: 0.15 (soft cap works, sort of) MLB Gini: 0.25 (luxury tax = weak deterrent) CFB Gini: 0.37 (no cap = free market) US Income: 0.39 (the whole economy) The bottom 50% of FBS schools control just 22% of total NIL spending. The top 10% control 35%. This is what a Gini of 0.37 looks like in practice: the rich schools aren’t just richer — they’re operating in a different financial universe. The Math: Projected Compression Under the EO The $20.5M revenue-share cap doesn’t eliminate inequality. It compresses it from the top. Current distribution (top 16 schools above cap): Avg spending: $32.2M Spending above cap: $11.7M avg excess Total excess: ~$187M across 16 schools Under $20.5M cap: All 16 schools capped at $20.5M max rev-share Spending above $20.5M must come from legitimate, verifiable NIL deals only New projected distribution: Top quartile avg: $20.5M (was $38.2M) Bottom quartile avg: $3.4M (unchanged) New ratio (top/bottom): 6.0x (was 11.2x) New Gini: ~0.20–0.25 That’s a 32–46% reduction in inequality. headline: Notre Dame Is Simultaneously the Most Protected and Most Vulnerable Program in College Football
deck: The executive order’s sports provisions help Notre Dame on every front: transfer limits favor their recruiting, NIL caps compress spending toward their level, and the 5-year eligibility rule suits their young roster. But the enforcement mechanism — threatening federal research funding — puts $200 million at risk for a private university already dealing with grant cancellations.
methods: Start with recruiting. Notre Dame signed the No. 8 class nationally in 2025, a ranking built almost entirely on high school prospects. Programs that rely on the portal to fill roster holes — Indiana brought in 18 transfers to fuel its 11–2 season — face a structurally smaller talent pool under the EO’s one-free-transfer limit. Notre Dame’s pipeline doesn’t shrink because it was never routed through the portal in the first place. Then there’s NIL. The EO’s proposed spending cap sits at approximately $20 million per program. Notre Dame already spends at or near that figure. Ohio State spends $38 million. Alabama spends $35 million. USC spends $33 million. A cap doesn’t hurt ND at all — it pulls everyone else down to ND’s level. That’s not a neutral outcome. That’s an advantage. The portal math is particularly telling. ND lost 18 players to the portal and gained only 8, || METHODS: The Math: Protected vs. Vulnerable Factor Analysis PROTECTED FACTORS IMPACT (1-10) ────────────────────────────────────────────────── 1. HS recruiting #8 nationally 8 / 10 2. NIL already at $20M cap 9 / 10 3. Portal net −10 (freeze helps) 7 / 10 4. 68% underclassmen (5-yr cap safe) 6 / 10 5. 100% media revenue retained 7 / 10 Total: 37 / 50 VULNERABLE FACTORS IMPACT (1-10) ────────────────────────────────────────────────── 1. $200M+ federal research at risk 9 / 10 2. Active grant cancellations ongoing 8 / 10 3. Private school, no state backstop 7 / 10 4. 1 voice vs. 4 conference blocs 6 / 10 5. Independence = no collective power 7 / 10 Total: 37 / 50 NET ASSESSMENT: 37 Protected, 37 Vulnerable This is the statistical expression of ND's paradox: the competitive upside and institutional downside are almost perfectly balanced. The EO helps the football program and threatens the university at nearly identical magnitudes. The difference: competitive gains are CERTAIN (the cap, the freeze, the eligibility rules exist). Institutional risks are CONDITIONAL (only triggered by enforcement action). ND's bet is that the gun is never fired. If it is, the damage exceeds the athletic gains by an order of magnitude. The symmetry is striking and almost certainly accidental. No one drafting sports policy was thinking about the NIL-to-federal-funding ratio of a specific independent Catholic university. But the math doesn’t care about intent. It cares about exposure. The Math: NIL-to-Federal-Funding Ratio — Who Carries the Most Risk? Federal NIL NIL/Research State School Research Spend Ratio Backstop? ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Michigan $1.6B $25M 1.6% Yes Ohio State $1.1B $38M 3.5% Yes USC $900M $33M 3.7% No Texas $800M $30M 3.8% Yes Alabama $600M $35M 5.8% Yes Georgia $500M $28M 5.6% Yes Notre Dame $200M $20M 10.0% No Interpretation: At Michigan, losing 10% of federal funding = $160M.

headline: The Rule That Would Have Prevented Cignetti’s Miracle Now Protects What He Built
deck: Curt Cignetti used 18 incoming transfers to turn 3–9 Indiana into an 11–2 CFP team. Under the executive order’s transfer limits, that instant rebuild becomes nearly impossible. The drawbridge rises after the king is inside — and mid-tier programs may never get that chance again.
methods: In December 2023, Curt Cignetti left James Madison — where he’d gone 52–9 across three seasons and an FCS-to-FBS transition — for an Indiana program coming off a 3–9 season. What happened next was the most dramatic single-season turnaround in modern Big Ten history. Cignetti brought 18 incoming transfers, essentially replacing half the roster in one offseason. The result: 11–2, a College Football Playoff berth, and a 7.5-win improvement that defied every historical precedent for the program. This wasn’t a gradual build. It was a roster transplant. Cignetti took the portal — the mechanism designed to give athletes freedom of movement — and used it as an organizational tool. He knew exactly what he needed, knew where to find it, and assembled a team that played like it had been together for years despite meeting in January. The 2025 Indiana season told a subtler story. Cignetti went 9–2, still excellent || METHODS: The Numbers: Portal Dependency vs. Blue Blood Recruiting Power Indiana 2024 roster composition: Incoming portal transfers: 18 players Holdover from 2023 roster: ~67 players Portal players as % of roster: 21% Portal players in starting lineup: ~11 of 22 (50%) Portal contribution to win share: estimated 60%+ Blue blood recruiting advantage (2024 cycle avg): Ohio State (#1): avg recruit rating .9350 Georgia (#2): avg recruit rating .9280 Notre Dame (#8): avg recruit rating .9120 Indiana (#40): avg recruit rating .8650 Rating gap, OSU vs. Indiana: .0700 That gap = ~3 stars vs. 4 stars at every position Over a 25-man class, the cumulative talent gap is roughly equivalent to adding 5 extra blue-chip players to Ohio State’s roster every year. Without the portal to close this gap: Indiana must out-develop opponents by ~15% to compensate for the recruiting deficit. Possible? Yes. Sustainable? Ask Boise State. The portal allowed Indiana to bypass the recruiting hierarchy entirely. For one glorious year, it didn’t matter that Ohio State signed better high schoolers. It mattered that Cignetti assembled better transfers. Remove that mechanism and the recruiting hierarchy reasserts itself — slowly, but inevitably. Projected Impact: 35–40% Portal Reduction on Mid-Tier Programs Current portal pool (2025): ~3,100 FBS entries Projected pool under EO (2026): ~1,900 FBS entries Reduction: ~1,200 fewer transfers Who disappears from the pool: Repeat transfers (28% of pool): ~870 players gone Deterred first-timers (~10%): ~310 players gone Total removed: ~1,180 players Impact by program type: Current Projected Change Portal In Portal In ─────────────────────────────────────── Blue bloods (OSU) 6 5 −17% Mid-tier (Indiana) 18 10 −44% Portal-heavy (CU) 28 15 −46% The math is cruel: programs that relied most on the portal lose the most transfers. Blue bloods barely notice. The competitive gap WIDENS. Mid-tier “instant rebuild” scenario: Old rules: 18 transfers → 7.5-win

headline: The Executive Order Isn’t Saving College Sports. It’s Restoring the Old Guard — With One Dangerous Asterisk.
deck: Transfer limits, NIL caps, and eligibility rules all favor the programs that were already winning. Blue bloods won 85% of national titles pre-portal. The portal briefly opened the door to upstarts. The EO narrows it again. But the enforcement mechanism — threatening federal research funding over sports rules — is a precedent that should worry everyone.
methods: Here is the argument in three sentences. Between 1970 and 2010, ten programs won 85% of national championships: Alabama, Ohio State, Notre Dame, USC, Oklahoma, Michigan, Nebraska, Florida State, Miami, and Texas. The transfer portal, NIL, and the expanded playoff briefly disrupted that monopoly — dropping blue-blood dominance to roughly 70% and letting TCU, Indiana, and Colorado crash the party. The executive order’s three pillars — transfer limits, NIL caps, and eligibility restrictions — each independently favor the old guard, and together they represent the most significant structural advantage handed to established programs since scholarship limits were standardized in 1973. This is not a conspiracy theory. Nobody in the White House sat down and said “let’s help Alabama.” The stated goals — athlete welfare, academic integrity, competitive balance — are defensible on paper. But regulatory design has consequences that diverge from stated intent, and the consequences here are remarkably one-directional. || METHODS: The Math: Blue Blood Title Share — Before, During, and After the Portal Era Blue Blood Share Notes ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Pre-Portal (1970-2010) 85% (34/40) 10 programs dominate Portal Era (2014-2025) 70% (8.4/12) TCU, Indiana, Colorado emerge Democratization Gap: -15 points Most parity in 50 years Projected EO Impact: Transfer limits: +5 pts (back to ~75%) NIL caps: +3 pts (to ~78%) Eligibility restrictions: +1 pt (to ~79%) Combined projection: 78-83% The portal opened a 15-point window of parity. The EO closes roughly 8-13 of those 15 points. Net result: partial restoration, not full reversion. The EO doesn’t fully restore the old order. It was never going to. The expanded playoff alone ensures more teams get a shot. But it narrows the funnel considerably. Where the portal era produced 4–5 legitimate contenders from outside the blue-blood club each year, the post-EO era likely produces 1–2. The door doesn’t close. It just gets a lot harder to push open. The Math: The Enforcement Mechanism Dwarfs What It’s Regulating What the EO regulates: Total NCAA revenue (2024): $1.3B Total P4 athletic dept revenue: $8.5B Estimated NIL spending (all FBS): $1.1B Total college sports economy: ~$11B What the EO uses as leverage: Annual federal research funding: $380B Federal grants to D1 institutions: $210B NIH alone: $47B NSF alone: $11B Ratio: $380B / $11B = 34.5x The enforcement mechanism is 34 times larger than the industry it’s regulating. Top research universities at risk: Johns Hopkins: $3.1B in federal grants U of Michigan: $1.8B Stanford: $1.7B Ohio State: $1.1B Notre Dame: $200M+ Using $380B in research funding to regulate $11B in sports spending is like using a howitzer to hang a picture frame. This is the dangerous asterisk. The EO’s enforcement mechanism isn’t a fine or a postseason ban or an NCAA sanction. It’s the implicit threat

headline: The JUCO Detour: College Baseball’s Portal Workaround Is Already Here
deck: The executive order limits athletes to one free transfer. But junior college players aren’t transferring — they’re arriving. The JUCO-to-D1 pipeline doesn’t trigger the portal’s one-transfer cap, and smart programs are already loading rosters with physically mature, battle-tested players who never burned their portal move. If you want to see the future of college baseball under this EO, look at the player who led the Big 12 in hitting last year: he came from a community college in Las Vegas.
methods: Brady Ballinger was an All-State first baseman at Green Valley High School in Henderson, Nevada. Good enough to earn Third Team All-American honors as a prep player. Not good enough, apparently, for a D1 scholarship out of the gate. So he did what an increasing number of smart athletes are doing: he went to the College of Southern Nevada, a JUCO powerhouse that has produced 30 MLB draft picks and sends an average of 12 players to four-year programs every year. At CSN in 2024, Ballinger hit .433/.548/.690 with 81 hits, 30 doubles, and 63 RBIs across 60 games. He was named Scenic West Athletic Conference Player of the Year. He helped CSN go 53–12 and finish fifth at the JUCO World Series. Then he went to Kansas. At Kansas in 2025 — his first D1 season — Ballinger led the team in batting average (.353), walks (56), slugging (.670), || METHODS: The Math: The JUCO Path vs. the Direct-Entry Path Under the EO PATH A: HIGH SCHOOL → D1 (DIRECT ENTRY) ────────────────────────────────────────── Year 1: Freshman at School A (5-year clock starts) Year 2: Sophomore at School A Year 3: Transfer to School B (FREE — one-time use) Year 4: Junior at School B Year 5: Senior at School B Portal transfers used: 1 of 1 Remaining moves: 0 (must sit out if transferring again) Risk: If School A is a bad fit, you burn your one transfer early and pray School B works. PATH B: HIGH SCHOOL → JUCO → D1 (THE DETOUR) ────────────────────────────────────────── Year 1: Freshman at JUCO (5-year clock starts) Year 2: Sophomore at JUCO (develop, compete, mature) Year 3: Junior at D1 School A (JUCO-to-D1, not a portal transfer) Year 4: Senior at D1 School A Year 5: 5th Year — or — transfer to School B (FREE) Portal transfers used: 0 of 1 Remaining moves: 1 (insurance policy still intact) Advantage: Arrive at D1 with more experience, more physical maturity, proven stats, AND a backup plan. The JUCO path doesn’t just avoid the portal restriction — it creates an insurance policy. The direct-entry athlete is all-in from Day 1 with no safety net. The JUCO-routed athlete carries a free transfer in reserve for the entirety of their D1 career. Under the EO, that optionality is worth more than it ever was before. The Numbers: D1 Baseball’s JUCO Connection in 2026
